questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Explain how the drainage system of Harappan cities indicate town planning.

answer.text: The drainage system shows careful town planning: urban centres at Harappa were well planned; drains were properly laid down; roads and streets were laid along an approximate grid pattern; streets with drains were laid out first and houses built along them afterwards; for domestic waste water to flow into the street drains, every house needed to have at least one wall along the street.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Explain why the seals and sealings were used by the Harappans.

answer.text: Seals and sealings were used by the Harappans to facilitate long-distance communication: a seal was pressed on the mouth of a bag of goods that was tied with a rope, leaving an impression (sealing); if the bag reached with the sealing intact it meant it had not been tampered with; the sealing also conveyed the identity of the sender.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: ‘Mohenjodaro was a planned Urban Centre.’ Support the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text: Mohenjodaro was a planned urban centre: it had a Citadel and a Lower Town, both walled; the Citadel was walled and constructed on mud-brick platforms; signs of planning include bricks of a standardised ratio; one of the most distinctive features was the carefully planned drainage system; roads and streets were laid out along an approximate grid pattern, intersecting at right angles, with streets and drains laid out first and houses built along them afterwards; every house needed at least one wall along a street so that domestic waste water could flow into the street drains; Lower Town buildings were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides, probably used for cooking and weaving; there were no windows in the walls along the ground level and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or courtyard; every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks with connected drains, and some had staircases to a second storey or roof; many houses had wells, often in a room that could be reached from outside — scholars estimate about 700 wells in Mohenjodaro in all.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “How artefacts are identified” — Processing of food required grinding equipment as well as vessels for mixing, blending and cooking. These were made of stone, metal and terracotta. This is an excerpt from one of the earliest reports on excavations at Mohenjodaro, the best-known Harappan site : Saddle querns ... are found in considerable numbers ... and they seem to have been the only means in use for grinding cereals. As a rule, they were roughly made of hard, gritty, igneous rock or sandstone and mostly show signs of hard usage. As their bases are usually convex, they must have been set in the earth or in mud to prevent their rocking. Two main types have been found: those on which another smaller stone was pushed or rolled to and fro, and others with which a second stone was used as a pounder, eventually making a large cavity in the nether stone. Querns of the former type were probably used solely for grain; the second type possibly only for pounding herbs and spices for making curries. In fact stones of this latter type are dubbed “curry stones” by our workmen and our cook asked for the loan of one from the museum for use in the kitchen. (From Ernest Mackay, Further Excavations at Mohenjodaro) (31.1) How do archaeologists classify their finds ? (31.2) How do archaeologists use present day analogies to understand ancient artefacts ? (31.3) How has Ernest Mackay described ‘Saddle quern’ in his book ?

answer.text:
(31.1) Archaeologists classify their finds on the basis of material, such as stone, clay, metal, bone or ivory, and in terms of function — deciding whether an artefact is a tool, an ornament, or something meant for both, or for ritual use.
(31.2) Archaeologists use present-day analogies to reconstruct the past through a study of the artefacts they unearth, such as seals, coins, remains of buildings, clay pots or burnt grains.
(31.3) Ernest Mackay described the saddle quern in his book as a stone used for grinding material with one's hand, produced by rocking or rolling the hand stone using parallel motions; pushing and pulling the hand stone in this way formed a shape looking like a saddle.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: Describe the distinct views of archaeologists on the Central authority of Harappa.

answer.text: Archaeologists hold distinct views on the central authority of Harappa: the archaeological record provides no immediate answer; a large building found at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace, though no spectacular finds were associated with it, and a stone statue was labelled the 'priest king' because archaeologists, familiar with Mesopotamian history and its priest-kings, found parallels in the Indus region — though it was never explained whether those who performed ritual practices also held political power; some archaeologists opine that Harappan society had no rulers and everybody enjoyed equal status, others feel there was no single ruler but separate rulers for separate cities, while yet others argue there was a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, evidence of planned settlements, the standardised ratio of brick sizes, and the establishment of settlements near sources of raw material; the last theory seems the most plausible, as it is unlikely entire communities could have collectively made and implemented such complex decisions.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Describe the town planning of Harappa.

answer.text: Town planning of Harappa: Harappa had a Citadel and a Lower Town; the Citadel was walled and constructed on mud-brick platforms, and the Lower Town was also walled, with buildings built on platforms and building activity restricted to a fixed area on the platforms; signs of planning include bricks of a standardised ratio, both sun-dried and baked; an efficient drainage system was an important feature, with roads and streets laid out in a grid pattern intersecting at right angles - streets with drains were laid out first and houses built along them afterwards, and every house had one wall along a street so domestic waste water could flow into the street drains; the Lower Town had residential buildings, with houses centred on a courtyard, rooms on all sides, and the courtyard as the centre of activities such as cooking and weaving; there were no windows in the walls at ground level, reflecting a concern for privacy, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or courtyard; every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks connected to street drains, some houses had remains of staircases to reach a second storey or the roof, and many houses had wells that could be reached from outside - Mohenjodaro alone had about 700 wells; the Citadel had structures used for public purposes, such as granaries and warehouses, and the Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides, with two flights of steps leading into the tank, rooms on three sides (one with a large well), and water from the tank flowing into a huge drain.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Describe the contributions of various archaeologists from 1875 till 1950 in discovering the Harappan civilization.

answer.text: Contributions of various archaeologists from 1875 till 1950 in discovering the Harappan Civilization: Alexander Cunningham was the first Director-General of the ASI, though he was initially confused about the significance of Harappan artefacts; Daya Ram Sahni discovered seals at Harappa in layers older than early historic levels and understood their significance, while Rakhal Das Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjo-daro and realised these sites were part of a single archaeological culture; S.N. Roy authored 'The Story of Indian Archaeology', highlighting Marshall's viewpoint; John Marshall, who brought experience of working in Greece and Crete, looked for patterns of everyday life and excavated along regular horizontal units, though this meant he ignored the stratigraphy of the mound, leading to loss of valuable information - in 1924 Marshall announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley to the world; R.E.M. Wheeler took over as Director-General of the ASI in 1944, recognised that it was necessary to follow the stratigraphy of the mound, and brought military precision to the practice of archaeology; specialists from the subcontinent and abroad have jointly worked at both Harappa and Mohenjo-daro since.

answer.text: Methods of irrigation used by the Harappans at different sites: (i) Traces of canals found at Shortughai in Afghanistan, used for agriculture. (ii) No definite evidence of canals in Punjab and Sindh, water drawn from wells for irrigation. (iii) Traces of water reservoirs found in Kutch, Gujarat, used to store water for irrigation. questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Explain how burials help in understanding the social and economic differences amongst the people in Harappan civilization.

answer.text: How burials help understand social and economic differences: (i) Bodies laid in pits with differences in the way the pits are made – in some cases the sides were lined with bricks. (ii) Some graves have pottery and ornaments, indicating a belief that these could be used in the afterlife. (iii) Ornaments have been found in burials of both men and women. (iv) Jewellery has been found even in the graves of poorer people, made of shell or copper. (v) A cemetery at Farmana in Haryana; a coffin burial found at Harappa. (vi) In some cases pottery is absent, indicating differences of wealth and status not always visible in burials. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Explain how did archaeologists identify the centres of craft production of the Harappan age.

answer.text: (a) How archaeologists identified centres of craft production of the Harappan age: (i) By looking for raw material such as stone nodules, shells, copper ores etc. (ii) Looking for unfinished objects, rejects and waste material. (iii) By looking for broken material. (iv) Waste was used for craft work. (v) Large waste pieces were used for making small objects. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) “The most distinctive feature of Harappan cities was Carefully planned drainage system.” Explain the statement.

answer.text: (b) Carefully planned drainage system as the most distinctive feature of Harappan cities: (i) Streets and drains were laid out first and houses built along them on a 'grid' pattern. (ii) Streets and drains cross at right angles. (iii) Every house was connected to the street drains. (iv) The main channels were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be removed for cleaning. (v) In some cases limestone was used for the covers. (vi) House drains first emptied into a sump or cesspit into which solid matter settled while waste water flowed out into the street drains. (vii) Very long drainage channels were provided at intervals with sumps for cleaning. (viii) Little heaps of material, mostly sand, have frequently been found lying alongside drainage channels, showing debris was not always carted away when the drain was cleared. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Explain the strategies adopted by Harappans to procure raw material for their craft production.

answer.text: (a) Strategies adopted by Harappans to procure raw material for craft production: (i) Many methods and strategies were used to procure raw material. (ii) Clay was locally available. (iii) Stone, timber and metal were procured from outside. (iv) Goods and people were transported by land and sea routes. (v) They established settlements such as Nageshwar and Balakot for shells, Shortughai (far-off Afghanistan) for lapis lazuli, Lothal near sources of carnelian, steatite (from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal like copper (from Rajasthan). (vi) They sent expeditions to areas where raw material was available, such as the Khetri region of Rajasthan (for copper) and South India (for gold). (vii) They communicated with local people; Harappan micro-beads found in these areas show such contact. (viii) Contact with distant lands – copper was probably brought from Oman; a distinctive Harappan jar was found at Omani sites; Mesopotamian texts mention contact with regions such as Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan and Meluhha. (ix) Bullock carts were used for transport, and boats on rivers/seas. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Explain how archaeologists have been able to reconstruct dietry practices of the Harappans.

answer.text: (b) How archaeologists reconstructed dietary practices of the Harappans: (i) The Harappans ate a wide range of plant products. (ii) Grains like wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame have been found at Harappan sites. (iii) Millets are found from sites in Gujarat. (iv) Finds of rice are rare. (v) Dietary practices are reconstructed from finds of charred grains and seeds, studied by archaeo-botanists (specialists in ancient plant remains). (vi) The Harappans also consumed animal products. (vii) Bones of animals such as cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig have been found at Harappan sites. (viii) Bones of wild species have also been found. (ix) Bones of fish and fowl are also found. (Any three to be explained)

questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “The most ancient system yet discovered” — About the drains, Mackay noted : “It is certainly the most complete ancient system as yet discovered.” Every house was connected to the street drains. The main channels were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be removed for cleaning. In some cases, limestone was used for the covers. House drains first emptied into a sump or cesspit into which solid matter settled while waste water flowed out into the street drains. Very long drainage channels were provided at intervals with sumps for cleaning. It is a wonder of archaeology that “little heaps of material, mostly sand, have frequently been found lying alongside drainage channels, which shows… that the debris was not always carted away when the drain was cleared”. From Ernest Mackay, Early Indus Civilisation, 1948. Drainage systems were not unique to the larger cities, but were found in smaller settlements as well. At Lothal for example, while houses were built of mud bricks, drains were made of burnt bricks. (31.1) Analyse the possible reason behind the uniformity in the drainage systems across the Harappan cities. (1) (31.2) Analyse the implications of finding little heaps of material, mostly sand, alongside drainage channels. (1) (31.3) Assess the impact of Harappan drainage system. (2)

answer.text:
31.1: The uniformity in the drainage system across Harappan cities was likely due to urban planning and engineering skills, and the possible presence of a central authority.
31.2: The little heaps of material, mostly sand, found alongside drainage channels imply that the Harappans had established regular maintenance practices for their drains, but the debris was not always carted away when the drain was cleared.
31.3: The advanced Harappan drainage system suggests a highly organised society with strong emphasis on public health and cleanliness; the integration of every house into the drainage network implies a relatively egalitarian approach to urban amenities, where sanitation services were accessible to all residents; the infrastructure likely improved quality of life by reducing waste-related health issues and promoting a cleaner living environment.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Archaeogenetic Research” — As you can see, a careful re-examination of the data can sometimes lead to a reversal of earlier interpretations. In this respect, it is necessary to mention the recent archaeogenetic research carried out at the site of Rakhigarhi. The site, located in Hisar district of Haryana, is the biggest Harappan city, spread over an area of 550 Hectare. In order to study the genetic history of the Harappans, DNA was extracted from the skeletal remains excavated at Rakhigarhi. This research was carried out by The Deccan College Deemed University, Pune in collaboration with Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad and The Harvard Medical College. The analysis of the data indicates that the Harappans are the indigenous people of this region. The genetic roots of the Harappans go back to 10,000 BCE. The DNA of the Harappans has continued till today and a majority of the South Asian population appears to be their descendants. Due to trade and cultural contacts of the Harappans with distant regions there is a mixture of genes in small quantity. The continuity without any break in genetic history as well as cultural history rules out large scale immigration of the so-called Aryans. This research also indicates that the people coming from bordering areas and distant regions were absorbed in the Indian society. At no stage, the genetic history of the Indians was either discontinued or broken. As the Harappans started moving towards Iran and Central Asia, their genes also gradually spread in these regions. The same team of researchers reconstructed 3D features of the Harappan people. The reconstructed facial features of the Harappans, male and female, show remarkable similarity with the modern population of Haryana. Thus, this study has indicated unbroken continuity for 5000 years in this region. (31.1) How does the research at Rakhigarhi contribute to understanding of ancient civilizations ? (1) (31.2) How does the research redefine our understanding of genetic history in South Asia ? (1) (31.3) What is the significance of extracting and analyzing DNA from the remains at Rakhigarhi ? (2)

answer.text:
31.1: The archaeogenetic research at Rakhigarhi contributes to understanding ancient civilizations by providing a model for research into Harappan origins.
31.2: The research redefines our understanding of genetic history in South Asia by showing that the DNA of the Harappans has continued till today, with a majority of the South Asian population appearing to be their descendants - a critical step forward in unravelling the mysteries of India's past.
31.3: The significance of extracting and analysing DNA from the remains at Rakhigarhi lies in the fact that the reconstructed facial features of the Harappans, male and female, show remarkable similarity with the modern population of Haryana, and the study indicates unbroken continuity for 5000 years in this region.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: Explain the views of archaeologists on the religious beliefs of the Harappans.

answer.text:
Views of archaeologists on the religious beliefs of the Harappans:
Early archaeologists labelled unusual or unfamiliar objects as having religious significance; terracotta figurines of women, heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses, were regarded as mother goddesses, and rare stone statuary of men was labelled the 'priest-king'.
Many structures have been assigned ritual significance, such as the Great Bath and fire altars found at Kalibangan and Lothal.
Attempts have been made to reconstruct religious beliefs by examining seals - those with plant motifs indicate nature worship, and some animals such as the one-horned 'unicorn' depicted on seals are seen as mythical, composite creatures.
In some seals a figure shown seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture, sometimes surrounded by animals, has been regarded as a depiction of 'proto-Shiva'; conical stone objects have been classified as lingas.
Many reconstructions of Harappan religion are made on the assumption that later traditions provide parallels with earlier ones.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) How do the archaeological discoveries at Harappa explain urban planning of the Indus Valley Civilization ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How archaeological discoveries at Harappa explain urban planning of the Indus Valley Civilization:
Harappa had a Citadel and a Lower Town, both walled, though the Citadel was constructed on higher mud platforms; roads and streets were laid out in a grid pattern, intersecting at right angles.
Buildings were built on platforms, with an efficient drainage system as an important feature; many houses had wells that could be reached from outside - Mohenjodaro alone had about 700 wells.
The Citadel had structures used for public purposes such as granaries and warehouses, while the Lower Town had residential buildings; houses were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides, and the courtyard was the centre of activities such as cooking and weaving - there were no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or courtyard.
Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, connected to the street drains; the Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides. Signs of planning include bricks of a standardised ratio.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) How have the roles and methodologies of archaeologists contributed to the understanding of Harappan Civilization over time ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How the roles and methodologies of archaeologists contributed to the understanding of Harappan Civilization over time:
Cunningham, the first director-general of the ASI, missed the significance of Harappan seals, as he used accounts left by Chinese Buddhist pilgrims to locate early (historical) settlements rather than earlier ones.
Daya Ram Sahni discovered seals at Harappa in layers older than early historic levels and understood their significance; Rakhal Das Bannerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro and understood these sites were part of a single archaeological culture; S.N. Roy authored 'The Story of Indian Archaeology', highlighting Marshall's viewpoint.
John Marshall, who brought experience of working in Greece and Crete, looked for patterns of everyday life and excavated along regular horizontal units; in 1924 he announced the discovery of a new (Indus Valley) civilisation to the world.
R.E.M. Wheeler recognised the need to follow the stratigraphy of the mound and classified objects according to the layer of soil in which they were found; specialists from the subcontinent and abroad have jointly worked at both Harappa and Mohenjodaro.
Later researchers include Vasant Shinde, who began archaeogenetic research at Rakhigarhi; B.B. Lal and Thapar, who began excavation at Kalibangan; and R.S. Bisht, who began excavation at Dholavira.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Examine the characteristic features of architecture of urban centres of Mohenjodaro.

answer.text:
The most unique feature of the Harappan civilisation was the development of urban centres; Mohenjodaro was the most important urban centre of that time, although the first site to be discovered was Harappa.
Settlements were divided into two sections - the lower town and the citadel; the lower town was walled with several buildings on the platform.
The citadel was the upper portion; once the platforms were in place, all building activity within the city was restricted to a fixed area on the platforms, so it seems the settlement was first planned and then implemented.
These cities had a carefully planned drainage system; roads and streets were laid down along a grid pattern.
Every house had its own bathroom; a large rectangular tank was also built, perhaps for public bathing.
Other signs of planning include bricks, which whether sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio, where the length and breadth were four and twice the height respectively.
Residential buildings were centred on a courtyard, with rooms on all sides.
They were concerned for privacy: there were no windows in the walls along the ground level.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Examine the causes and the evidences of the collapse of the Harappan civilisation.

answer.text:
Causes of the collapse: several explanations have been put forward - climatic changes damaged the civilisation, deforestation was another cause, excessive floods caused much harm, shifting and/or drying up of rivers, and overuse of the landscape; the combined impact of all these causes may have led to the collapse.
Evidence: by 1800 BCE most of the mature Harappan sites were abandoned; there is evidence of disappearance of distinct artefacts of the civilisation - weights, seals, beads and trade all disappeared; house construction techniques deteriorated; the script and pottery disappeared; and there was decline and abandonment of cities.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Imagine you are writing a research project on Harappan agriculture. Which three informations on archaeological evidence would you cite to explain it ?

answer.text:
The prevalence of agriculture is indicated by finds of grain.
Representations on seals and terracotta sculpture indicate that the bull was known to them; archaeologists extrapolate from this that oxen were used for ploughing.
Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali.
Archaeologists have also found evidence of a ploughed field at Kalibangan (Rajasthan), associated with Early Harappan levels; the field had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting two different crops were grown together.
Traces of canals have been found at the Harappan site of Shortughai in Afghanistan; water drawn from wells was used for irrigation, and water reservoirs found in Dholavira (Gujarat) may have been used to store water for agriculture.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Imagine your school is hosting an exhibition on the Harappan civilization and you are responsible for the section on the Harappan script. Which three aspects of it would you explain to the visitors ?

answer.text:
Harappan seals usually have a line of writing, probably containing the name and title of the owner.
The motif (generally an animal) conveyed a meaning to those who could not read.
Most inscriptions are short, the longest containing about 26 signs; the script remains undeciphered till date.
It was evidently not alphabetical, as it has too many signs - somewhere between 375 and 400.
It is apparent that the script was written from right to left, as some seals show wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left; it is found on a variety of objects - seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods, even an ancient signboard.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (a) Imagine you are doing research on Harappan beads and jewellery. Which three aspects would you understand about Harappan craft production and trade from it ? Explain.

answer.text:
A variety of materials were used to make beads - stones like carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite, metals like copper, bronze and gold, and shell, faience and terracotta.
The shapes were numerous: disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel, segmented; they were decorated with painting, incising and designs etched onto them, with different techniques used according to the material.
The red colour of carnelian was obtained by firing the yellowish raw material at various stages of production; grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process of making beads and jewellery.
Nageshwar and Balakot were important production centres; procurement of materials for craft production suggests trade relations with Mesopotamia, Bahrain, Oman etc.

questions.chapter: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
questions.text: (b) Imagine you are a part of a student archaeology workshop where you have to explain about Harappan burial sites and jewellery. Which three aspects would you present to your classmates about it ? Explain.

answer.text:
In Harappan sites the dead were generally laid in pits; some were buried in hollowed out spaces lined with bricks, perhaps to indicate social differences.
Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps indicating a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.
Jewellery has been found in burials of both men and women; on the whole, Harappans did not believe in burying precious things with the dead.

questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Capturing elephants for the army” — The Arthashastra lays down minute details of administrative and military organisation. This is what it says about how to capture elephants: “Guards of elephant forests, assisted by those who rear elephants, those who enchain the legs of elephants, those who guard the boundaries, those who live in forests, as well as by those who nurse elephants, shall, with the help of five or seven female elephants to help in tethering wild ones, trace the whereabouts of herds of elephants by following the course of urine and dung left by elephants.” According to Greek sources, the Mauryan ruler had a standing army of 600,000 foot-soldiers, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants. (31.3) Elephants were captured by the Mauryan rulers to raise the military strength of the army; according to Greek sources, the Mauryan ruler had a standing army of 9,000 elephants.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (a) How were the inscriptions of Maurya period deciphered ? Explain the limitations of epigraphy. $2 + 6 = 8$

answer.text: Inscriptions of the Maurya period were deciphered by James Prinsep, an officer in the mint of the East India Company, who deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi, the two scripts used in the earliest inscriptions; he matched inscriptions in terms of content, style, language and palaeography, and discovered that Asoka was the name of the ruler, while devanampiya and piyadassi were titles used for him in many inscriptions. Limitations of epigraphy: there are technical limitations in studying inscriptions; in some inscriptions the letters are very faintly engraved, some inscriptions are damaged and letters are missing, making reconstructions uncertain; it is not always easy to be sure of the exact meaning of words used; several thousand inscriptions were made but only some hundreds have been discovered, and not all of these have been deciphered, published and translated; politically and economically significant matters are recorded in inscriptions, but routine agricultural practices and the joys and sorrows of daily existence are not found in them.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (b) How do Historians come to know about Maurya period ? Explain the administrative structure of Mauryan empire. $4 + 4 = 8$

answer.text: Historians come to know about the Mauryas from: archaeological finds, especially sculptures, buildings and monasteries; the account of Megasthenes, called Indica, which survives in fragments; the Arthashastra, composed by Kautilya; later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic literature; Sanskrit literary works written about the Mauryas; and the inscriptions of Asoka on rocks and pillars. Administrative structure of the Mauryan Empire: there were five major political centres — the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, all mentioned in Asokan inscriptions; administrative control was strongest around the capital and provincial centres, which were carefully chosen (Taxila and Ujjayini being on important long-distance trade routes); there was a committee with six subcommittees coordinating military activity, looking after the navy, transport and provisions, foot-soldiers, horses, chariots and elephants respectively; Asoka also tried to hold the empire together by propagating dhamma, whose principles were simple and universally applicable, appointing special officers called Dhamma Mahamatta to spread its message, and appointing Pativedakas to collect people's needs and report directly to the king.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (a) “Between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, Magadha became the most powerful Mahajanapada.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: Between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, Magadha became the most powerful Mahajanapada: agriculture was especially productive in the Magadha region; iron mines were accessible there, providing resources for tools and weapons; elephants, an important component of the army, were found in its forests; the Ganga and its tributaries provided a means of cheap and convenient communication; Buddhist and Jaina writers who wrote about Magadha attributed its power to these factors and to its ambitious kings, of whom Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and Mahapadma Nanda are the best known, along with the ministers who helped implement their policies; and the strategic location of its capitals, Rajgir and later Pataliputra.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (b) “Several urban centres emerged in the sub-continent from the sixth century BCE.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: Several urban centres emerged in the sub-continent from the sixth century BCE: these were the capitals of Mahajanapadas; virtually all major towns were located along routes of communication — some, such as Pataliputra, were situated on riverine routes, others, such as Ujjayini, were along land routes, and yet others, such as Puhar, were near the coast from where sea routes began; many cities, like Mathura, were bustling centres of commercial, cultural and political activity.

questions.text: Describe any three features of ancient numismatics.

answer.text: Features of ancient numismatics: exchanges were facilitated by the introduction of coinage; punch-marked coins, made of silver and copper (such as Mauryan coins), were the earliest to be used; merchants, bankers and townspeople also issued coins; images and names of kings appeared on coins issued by the Indo-Greeks and Kushanas, and the Kushanas issued the first gold coins, identical in weight to those issued by contemporary Roman and Parthian rulers; hoards of Roman coins have been found, indicating coins were used for long-distance trade; coins were also issued by tribal republics of Punjab and Haryana, called the Yaudheyas, and gold coins were issued by the Gupta rulers - coins were thus made of silver, copper and gold.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (a) Examine the nature and characteristics of the land grants in ancient Indian society.

answer.text:
Nature and characteristics of land grants in ancient Indian society:
Land grants were recorded on copper plates and stone, indicating who received the land; most inscriptions were in Sanskrit, though some were in local languages like Tamil and Telugu.
Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of a powerful ruler, gave land grants, having access to land as a powerful lady.
Land grants were given to rural peasants and Brahmins, and may have been part of a strategy to expand cultivable areas.
Some historians feel land grants were a sign of weak rulers losing control over samantas, while surviving records are generally about religious institutions or Brahmanas.
There were regional variations in the size of land donated; villagers were expected to obey the new lord and pay dues, and agrahara land granted to Brahmins was usually tax-exempt.
Land grants provide insight into the relationship between cultivators and the state.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (b) Examine the various strategies used to enhance agricultural output from the sixth BCE onwards.

answer.text:
Strategies used to enhance agricultural output from the sixth century BCE onwards:
Shifting to plough agriculture in the fertile river valleys, using iron-tipped ploughshares.
The alluvial soils of the Ganga valley with good rainfall favoured crop growth; paddy production increased dramatically with the introduction of transplantation.
Semi-arid areas could not adopt this improved technology; hilly tracts of the North-east and parts of central India practised hoe agriculture instead.
Irrigation was another strategy, using wells, tanks and canals; because of these variations, the benefits of increased production were uneven.
Communities as well as individuals organised the construction of irrigation works.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (a) In what ways do the challenges of inscriptional evidences restrict our ability to understand the past ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
Challenges of inscriptional evidence restrict our ability to understand the past:
Histories of ancient rulers have been reconstructed from literature, coins and inscriptions including prashastis, but there are technical limitations - letters may be very faintly engraved, leading to uncertainty in reconstruction, and inscriptions may be damaged or have missing letters.
It is not always easy to be sure of the exact meaning of words used, some of which may be specific to a particular place or time, leading scholars to debate alternative readings; a few inscriptions remain undeciphered, and not all of the several thousand discovered have been deciphered, published and translated.
Many more inscriptions must have existed but have not survived the ravages of time, so what is available today is probably only a fraction of what was originally inscribed.
Not everything we consider politically or economically significant was necessarily recorded in inscriptions - routine agricultural practices and the joys and sorrows of daily existence find no mention, as inscriptions focus more often on grand, unique events.
The content of inscriptions almost invariably reflects the perspective of the persons who commissioned them (often kings, e.g. Ashoka's edicts, or land grants such as Prabhavati Gupta's), so inscriptions need to be corroborated with other evidence, and epigraphy alone does not provide a full understanding of political and economic history.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: (b) In what ways do coins serve as valuable sources for understanding the ancient period ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
Coins serve as valuable sources for understanding the ancient period:
Coins act as an important archaeological source; punch-marked coins of silver and copper (from c. sixth century BCE) were amongst the earliest to be minted and used, and the material used indicates economic conditions.
Numismatists have studied coins to reconstruct possible commercial networks; coins were issued by kings, merchants, bankers and townspeople.
The first coins to bear the names and images of rulers were issued by the Indo-Greeks; the widespread use of gold coins indicates the enormous value of transactions taking place.
The Kushanas issued the largest hoards of gold coins from the first century CE, virtually identical in weight to those issued by contemporary Roman emperors and Parthian rulers of Iran; coins were also issued by tribal republics such as the Yaudheyas of Punjab and Haryana, facilitating long-distance transactions from which kings also benefited.
Gold coins issued by the Gupta rulers, especially the earliest issues, are remarkable for their purity, and depicted hierarchies of ruling kings; from c. sixth century CE onwards, finds of gold coins taper off.

questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “The Anguish of the King” — When the king Devanampiya Piyadassi had been ruling for eight years, the (country of the) Kalingas (present-day coastal Orissa) was conquered by (him). One hundred and fifty thousand men were deported, a hundred thousand were killed, and many more died. After that, now that (the country of) the Kalingas has been taken, Devanampiya (is devoted) to an intense study of Dhamma, to the love of Dhamma, and to instructing (the people) in Dhamma. This is the repentance of Devanampiya on account of his conquest of the (country of the) Kalingas. For this is considered very painful and deplorable by Devanampiya that, while one is conquering an unconquered (country) slaughter, death and deportation of people (take place) there… (31.1) How did king Devanampiya Piyadassi's conquest of Kalinga influence his approach to governance ? (31.2) How did Kalinga's conquest change the king's actions towards his subjects ? (31.3) How did the king's transformation shape the spread of Dhamma ?

answer.text:
31.1: King Devanampiya Piyadassi's (Ashoka's) conquest of Kalinga had a great impact on him - he regretted the violence and suffering it caused, devoted himself to Dhamma, appointed Dhamma Mahamatas, became compassionate and generous, and preached non-violence, instructing his people to be humane, respectful and ethical.
31.2: Kalinga's conquest changed the king's actions towards his subjects - it led him to devote himself to Dhamma, become compassionate and generous, preach non-violence, stop the killing of animals in his kitchen, and instruct his people to be humane, respectful and ethical.
31.3: The king's transformation shaped the spread of Dhamma - he appointed Dhamma Mahamatas, adopted and promoted Dhamma through pillars and rock edicts, sent ambassadors to various places, stopped the killing of animals in his kitchen, and Dhamma became his guiding principle.

answer.text:
31.1 Rivers served as natural transport routes, providing cheap, efficient transport and connectivity, promoting trade.
31.2 Large amounts of goods were traded between India and other countries because India, being a rich country, provided many articles like pepper, cinnamon, crude, topaz and minerals; other countries needed these goods, so trade flourished.
31.3 Archaeological evidence proves that precious and semi-precious stones were found in Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu; some precious stones were brought from other sites along the coast; the availability of these stones gave rise to the setting up of the bead-making industry.

questions.chapter: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies
questions.text: Describe any three features of the Mauryan administration.

answer.text:
There were five major political centres in the empire, with the capital at Pataliputra; the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri are all mentioned in Ashokan inscriptions.
The vast empire did not have a uniform administrative system; the regions included within the empire were diverse - contrast the hilly terrain of Afghanistan with the coast of Orissa.
Administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres; Taxila and Ujjayini were situated on important long-distance trade routes, while Suvarnagiri (the golden mountain) was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka.
Communication along both land and riverine routes was vital for the existence of the empire; Megasthenes mentions a committee with six subcommittees for coordinating military activity, and Ashoka also tried to hold his empire together by propagating dhamma.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: How is Mahabharata a dynamic text ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: The Mahabharata is a dynamic text because: it is available in various languages; it contains several stories; the epic has been retold in various ways; it has been depicted in sculpture; it has been depicted in paintings; and it has inspired plays, dance and narrations across centuries.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “A Tiger-like Husband” — This is a summary of a story from the Adi Parvan of the Mahabharata : The Pandavas had fled into the forest. They were tired and fell asleep; only Bhima, the second Pandava, renowned for his prowess, was keeping watch. A man-eating rakshasa caught the scent of the Pandavas and sent his sister Hidimba to capture them. She fell in love with Bhima, transformed herself into a lovely maiden and proposed to him. He refused. Meanwhile, the rakshasa arrived and challenged Bhima to a wrestling match. Bhima accepted the challenge and killed him. The others woke up hearing the noise. Hidimba introduced herself, and declared her love for Bhima. She told Kunti: “I have forsaken my friends, my dharma and my kin; and good lady, chosen your tiger-like son for my man ... whether you think me a fool, or your devoted servant, let me join you, great lady, with your son as my husband.” Ultimately, Yudhisthira agreed to the marriage on condition that they would spend the day together but that Bhima would return every night. The couple roamed all over the world during the day. In due course Hidimba gave birth to a rakshasa boy named Ghatotkacha. Then the mother and son left the Pandavas. Ghatotkacha promised to return to the Pandavas whenever they needed him. (31.1) How was Hidimba’s culture different from Pandavas ? (31.2) Why did Kunti approve Hidimba’s plea for Bhima ? (31.3) How did this incident prove Kunti’s far sightedness ?

answer.text:
(31.1) Hidimba belonged to the Rakshasa clan, who were man-eaters and existed beyond the four varnas — this made her culture different from that of the Pandavas.
(31.2) Kunti approved Hidimba's plea on the condition that Bhima would spend the day with Hidimba but would return to the Pandavas at night.
(31.3) This incident proved Kunti's far-sightedness because she was a farsighted person who knew that Hidimba and her child would be of great help to the Pandavas in their time of need; indeed, the same thing happened later when Ghatotkacha (Hidimba and Bhima's son) promised to return to the Pandavas whenever they needed him.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Why is Mahabharata considered as a dynamic text ? Explain.

answer.text: The Mahabharata is considered a dynamic text because its growth did not stop with the Sanskrit version — over the centuries, versions of the epic were written in a variety of languages through an ongoing process of dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts; several stories that originated in specific regions or circulated among certain people found their way into the epic, and its central story was often retold in different ways; episodes from the Mahabharata were depicted in sculpture and painting, and it provided themes for a wide range of performing arts — plays, dance and other kinds of narration; it combines narrative and didactic aspects and is meant to be a dramatic, moving story carrying a social message; the Bhagavad Gita, a part of the Mahabharata, contains the advice of Shri Krishna to Arjuna.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “According to Brahmanical theory, only Kshatriyas could be kings in the early states, however several other ruling lineages probably had different origins.” Explain the statement with examples from ancient India.

answer.text: According to Brahmanical theory only Kshatriyas could be kings in the early states, but this prescription does not hold good, as several other ruling lineages probably had different origins: as per Brahmanical texts, the Mauryas were of low origin; the Shungas and the Kanvas were Brahmins, not Kshatriyas; the Shakas, who came from Western Asia, were considered Mlecchas, and Rudradaman, a Shaka ruler, was a powerful 'Mlechchha'; Gautamiputra Satakarni was also a Brahmin, and he entered into a marriage alliance with the Rudradaman kin, even though the Satavahanas claimed to be Brahmanas; the Brahmanical theory therefore does not hold good — it was ultimately the powerful person who became king.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “Given the diversity of the sub-continent, there have been populations in early states, whose social practices were not influenced by the Brahmanical ideas.” Explain the statement.

answer.text: Given the diversity of the sub-continent, there have been populations in early states whose social practices were not influenced by Brahmanical ideas: many groups of people refused to follow the Brahmanical varna order, and were called uncivilised or even animal-like; these were forest dwellers whose main occupation was hunting and gathering — Eklavya is supposed to belong to such a group, called nishada; some of these people were nomadic pastoralists, and some groups were labelled Mlecchhas; some people outside the Brahmanical system were called untouchables, and some groups did polluting jobs like handling corpses or dead animals, and were often called Chandalas.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Analyse the elements examined by historians on Mahabharata as a text.

answer.text: Elements examined by historians on the Mahabharata as a text: Language - the original version of the Mahabharata was in Sanskrit, and the Sanskrit used in the epic is simpler than Vedic Sanskrit; Content - historians classify the contents of the Mahabharata under two broad heads, narrative and didactic, with the epic revolving around two sets of warring cousins; Author - the original story was probably composed by charioteer-bards known as sutas, though it is attributed to the sage Vyasa; Dates - sutas circulated the story orally for many decades before Brahmanas took to writing it down much later; historians also examine its intended audience, the kind of text it is (didactic and narrative), the fact that it is a dynamic text, its many regional variations, and the socio-cultural context in which it was written.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “Historians have studied many rules and varied practices of familial ties during the Mahabharata period.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: Familial relations during the Mahabharata period: (i) Kinship and blood relationships. (ii) Tradition and rituals. (iii) Gotra system and each gotra named after a vedic seer. (iv) Endogamy and exogamy. (v) Polyandry, e.g. marriage of Draupadi with the Pandavas, and Polygyny, e.g. many Satavahana rulers had more than one wife. (vi) Metronymics, e.g. the list of successive generations of teachers and students given in the Brihadranyaka Upanishada. (vii) Eight forms of marriage recognized by the Dharamshastras and Dharmasutras. (viii) Guru-Shishya relationships were quite prevalent. (ix) Importance of sons for the continuity of the patrilineage. (x) No claims of daughters on the resources of household. (xi) Kanyadaan was considered an important religious duty of the father. (xii) Codes of social behaviour were laid down in Dharamshastras and Dharmsutras, e.g. Manusmriti. (Any eight to be explained)

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “There are various elements on which historians have analysed Mahabharata and called it a dynamic text.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: Mahabharata as a dynamic text – various elements: (i) Authors – composition by charioteer bards/sutas which was circulated orally; later Brahmans began to commit it to writing and the author is traditionally considered to be Sage Vyas. (ii) Dates – a phase of the composition of the text between c.200 BCE and 200 CE. (iii) Didactic (rules and regulations about social norms) and Narrative portions (stories). (iv) Language – simpler Sanskrit than that of the Vedas and the Prashastis, later written in a variety of languages. (v) Search for convergence – vivid description of battles, forests, palaces and settlements. (vi) Role of the archaeologist, Dr. B.B. Lal. (vii) Episode of Draupadi's marriage with the Pandavas related to polyandry. (viii) Ongoing dialogue between peoples. (ix) Stories from Mahabharata reflect in various performing arts – Music, Dance, Theatre, Sculpture, Painting, Narrative, Bhagavad Gita. (Any eight to be explained)

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “In the ancient India, the Kingship was not only with Kshatriyas but also with Non-Kshatriyas.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: (a) Kingship of Kshatriyas and Non-Kshatriyas in ancient India: Kshatriya rulers – according to the shastras only Kshatriyas could be kings, e.g. Mahapadmananda, Ajatashatru; according to the Brahmanas kings ought to have been Kshatriyas, e.g. Pandavas, Kauravas, Pratiharas, Guptas, Palas, Rashtrakutas; they followed the Manusmriti and Dharmashastras. (Any four to be explained) Non-Kshatriya rulers – several important ruling lineages probably had different origins; the social background of the Mauryas has been hotly debated, and Brahminical texts describe them as of low origin; the Shungas and Kanvas, immediate successors of the Mauryas, were Brahmins/non-Kshatriyas; the Shakas who came from Central Asia were regarded as mlechchhas; the Satavahana ruler claimed to be a Brahmin; putting kings in the framework of caste was often difficult; only those who could command resources and muster support could become king, other than Kshatriyas. (Any four to be explained)

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “In the ancient Indian subcontinent there were populations beyond the influence of Brahminical idea of four Varnas.” Explain this statement with examples.

answer.text: (b) Populations beyond the influence of the Brahminical idea of four Varnas: (i) There were populations whose social practices were not influenced by Brahminical ideas. (ii) They were described as odd, uncivilized or even animal-like. (iii) Many of them were forest dwellers, hunters and gatherers. (iv) Categories such as Nishad, to which Eklavya was supposed to have belonged. (v) 'Rakshasa' was used to describe people whose practices differed from those laid down in Brahmanical texts. (vi) Nomadic pastoralists could not be accommodated within the framework of settled agriculturists. (vii) Mlechchhas, being non-Sanskrit speakers, were also considered low. (viii) The social category of untouchables developed; Fa-Xian also wrote about the untouchables. (ix) Chandals were placed at the very bottom of the social hierarchy. (x) Matanga. (Any eight to be explained)

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: How was patriliny system important among the elite families from sixth century BCE onwards. Explain with examples.

answer.text: Importance of the patriliny system among elite families from the sixth century BCE: (i) Patriliny means tracing descent from father to son, grandson etc. (ii) Under patriliny, sons could claim the resources (including the throne, in the case of kings) of their fathers when the latter died. (iii) In the conflict between the Pandavas and Kauravas, the Pandavas emerged victorious and patrilineal succession was proclaimed. (iv) Most ruling dynasties from the sixth century BCE onwards claimed to follow this system. (v) Mantras in the Rig Veda show the importance of patriliny. (vi) This practice was followed by wealthy men and Brahmanas. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “There were specific features of the familial relationship during the Mahabharata period.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Features of familial relationships during the Mahabharata period:
Families were usually parts of larger networks of people defined as relatives; familial ties, though regarded as 'natural' and based on blood, were defined in many different ways.
The Mahabharata describes a feud over land and power between the Kauravas and the Pandavas, cousins belonging to a single ruling family.
The Pandavas emerged victorious and proclaimed patrilineal succession; while patriliny existed before this feud, the story of the Mahabharata reinforced the ideal.
Under patriliny, sons could claim resources (including the throne) of their fathers, though there were variations - sometimes brothers succeeded one another or other kinsmen claimed the throne, and in exceptional circumstances women inherited the throne or ancestral property, e.g. Prabhavati Gupta.
The Brahmins laid down codes of social behaviour, which were not followed by everybody, though many common people did follow these rules.
There were eight different kinds of marriage - e.g. Draupadi's marriage, Bhima's marriage to Hidimba.
Gotra rules were not followed by all ruling dynasties, e.g. the Satavahanas.
Mothers had an important place in the family, but their advice was not always upheld, e.g. Kunti and Gandhari.
Respect was shown on the basis of hierarchy - caste and gender.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “The political power or kingship was rarely dependent on birth as Kshatriyas but also open to anyone who could muster support and resources.” Explain the statement with the examples from sixth century BCE onwards.

answer.text:
Political power/kingship was rarely dependent on birth as Kshatriyas and was open to anyone who could muster support and resources:
According to the Dharmashastras and Dharmasutras, only Kshatriyas could be kings, but this prescription was not followed universally.
Several important ruling lineages probably had different origins.
Buddhist texts suggest the Mauryas had a Kshatriya background, while Brahmanical texts describe them as being of 'low' origin.
The Shungas and Kanvas who ruled were Brahmins.
The Shakas, who came from Central Asia, were regarded as Mlechchhas, though some powerful Mlechchhas were familiar with Sanskritic traditions.
The Satavahana dynasty claimed to be Brahmanas - e.g. Gotami Puta Siri Satakani claimed to be a unique Brahmin and destroyer of the pride of the Kshatriyas.
All this shows that anyone who could muster support could become a king.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Why is Mahabharata called a dynamic text ? Choose the most suitable option from the following.
options: It remains unchanged and consistent in all versions.
It has been reinterpreted across various contexts.
It focuses solely on historical facts.
It is a fixed text with no variations over time.

answer.text: It has been reinterpreted across various contexts.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “Historians consider several elements when they analyse the Mahabharata.” Substantiate the statement with suitable examples.

answer.text:
Historians consider several elements when they analyse the Mahabharata:
Language - it was written in Sanskrit and translated into various languages.
It contains didactic sections with prescriptions about social norms; between c. 200 and 400 CE, large didactic sections resembling the Manusmriti were added, attributed to a sage named Vyasa; it is also a text on authority and governance.
The original story was probably composed by charioteer-bards known as sutas and circulated orally; from the fifth century BCE, Brahmanas took over the story and began committing it to writing.
It is a dynamic text - several stories that originated in specific regions or circulated among certain people found their way into the epic, and the central story was often retold in different ways.
It reflects socio-cultural elements such as social hierarchy, gender roles, family structures and forms of marriage.
Mahabharata stories were depicted in sculpture and painting, and provided themes for performing arts - plays, dance and other narrations.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “Many communities during the Mahabharata period had different social practices from Brahmanical ideas.” Substantiate the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Many communities during the Mahabharata period had different social practices from Brahmanical ideas:
The varna system laid down divisions of the four main varnas, but this was not followed by everybody.
Nishadas, forest dwellers such as Ekalavya, did not fit into this scheme.
Rakshasa marriage is exemplified by Bhima's marriage to Hidimba.
Categories of untouchables and chandalas existed outside the varna framework.
Rulers such as the Shakas were regarded as Mlechchhas (barbarians/outsiders) by Brahmanas, yet the best-known Satavahana ruler, Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani, claimed to be both a unique Brahmana and a destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas - showing the presence of non-Kshatriya kings in power.
Gotra rules on marriage were not always followed by all ruling dynasties.
Succession could be patrilineal, though in exceptional cases women like Prabhavati Gupta held resources; generally women could not claim a share of family resources.
Occupational groups like goldsmiths (suvarnakara) did not easily fit into the fourfold varna system.

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the narrative sections of the Mahabharata ?

answer.text: They contain compiled stories

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) Describe the processes adopted by V.S. Sukthankar and his team in preparing the critical edition of the Mahabharata.

answer.text:
Processes adopted by V.S. Sukthankar and his team in preparing the critical edition of the Mahabharata:
The team, led by V.S. Sukthankar, a noted Sanskritist, started working in 1919.
They collected Sanskrit manuscripts of the text, written in various scripts, from different parts of the country, and compared verses from each manuscript.
Two things became apparent - there were several common elements in the Sanskrit versions of the story, and there were also enormous regional variations.
They selected common verses and published these in several volumes, while regional variations were documented in footnotes and appendices to the main text; taken together, more than half of the 13,000 pages of the critical edition are devoted to these variations.
The project was completed in 47 years.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) Describe different patterns of marriages that influenced familial relations during the Mahabharata period.

answer.text:
Different patterns of marriage that influenced familial relations during the Mahabharata period:
Endogamy/gotra endogamy - marriage within the gotra.
Exogamy/gotra exogamy - marriage outside the gotra.
Polygyny - the practice of a man having several wives.
Polyandry - the practice of a woman having several husbands, e.g. Draupadi's marriage.
Polygamy - the practice of having more than one spouse; the Manusmriti mentions eight forms of marriage.
There were also marriages outside the Brahmanical system, e.g. Bhima's marriage to Hidimba.

questions.text: (a) Examine the duties to be performed by Kshatriyas as codified in Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras in the ancient India.

answer.text:
Duties to be performed by Kshatriyas as codified in the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras:
Kshatriyas were to engage in warfare and protect the people.
They had to administer justice to the common man, study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed, and make gifts.
Kings were mainly drawn from the Kshatriya varna.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) Examine any three ways evolved by Brahmanas to enforce the norms of the Varna order in the ancient India.

answer.text:
Ways evolved by Brahmanas to enforce the norms of the varna order in ancient India:
Brahmanas asserted and proclaimed that the varna order was of divine origin.
They advised the king to ensure implementation of the varna order.
They said that social status was determined by birth.
Brahmanas referred to the Purusha Sukta hymn to enforce the varna order.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) How did different types of marriages reflect the social systems of ancient India during the Mahabharata Period ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How different types of marriages reflected the social system of ancient India during the Mahabharata period:
Endogamy refers to marriage within a unit - this could be a kin group, caste, or a group living in the same locality; exogamy refers to marriage outside the unit.
Girls were married at the right time and to the right person; kanyadaan was an important religious duty of the father, and women gave up their father's gotra and adopted that of their husbands on marriage.
Polyandry was the practice of a woman having several husbands, e.g. Draupadi; polygyny was the practice of a man having several wives, e.g. Arjuna.
The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras recognised eight forms of marriage - the first four were considered good, while the remaining were condemned; these rules were not followed the same way everywhere.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) How did familial relations impact the social systems of India during the Mahabharata Period ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How familial relations impacted the social systems of India during the Mahabharata period:
Families are usually parts of larger networks of people defined as relatives; family ties are often regarded as 'natural' and based on blood, but are defined in many different ways - some societies regard cousins as blood relations, others do not.
The Mahabharata describes a feud over land and power between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, belonging to the same ruling family; their conflict ended in a battle in which the Pandavas emerged victorious and proclaimed patrilineal succession.
The idea of patriliny had existed before this feud, and the Mahabharata story reinforced this ideal; under patriliny, sons could claim the resources of their father when he died, including the throne in the case of kings, and most ruling dynasties from the sixth century BCE claimed to follow this system, though in some situations brothers succeeded one another, and in exceptional circumstances women inherited the throne.
Marriage rules - according to the Manusmriti, eight forms of marriage were in practice; the epic also shows the role of mothers, e.g. the advice of Kunti and Gandhari, and depicts various social situations such as Draupadi's marriage, along with the desire for sons and the gotra of women; respect was shown on the basis of hierarchy.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : “A Mother's Advice” — The \textit{Mahabharata} describes how, when war between the Kauravas and the Pandavas became almost inevitable, Gandhari made one last appeal to her eldest son Duryodhana. By making peace you honour your father and me, as well as your well-wishers… it is the wise man in control of his senses who guards his kingdom. Greed and anger drag a man away from his profits; by defeating these two enemies a king conquers the earth… You will happily enjoy the earth, my son, along with the wise and heroic Pandavas…. There is no good in a war, no law (\textit{dharma}) and profit (\textit{artha}), let alone happiness; nor is there (necessarily) victory in the end – don't set your mind on war… Duryodhana did not listen to this advice and fought and lost the war. (31.1) Explain the main cause of conflict between Kauravas and Pandavas. (31.2) Why did Gandhari advice Duryodhana not to fight ? (31.3) Why did Duryodhana not listen to the advice of his mother, Gandhari ?

answer.text:
31.1 The basic cause of conflict between the Kauravas and Pandavas was to have supremacy over land and power; the Kurus were a dominant group and wanted power to rule under all circumstances.
31.2 Gandhari advised Duryodhana not to fight because by making peace Duryodhana would honour his parents and well-wishers; greed and anger drag a man away from his profits; there is no good in a war, no law (dharma), no profit or happiness, and there is no victory at the end of the war.
31.3 Duryodhana did not listen to his mother Gandhari's advice because he wanted to be the ruler; he was jealous and greedy; and he did not want to make peace with the Pandavas.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) “\textit{Mahabharata} is considered as a dynamic text.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
The growth of the Mahabharata did not stop with the Sanskrit version; the epic was written in a variety of languages.
The epic was an ongoing process of dialogue between peoples, communities, and those who wrote the texts.
Several stories that originated in specific regions or circulated amongst certain people found their way into the epic; the central story was often retold in different ways.
Many episodes were depicted in sculpture and painting; it provided themes for a wide range of performing arts - plays, dance and other kinds of narrations.
It is depicted in sculpture and relief carvings in temples, and gave rise to texts like the Bhagavad Gita.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) “\textit{Mahabharata} reinforced the ideas of familial values.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Familial ties are often regarded as 'natural' and based on blood, but they are defined in many different ways; some societies regard cousins as blood relations, whereas others do not.
Patriliny means tracing descent from father to son to grandson, leading to patrilineal succession; in exceptional circumstances, women such as Prabhavati Gupta exercised power.
Sons were important for the continuity of the patrilineage; daughters had no claims to the resources of the household, and were married outside the kin - a system called exogamy.
Kanyadana, the gift of a daughter in marriage, was an important religious duty of the father.
People were classified into gotras; women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt their husband's on marriage, and members of the same gotra could not marry.
Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from that of the mother), suggesting mothers were important, though caution is needed before drawing conclusions.
Proper social roles are illustrated by examples like Drona and Eklavya, and Bhima and Hidimba.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (a) Describe the examples which show that Brahmanical ideas on kinship, marriage and ruling lineage were not universally followed during the early historical period in India.

answer.text:
The Mahabharata describes a feud over land and power between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, who belonged to a single ruling family, that of the Kurus, a lineage dominating one of the janapadas.
Most ruling dynasties claimed to follow patrilineal succession, although there were variations: sometimes brothers succeeded one another, sometimes other kinsmen claimed the throne, and in very exceptional circumstances women such as Prabhavati Gupta exercised power.
The concern with patriliny was not unique to ruling families - it is evident in mantras in ritual texts such as the Rigveda, and was possibly shared by wealthy men and Brahmanas.
The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras recognised as many as eight forms of marriage; the first four were considered 'good' while the remaining were condemned - possibly practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms.
The names of women who married Satavahana rulers indicate many had names derived from their father's gotra, such as Gotama and Vasistha.
Endogamy, or marriage within the kin group, was prevalent amongst several communities in south India; such marriages amongst kinfolk ensured a close-knit community.
Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from that of the mother).
According to the Shastras, only Kshatriyas could be kings, but several important ruling lineages probably had different origins - the social background of the Mauryas is debated, the Shakas who came from Central Asia were regarded as mlechchhas by the Brahmanas, and Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani of the Satavahana dynasty claimed to be both a unique Brahmana and a destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas, while also entering a marriage alliance with the kin of Rudradaman.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: (b) Describe the process undertaken by V.S. Sukthankar and his team in preparing the critical edition of the \textit{Mahabharata}.

answer.text:
In 1919, under the leadership of Indian Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar, a team comprising dozens of scholars initiated the task of preparing a critical edition of the Mahabharata.
It meant collecting Sanskrit manuscripts of the text, written in a variety of scripts, from different parts of the country; the team worked out a method of comparing verses from each manuscript.
They selected the verses that appeared common to most versions and published these in several volumes, running into over 13,000 pages; the project took 47 years to complete.
Two things became apparent: there were several common elements in the Sanskrit versions of the story evident in manuscripts from all over the subcontinent, and there were enormous regional variations in the ways the text had been transmitted over the centuries.
These variations were documented in footnotes and appendices - more than half the 13,000 pages are devoted to them; they are reflective of the complex processes that shaped early and later social histories, through dialogues between dominant traditions and resilient local ideas and practices, characterised by moments of conflict as well as consensus.
Our understanding of these processes is derived primarily from texts written in Sanskrit by and for Brahmanas; scholars subsequently began studying other traditions, from works in Pali, Prakrit and Tamil, which indicated that the ideas in normative Sanskrit texts were on the whole recognised as authoritative.

questions.chapter: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Eight forms of marriage” — Here are the first, fourth, fifth and sixth forms of marriage from the \textit{Manusmriti} : First: The gift of a daughter, after dressing her in costly clothes and honouring her with presents of jewels, to a man learned in the Veda whom the father himself invites. Fourth: The gift of a daughter by the father after he has addressed the couple with the text, “May both of you perform your duties together,” and has shown honour to the bridegroom. Fifth: When the bridegroom receives a maiden, after having given as much wealth as he can afford to the kinsmen and to the bride herself, according to his own will. Sixth: The voluntary union of a maiden and her lover … which springs from desire … (31.1) Explain why jewels and costly clothes were given in the first form of marriage. (31.2) Explain the underlying idea behind the father honouring the bridegroom in the fourth form of marriage. (31.3) How had these marriages influenced the social practices in the later Indian society ?

answer.text:
31.1 Jewels and costly clothes were given in the first form of marriage to symbolize honour towards the bride and bridegroom, to provide financial assistance, and because it was directly related to status in society.
31.2 In the fourth form of marriage, the father honoured the bridegroom, reflecting the father's approval and blessings.
31.3 These marriages influenced later Indian society in the custom of performing rituals in marriages, the practice of dowry, and the role of wealth in marriage.

questions.text: (a) “The Stupa at Sanchi is among the best preserved monuments of the earliest times.” Explain the statement.

answer.text: The Stupa at Sanchi is among the best preserved ancient monuments because it escaped destruction: it was of great interest to Europeans; the French sought permission of Shah Jahan Begum to take away the eastern gateway to keep in their museum, and the English wanted to do the same; the Begum refused, and they had to be content with plaster copies; the Begums of Bhopal provided money for the preservation of the monument and also funded a museum and guest house in the Stupa complex; due to the wise decisions of the Begums, and the good luck of escaping the eyes of railway contractors and builders, it survives today as a key archaeological site and one of the best preserved monuments of the earliest times.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Explain the growth of Puranic Hinduism.

answer.text: The growth of Puranic Hinduism: Vaishnavism, a part of Puranic Hinduism, worships Vishnu; in the Shaivite tradition, Shiva is the chief deity; the worship of these deities was considered a bond between the deity and the worshipper; in Vaishnavism there are many incarnations or avatars (ten avatars are recognised) — it was believed that whenever there was disorder on earth, an avatar appeared to save people from evil forces, and each avatar came to be recognised as a local deity; Shiva was symbolised mainly in the form of a linga, though occasionally represented in human form too; deities in human form depicted a complex set of ideas and attributes through symbols such as head-dresses, ornaments and weapons.
