questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) Describe the main teachings of Buddhism.

answer.text: Main teachings of Buddhism: the world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing; it is soulless (anatta), as there is nothing permanent or eternal in it; within this transient, soulless world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to existence; by following the path of moderation between severe penance and self-indulgence, human beings can rise above these worldly troubles; the Buddha regarded the social world as a creation of humans rather than of divine origin, and advised people to be humane and ethical, expecting individual effort to transform social relations; he emphasised individual agency and righteous action as the means to escape the cycle of rebirth and attain self-realisation.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Describe the teachings of Jainism.

answer.text: Teachings of Jainism: the important idea in Jainism is that the entire world is animated — even stones, rocks and water have life; non-injury to living beings, especially humans, animals, plants and insects, is central to Jainism, and the principle of ahimsa has left its mark on Indian thinking; the cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma; asceticism and penance are required to free oneself from the cycle of karma, and this can be achieved only by renouncing the world.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) Why is the mid-first millennium BCE often regarded as a turning point in world history ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: The mid-first millennium BCE is often regarded as a turning point in world history: this period saw the emergence of thinkers such as Zarathustra in Iran, Kong Zi (Confucius) in China, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle in Greece, and Mahavira and Gautama Buddha in India, who tried to understand the mysteries of existence and the relationship between human beings and the cosmic order; it was also a time when new kingdoms and cities were developing all over the world, and social and economic life was changing in a variety of ways in the Ganga valley; the early Vedic tradition was one of the pre-existing traditions of thought — the Rig Veda consists of hymns in praise of deities such as Agni, Indra and Soma, chanted when sacrifices were performed, where people prayed for cattle, sons, good health and long life; at first sacrifices were performed collectively, but more elaborate sacrifices such as the Rajasuya and Ashvamedha were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests to conduct the rituals; the Upanishads reflect a new questioning of this tradition.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) How have Art historians tried to understand Buddhism through the sculptures of Sanchi Stupa ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: Art historians have tried to understand Buddhism through the sculptures of Sanchi Stupa: they have carefully studied the sculpture at Sanchi and identified many scenes from the Vessantara Jataka, the story of a generous prince who gave away everything to a Brahmana and went to live in the forest with his wife and children; the Buddha's presence is shown through symbols — an empty seat represents his meditation, a stupa represents the Mahaparinibbana, a wheel represents his first sermon delivered at Sarnath, and a tree symbolises an event in his life; a Brahmanical tradition motif, the shalabhanjika (a beautiful woman swinging from the edge of the gateway), derived from Sanskrit tradition, was used as a decoration of the stupa; many people who turned to Buddhism enriched it with their own pre-Buddhist and even non-Buddhist beliefs, practices and ideas; some of the finest depictions of animals are found at Sanchi Stupa, later used as symbols of human attributes — elephants signify strength and wisdom, along with horses, monkeys and battle scenes; the Gaja Lakshmi motif is identified by some as the mother of the Buddha, by others with the goddess of good fortune; and serpent motifs found on several pillars seem to be derived from other popular traditions.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Why was Buddha considered as one of the most influential teachers of his time ? Explain.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: Read the following source and answer the questions that follow : “The Therigatha” — This unique Buddhist text, part of the Sutta Pitaka, is a collection of verses composed by bhikkhunis. It provides an insight into women’s social and spiritual experiences. Punna, a dasi or slave woman, went to the river each morning to fetch water for her master’s household. There she would daily see a Brahmana performing bathing rituals. One morning she spoke to him. The following are verses composed by Punna, recording her conversation with the Brahmana : I am a water carrier : / Even in the cold / I have always gone down to the water / frightened of punishment / Or the angry words of high class women. / So what are you afraid of Brahmana, / That makes you go down to the water / (Though) your limbs shake with the bitter cold ? The Brahmana replied: / I am doing good to prevent evil; / anyone young or old / who has done something bad / is freed by washing in water. Punna said : / Whoever told you / You are freed from evil by washing in the water ? .... / In that case all the frogs and turtles / Would go to heaven, and so would the water snakes / and crocodiles! / (Instead) Don’t do that thing, / the fear of which / leads you to the water. / Stop now Brahmana! / Save your skin from the cold ... (31.1) How does the text provide an insight into Punna’s spiritual experience ? (31.2) How is Punna reflected as an awakened soul ? (31.3) Which of the teachings to Buddha are evident in the composition ?

answer.text:
(31.1) This text provides insight into Punna's spiritual experience as she realised that customs and rituals have no meaning - one cannot be freed from sins merely by bathing in water, she did not believe in the caste system, and she believed one should not commit sins in the first place, reflecting on truth and reality.
(31.2) Punna is reflected as an awakened soul because she understood that individual effort is what matters most for self-realisation and nibbana, and she tried to convince the Brahmin through reason and persuasion, understanding the path of divinity and the true meaning of the self, and realising that rituals are meaningless.
(31.3) Teachings of the Buddha evident in this composition include his urging people to seek enlightenment through spiritual experience, his view of the social world as the creation of humans, the importance he gave to good conduct, values and good deeds, his condemnation of rituals, his denouncement of the caste system, his effort to convince people through reason and persuasion, his advocacy of the path of moderation, and his emphasis on individual effort.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Fatalists and materialists ?” — Here is an excerpt from the Sutta Pitaka, describing a conversation between King Ajatasattu, the ruler of Magadha, and the Buddha : On one occasion King Ajatasattu visited the Buddha and described what another teacher, named Makkhali Gosala, had told him : “Though the wise should hope, by this virtue … by this penance I will gain karma … and the fool should by the same means hope to gradually rid himself of his karma, neither of them can do it. Pleasure and pain, measured out as it were, cannot be altered in the course of samsara (transmigration). It can neither be lessened or increased … just as a ball of string will when thrown unwind to its full length, so fool and wise alike will take their course and make an end of sorrow.” And this is what a philosopher named Ajita Kesakambalin taught : “There is no such thing, O king, as alms or sacrifice, or offerings … there is no such thing as this world or the next … A human being is made up of the four elements. When he dies the earthy in him returns to the earth, the fluid to water, the heat to fire, the windy to air, and his senses pass into space … The talk of gifts is a doctrine of fools, an empty lie … fools and wise alike are cut off and perish. They do not survive after death.” The first teacher belonged to the tradition of the Ajivikas. They have often been described as fatalists : those who believe that everything is predetermined. The second teacher belonged to the tradition of the Lokayatas, usually described as materialists. Texts from these traditions have not survived, so we know about them only from the works of other traditions. (31.1) Analyse the views of Makkhali Gosala on karma. (31.2) How did Ajita Kesakambalin describe the relations of human beings with the four elements of nature. (31.3) Differentiate between the views of a Fatalist and a Materialist in reference to this source.

answer.text: 31.1 Views of Makkhali Gosala on karma: follow all virtues; pleasure and pain are predetermined. (Any one point) 31.2 How Ajita Kesakambalin described the relations of human beings with the four elements of nature: human beings are made up of four elements – Earth, Water, Fire and Air. 31.3 Difference between the views of a Fatalist and a Materialist: Fatalist – all events and actions are predetermined, individuals are passive observers; Materialist – universe is a system by nature, events and outcomes are the result of physical processes, emphasis on material wellbeing. questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: How does the Sanchi Stupa reflect the religious and cultural beliefs of ancient India ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
The Sanchi Stupa reflects the religious and cultural beliefs of ancient India:
Its development reflects the evolution of Buddhist practices and beliefs.
The gateways (toranas) are adorned with scenes from the Buddha's life and Jataka tales, illustrating the growing importance of narrative traditions in Buddhism.
Inscriptions at Sanchi reveal donations from various social groups, and reliefs on the gateways depict scenes of city life, showing the growing urbanisation of ancient India and Buddhism's appeal to urban populations.
The shalabhanjika motif suggests that many people who turned to Buddhism enriched it with their own pre-Buddhist beliefs, practices and ideas - motifs like Gajalakshmi and serpents, and fine depictions of animals such as elephants, horses, monkeys and cattle, are also found.
The stupa architecture, exemplified by the Sanchi complex, is a multifaceted cultural artefact that embodies core Buddhist principles while also reflecting the political aspirations of rulers, the social dynamics of communities, and the artistic and technological achievements of the time.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) Examine how the sculptural elements are integrated within the architectural framework of the Sanchi Stupa.

answer.text:
How sculptural elements are integrated within the architectural framework of the Sanchi Stupa:
Art historians have identified many scenes from the Vessantara Jataka - the story of a generous prince who gave away everything to a Brahmana and went to live in the forest with his wife and children.
The Buddha's presence is shown through symbols - an empty seat represents his meditation, a stupa represents his Mahaparinibbana, a wheel represents his first sermon at Sarnath, and a tree symbolises an event in his life.
The popular Shalabhanjika motif - a beautiful woman swinging from the edge of the gateway - was regarded as a decoration of the stupa, derived from Sanskrit tradition.
Some of the finest depictions of animals (used as symbols of human attributes, e.g. elephants for strength and wisdom) are found at Sanchi, including horses and monkeys; the Gajalakshmi motif is seen as the mother of the Buddha, or identified with the goddess of good fortune, and serpents found on several pillars seem derived from other popular traditions.
James Fergusson considered Sanchi to be a centre of tree and serpent worship, as he was not familiar with Buddhist literature.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Examine the relationship between Puranic Hinduism and devotional practices.

answer.text:
Relationship between Puranic Hinduism and devotional practices:
The notion of a saviour became popular; Vaishnavism, part of Puranic Hinduism, worships Vishnu, while in the Shaivite tradition Shiva is the chief deity - the worship of these deities is considered a bond between the deity and the worshipper.
In Vaishnavism there are many incarnations or avatars - ten avatars have been recognised, and it is presumed that whenever there was disorder on earth, an avatar appeared to save people from evil forces; each avatar is recognised as a local deity.
Shiva is symbolised in the form of a linga and is also represented in human form; deities in human form depicted a complex set of ideas, with attributes represented through symbols such as head-dresses, ornaments and weapons (ayudhas).
This relationship is reflected in the construction of temples, and the compilation of stories of the deities in the Puranas, compiled by Brahmanas, which became available to women and shudras; there is also a trinity of gods, depiction of deities as figures with multiple arms/heads or with combinations of human and animal forms, and sculptures vividly depicting stories from the epics/Puranas, e.g. the rock-cut sculptural panel at Mahabalipuram, and sculptures of Shiva and Vishnu.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) “The Buddha was considered as one of the most influential teachers of his times.” In the light of this statement, explain his teachings.

answer.text:
The Buddha was considered one of the most influential teachers of his times - his teachings:
He taught that the world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing, and soulless (anatta), with nothing permanent or eternal in it; sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence, but by following the path of moderation human beings can rise above worldly troubles.
In Buddhism the concept of god was irrelevant; he regarded the social world as the creation of human beings, and advised kings and gahapatis to be humane and ethical, expecting individual effort to transform social relations.
He taught Dhamma, the path of righteous living, and propagated the middle path or path of moderation, along with the eightfold path; he told his disciples, 'Be lamps unto yourselves as all of you must work out your own liberation.'
His teachings had a profound impact on people and were easy to comprehend, spreading to China, Japan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand and Indonesia.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Explain the features of Puranic Hinduism in ancient India.

answer.text:
Features of Puranic Hinduism in ancient India:
Vaishnavism is part of Puranic Hinduism, in which Vishnu is worshipped; in the Shaivite tradition, Shiva is the chief deity - worship of these deities is considered a bond between the deity and the worshipper.
In Vaishnavism there are many incarnations or avatars - ten avatars have been recognised, and it is presumed that whenever there was disorder on earth, an avatar appeared to save people from evil forces; each avatar is recognised as a local deity.
Shiva is symbolised in the form of a linga and also represented in human form; deities in human form depicted a complex set of ideas, with attributes represented through symbols such as head-dresses, ornaments and weapons.
This is reflected in the structure and construction of temples.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) How did Buddha attain enlightenment ? Explain.

answer.text:
Buddha's journey into the world outside was traumatic; he was deeply anguished when he saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse.
He realised in that moment that decay and destruction of the human body was inevitable.
He also saw a homeless mendicant who, it seemed to him, had come to terms with old age, disease and death, and found peace.
Soon after, he left the palace and set out in search of his own truth; Siddhartha explored several paths including bodily mortification which led him to a situation of near death.
Abandoning these extreme methods, he meditated for several days and finally attained enlightenment, after which he came to be known as the Buddha or the Enlightened One.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “How Buddhist texts were prepared and preserved” — The Buddha (and other teachers) taught orally – through discussion and debate. Men and women (perhaps children as well) attended these discourses and discussed what they heard. None of the Buddha's speeches were written down during his lifetime. After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of “elders” or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali in present-day Bihar). These compilations were known as \textit{Tipitaka} – literally, three baskets to hold different types of texts. They were first transmitted orally and then written and classified according to length as well as subject matter. The \textit{Vinaya Pitaka} included rules and regulations for those who joined the \textit{sangha} or monastic order; the Buddha's teachings were included in the \textit{Sutta Pitaka}; and the \textit{Abhidhamma Pitaka} dealt with philosophical matters. Each \textit{pitaka} comprised a number of individual texts. Later, commentaries were written on these texts by Buddhist scholars. As Buddhism travelled to new regions such as Sri Lanka, other texts such as the \textit{Dipavamsa} (literally, the chronicle of the island) and \textit{Mahavamsa} (the great chronicle) were written, containing regional histories of Buddhism. Many of these works contained biographies of the Buddha. Some of the oldest texts are in Pali, while later compositions are in Sanskrit. When Buddhism spread to East Asia, pilgrims such as Fa Xian and Xuan Zang travelled all the way from China to India in search of texts. These they took back to their own country, where they were translated by scholars. Indian Buddhist teachers also travelled to faraway places, carrying texts to disseminate the teachings of the Buddha. Buddhist texts were preserved in manuscripts for several centuries in monasteries in different parts of Asia. Modern translations have been prepared from Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan texts. (31.1) Explain why Buddha's speeches were not written down during his lifetime. (31.2) Assess the impact of orally transmitting texts before writing them down for preservation. (31.3) Explain the differences between the \textit{Vinaya Pitaka} and \textit{Sutta Pitaka}.

answer.text:
31.1 Buddha's speeches were not written down during his lifetime because they were taught orally, and discussed by his followers through discussion and debate.
31.2 Orally transmitting texts led to interaction and debate: men, women and children attended these discourses and discussed what they heard; after his death, his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of 'elders' or senior monks at Vesali, as a reliable form of preservation.
31.3 The Vinaya Pitaka included rules and regulations for those who joined the sangha or monastic order; the Buddha's teachings were included in the Sutta Pitaka.

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (a) Describe the teachings and principles of Buddhism.

answer.text:
The world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing; it is soulless (anatta) as there is nothing permanent or eternal, and sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence.
The Path of Moderation between severe penance and self-indulgence is to be followed; Buddha emphasised righteous living (dhamma) as the means to escape the cycle of rebirth and attain nibbana.
Humans have to rise above worldly pleasures; Buddha regarded the social world as the creation of humans rather than of divine origin, and advised kings and gahapatis to be humane and ethical.
Individual effort was expected to transform social relations; all should strive for attaining self-realisation ('Be lamps unto yourselves').

questions.chapter: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments
questions.text: (b) Describe the main ideas of Jainism along with its spread across India in the ancient period.

answer.text:
Mahavira was preceded by 23 other teachers or tirthankaras - literally, those who guide men and women across the river of existence; the most important idea in Jainism is that the entire world is animated, even stones, rocks and water have life.
Non-injury to living beings, especially humans, animals, plants and insects, is central to Jaina philosophy; the principle of ahimsa has left its mark on Indian thinking as a whole.
The cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma; asceticism and penance are required to free oneself from the cycle of karma, achieved only by renouncing the world, so monastic existence is a necessary condition of salvation.
Jaina monks and nuns took five vows: to abstain from killing, stealing and lying; to observe celibacy; and to abstain from possessing property.
Jainism spread to many parts of India as Jaina scholars produced a wealth of literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil; manuscripts were carefully preserved in libraries attached to temples, and stone sculptures associated with the tradition have been recovered from several sites throughout the subcontinent.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: Describe any three experiences of Ibn Battuta in India.

answer.text: Experiences of Ibn Battuta in India: he described the coconut as looking like a date palm, its fruit resembling a man's head; he described the paan plant, grown for its leaves; he found Indian cities in the subcontinent full of exciting opportunities, resources and skills, and densely populated and prosperous; bazaars were places of economic transactions as well as the hub of social and cultural activities, with performances by dancers, musicians and singers; he described Delhi and Daulatabad as vast cities with a great population, the largest in India; he noted the fertility of the soil, which allowed farmers to cultivate two crops a year, and networks of trade and commerce; Indian textiles, particularly cotton cloth, fine muslins, silks, brocade and satin, were in great demand; he described a unique, efficient postal system (uluq and dawa); he noted that slaves were openly sold in markets and regularly exchanged as gifts, with considerable differentiation among slaves; and he found travelling insecure, as he himself was attacked by bands of robbers several times.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (a) Explain the views of Ibn Battuta on Indian cities.

answer.text: Ibn Battuta's views on Indian cities: he found Indian cities full of opportunities, densely populated and prosperous; most cities had crowded streets and bright, colourful markets stacked with goods; he described Delhi as a vast city with a great population, the largest in India, and Daulatabad as no less, easily rivalling Delhi in size; he described all the different gates of the city of Delhi, and also described public performances by dancers, musicians and singers in the city of Daulatabad; the bazaars were not only places of economic transactions but also the hub of social and cultural activities.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (b) Explain how Bernier found the crown ownership of land as being harmful for both the state and its people in the Mughal Empire.

answer.text: Bernier found the crown ownership of land harmful for both the state and its people in the Mughal Empire: the emperor owned all the land and distributed it among his nobles, which had a disastrous effect on society and economy, since the land could not be passed on to the peasants or their children; as a result, no long-term investment was made on land, the peasantry was in decline, and nobody was interested in improving the condition of land and agriculture; according to Bernier there was an absence of a middle class in the Mughal Empire; he saw the Mughal Empire and its king as the 'kings of beggars and barbarians'.

questions.text: Read the following source and answer the questions that follow : “Education and Entertainment” — This is what Ibn Juzayy, who was deputed to write what Ibn Battuta dictated, said in his introduction : A gracious direction was transmitted (by the ruler) that he (Ibn Battuta) should dictate an account of the cities which he had seen in his travel, and of the interesting events which had clung to his memory, and that he should speak of those whom he had met of the rulers of countries, of their-distinguished men of learning, and their pious saints. Accordingly, he dictated upon these subjects a narrative which gave entertainment to the mind and delight to the ears and eyes, with a variety of curious particulars by the exposition of which he gave edification and of marvellous things, by referring to which he aroused interest. (32.1) Why did the Sultan of Morocco insist Ibn Battuta to dictate the story of his travel to Ibn Juzayy ? (32.2) Highlight the places Ibn Battuta explored during his travel. (32.3) What do Ibn Battuta’s travel account reveal about the things he noted in India ?

answer.text:
(32.1) The Sultan of Morocco insisted that Ibn Battuta dictate the story of his travels to Ibn Juzayy so that an account of the cities he had seen on his travels could be recorded, to record interesting events and experiences in different countries, as the Sultan was interested in knowing about the people of different countries and it would entertain the audience.
(32.2) Ibn Battuta explored places such as Mecca, Syria, Iraq, Persia, Yemen, Oman, the coast of East Africa, Sind, Delhi, the Maldives and China, along with North Africa, West Asia, parts of Central Asia, and parts of the Indian subcontinent including Assam, West Bengal, Delhi and Daulatabad, as well as Sri Lanka and Sumatra.
(32.3) Ibn Battuta's travel accounts reveal that in India he noted the coconut and the paan; he found Indian cities densely populated and prosperous, full of opportunities, and gave descriptions of Delhi and Daulatabad; bazaars were hubs of social, economic and cultural activity in the towns, part of inter-Asian networks of trade and commerce, and he described a unique postal/communication system; he also noted that slaves were openly sold in markets and that travel was unsafe.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (a) Examine Bernier's description of Crown ownership of land and lack of private property during Mughal India.

answer.text: (a) Bernier's description of Crown ownership of land and lack of private property in Mughal India: (i) Bernier was a firm believer in the virtues of private property. (ii) He saw Crown ownership of land as harmful for both the state and its people. (iii) He claimed the Mughal emperor owned the entire land and distributed it among his nobles. (iv) This had disastrous consequences for both economy and society. (v) Owing to Crown ownership, peasants could not pass land to their children. (vi) They were averse to any long-term investment in sustenance and expansion of production. (vii) The absence of private property in land prevented the emergence of a class of 'improving' landlords. (viii) Some private property must have existed for peasants' personal use. (ix) There was no middle state in India. (x) It led to uniform ruination of agriculture. (xi) There was excessive oppression of the peasantry. (xii) There was a continuous decline in living standards of all sections except the ruling aristocracy. (xiii) He viewed Indian society as consisting of undifferentiated masses of impoverished people, subjugated by a small, rich and powerful ruling class. (Any eight to be explained)

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (b) Examine Ibn-Battuta's views on Delhi & Daulatabad during his travel.

answer.text: (b) Ibn-Battuta's views on Delhi and Daulatabad: Ibn Battuta found these cities full of exciting opportunities for those with drive, resources and skills. (i) They were densely populated and prosperous except for occasional disruptions from wars and invasions. (ii) Cities had crowded streets and bright, colourful markets stacked with a wide variety of goods. (iii) He described Delhi as a vast city with a great population, the largest in India. (iv) Daulatabad (in Maharashtra) easily rivalled Delhi in size. (v) Delhi covered a wide area with a large population. (vi) There were store-houses for edibles, magazines, ammunition, ballista and siege machines. (vii) Grains stored in the ramparts could last a long time without rotting. (viii) Horsemen and infantrymen moved from one end of the city to another. (ix) There were 28 gates called darwaza; the Budaun darwaza was the greatest, inside the Mandwi darwaza. (x) There was a grain market adjacent to the Gul darwaza, and an orchard. (xi) In Daulatabad there was a market place for male and female singers, known as Tarababad, one of the greatest and most beautiful bazaars. (xii) Shops were decorated with carpets, and there were mosques for offering prayers. (xiii) There was a fine cemetery with domes or arches over graves. (xiv) Bazaars were hubs of social and cultural activity, with spaces marked for public performances by dancers, singers and musicians. questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “A warning for Europe” — Bernier warned that if European kings followed the Mughal model : Their kingdoms would be very far from being well-cultivated and peopled, so well built, so rich, so polite and flourishing as we see them. Our kings are otherwise rich and powerful; and we must avow that they are much better and more royally served. They would soon be kings of deserts and solitudes, of beggars and barbarians, such as those are whom I have been representing. (the Mughals) … We should find the great Cities and the great Burroughs (boroughs) rendered uninhabitable because of ill air, and to fall to ruine (ruin) without anybodies (anybody) taking care of repairing them; the hillocks abandon'd, and the fields overspread with bushes, or fill'd with pestilential marishes (marshes), as hath been already intimated. (32.1) Mention any one prominent contribution of Bernier. (1) (32.2) How did Bernier describe the difference between European kingdom and the Mughal territories ? (1) (32.3) Explain Bernier's views on the socio-economic status of people under Mughal rule. (2)

answer.text:
32.1: Bernier wrote a book on India, 'Travels in the Mughal Empire', and made a comparative study of the East and the West.
32.2: Bernier described European kingdoms as well cultivated, rich, populous, polite and flourishing, in contrast to what he perceived as the desolate and neglected state of the Mughal territories; he warned that if European kings followed the Mughal model, they would fall into ruin.
32.3: Bernier believed the absence of private property in land prevented the emergence of a class of 'improving' landlords, leading to uniform ruination of agriculture, excessive oppression of the peasantry and a continuous decline in the living standards of all sections of society except the ruling aristocracy; people were reduced to beggars and barbarians; artisans had no incentive to improve the quality of their manufactures since profits were appropriated by the state; however, there did exist a prosperous merchant community engaged in long-distance exchange.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (a) 'Francois Bernier contrasted what he saw in India with the situation in Europe.' Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Francois Bernier contrasted what he saw in India with the situation in Europe:
In India there was a lack of private property in land, unlike Europe; Bernier believed private property had its own virtues, but in India the entire land was under the crown.
Due to crown ownership, land holders could not pass on land to their children, and this led to a continuous decline in living standards, unlike in Europe.
India had either rich or poor with no middle class, and he projected the Mughal state as tyrannical, unlike Europe.
In India artisans had no incentive to improve quality since profits were appropriated by the Indian state, and manufacturing was on the decline.
By the 16th century, 15% of the Indian population lived in towns, a higher proportion than in Europe, yet Indian society consisted of impoverished poor people subjugated by a small minority of the rich and powerful.
The absence of private property prevented the emergence of a class of improving landlords.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (b) 'Ibn-Battuta has written extensively about his experience in India.' Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Ibn Battuta wrote extensively about his experience in India:
Cities in the Indian subcontinent were full of exciting opportunities, populated and prosperous; most cities had crowded streets full of bright lights, and markets stacked with a variety of goods.
Ibn Battuta described Delhi as vast with a great population; most bazaars had a mosque and a temple.
The system of communication was very good, encouraging merchants; trade routes were supplied with inns and guest houses, and the postal system was efficient.
He mentioned his unfamiliarity with paan and coconut, noted spaces marked for public performances by dancers, musicians and singers, and found Indian agriculture productive.
The subcontinent was well integrated with the Inter-Asian network of trade and commerce; Indian manufactures were in great demand in West Asia and South-East Asia.
He also mentions that the practice of slavery was very common in India.

I set out alone, having neither fellow-traveller... nor caravan whose party I might join, but swayed by an overmastering impulse within me and a desire long-cherished in my bosom to visit these illustrious sanctuaries. So I braced my resolution to quit all my dear ones, female and male, and forsook my home as birds forsake their nests ... My age at that time was twenty-two years.” Ibn Battuta returned home in 1354, about 30 years after he had set out. questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (a) Analyse the observations, critical insights and reflections provided by Bernier while he travelled in Mughal India.

answer.text:
Observations, critical insights and reflections provided by Bernier while he travelled in Mughal India:
He observed crown ownership of land and the absence of private property, which meant there was no incentive for improving landlords, and landholders could not pass on their land to their children.
He noted there was no middle class - Indian society consisted of undifferentiated masses of impoverished people, suppressed by a few rich, with the king himself being 'a king of beggars and barbarians'.
He described the ruination of agriculture and the miserable condition of peasants; artisans had no incentive and manufactures were in decline, even though he observed that vast quantities of the world's precious metals flowed into India, and noted the existence of a prosperous merchant community engaged in long-distance exchange.
He described a continuous decline in the living standards of the people, with cities and towns ruined and contaminated with 'ill air', and fields 'overspread with bushes' and full of 'pestilential marishes'.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: (b) “Ibn Battuta's accounts provide important insights into the Indian society of that time.” Justify the statement.

answer.text:
Ibn Battuta's account provides important insights into Indian society of that time:
He observed that social inequities were a natural state of affairs; slaves were openly sold in markets and used as a commodity, exchanged as gifts - he himself purchased horses, camels and slaves as gifts for the Sultan.
There was considerable differentiation among slaves - female slaves, experts in music and dance, were also used to spy on nobles, while others were used for domestic labour or to carry women and men on palanquins/dola; the price of female slaves was low.
He described cities in the subcontinent as full of exciting opportunities, densely populated and prosperous, with crowded streets and bright, colourful markets; bazaars were places of economic, social and cultural transactions, most having both a mosque and a temple, with spaces marked for public performances by dancers, musicians and singers.
Towns derived their wealth from the surplus of villages; agriculture was very productive, and there was an effective communication system (uluq and dawa) and an effective network of inter-Asian trade and commerce, with trade routes well supplied with inns and guest houses; Indian manufactures were in great demand, and he noted the credit system and his unfamiliarity with coconut and paan.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “The imperial \textit{karkhanas}” — Bernier is perhaps the only historian who provides a detailed account of the working of the imperial \textit{karkhanas} or workshops: Large halls are seen at many places, called \textit{karkhanas} or workshops for the artisans. In one hall, embroiderers are busily employed, superintended by a master. In another, you see the goldsmiths; in a third, painters; in a fourth, varnishers in lacquer-work; in a fifth, joiners, turners, tailors and shoe-makers; in a sixth, manufacturers of silk, brocade and fine muslins … The artisans come every morning to their \textit{karkhanas} where they remain employed the whole day; and in the evening return to their homes. In this quiet regular manner, their time glides away; no one aspiring for any improvement in the condition of life wherein he happens to be born. (32.1) How did Bernier's description reflect the economic significance of the \textit{karkhanas} in the Mughal empire ? (32.2) How did the crafts in the \textit{karkhanas} reflect the cultural diversity of the Mughal empire ? (32.3) Analyse the relationship between the Mughal empire and its artisans.

answer.text:
32.1: Bernier's description reflected the economic significance of the Karkhanas in the Mughal empire, as they were a centre of production and were also used as a trading centre.
32.2: The crafts in the Karkhanas reflected the cultural diversity of the Mughal empire, as different craftsmen - goldsmiths, shoemakers, tailors, varnishers and painters - worked together in the karkhana.
32.3: The relationship between the Mughal empire and its artisans was that the empire established karkhanas for artisans to work in; artisans such as goldsmiths, embroiderers, painters, varnishers, tailors and shoemakers all worked together in the karkhanas, and Mughal kings and others became customers for the goods produced there.

questions.text: “Ibn Batuta was amazed by the efficiency of Indian postal system.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
The state took several measures to encourage merchants.
Almost all the trade routes were supplied with inns and guest houses.
The postal system allowed merchants to send information and remit credit across long distances.
It allowed the dispatch of goods at short notice.
The postal system was so efficient that while it took fifty days to reach Delhi from Sind, news reports of spies would reach the Sultan through the postal system in just five days.
The postal system was of two kinds: the horse post (uluq), run by royal horses stationed at a distance of every four miles, and the foot-post (dawa) with three stations per mile.
The foot-post was quicker than the horse-post, and was often used to transport the fruits of Khurasan to India.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “A warning for Europe” — Bernier warned that if European kings followed the Mughal model : Their kingdoms would be very far from being well cultivated and peopled, so well built, so rich, so polite and flourishing as we see them. Our kings are otherwise rich and powerful; and we must avow that they are much better and more royally served. They would soon be kings of deserts and solitudes, of beggars and barbarians, such as those are whom I have been representing (the Mughals). … We should find the great Cities and the great Burroughs (boroughs) rendered uninhabitable because of ill air, and to fall to ruine (ruin) without any bodies (anybody) taking care of repairing them; the hillocks abandon'd, and the fields overspread with bushes, or fill'd with pestilential marishes (marshes), as hath been already intimated. (32.1) Why did Bernier warn their European kings against following Mughal model of kingship ? (32.2) Mention any one difference between Mughal \& European land-ownership. (32.3) How did Bernier's description influence the western theorists from 18$^{th}$ century onwards ? Explain.

answer.text:
32.1 The Mughal kingdom was far from being well cultivated, populated, rich, polite, well-built and flourishing; Bernier considered the Mughal emperor the 'King of Beggars and barbarians', and warned European kings against following this model of kingship.
32.2 A fundamental difference between Mughal India and Europe was the lack of private property in land in the former; in Mughal India the crown was the owner of the land.
32.3 Bernier's descriptions influenced Western theorists from the eighteenth century onwards: the French philosopher Montesquieu used this account to develop the idea of oriental despotism, believing rulers in the oriental world enjoyed unlimited power and absolute authority, keeping subjects in subjugation and poverty; this idea was further developed as the concept of the Asiatic Mode of Production by Karl Marx in the nineteenth century.

questions.chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “How Silver Came to India” — This excerpt from Giovanni Careri's account (based on Bernier's account) gives an idea of the enormous amount of wealth that found its way into the Mughal Empire : That the Reader may form some idea of the Wealth of this (Mughal) Empire, he is to observe that all the Gold and Silver, which circulates throughout the World at last Centres here. It is well known that as much of it comes out of America, after running through several Kingdoms of Europe, goes partly into Turky (Turkey), for several sorts of Commodities; and part into Persia, by the way of Smirna for Silk. Now the Turks not being able to abstain from Coffee, which comes from Hyeman (Oman), and Arabia … nor Persia, Arabia, and the Turks themselves to go without the commodities of India, send vast quantities of Mony (money) to Moka (Mocha) on the Red Sea, near Babel Mandel; to Bassora (Basra) at the bottom of the Persian Gulgh (Gulf); … which is afterwards sent over in Ships to Indostan (Hindustan). Besides the Indian, Dutch, English, and Portuguese Ships, that every Year carry the Commodities of Indostan to Pegu, Tanasserri (parts of Myanmar), Siam (Thailand), Ceylon (Sri Lanka) … the Maldive Islands, Mozambique and other Places, must of necessity convey much Gold and Silver thither, from those Countries. All that the Dutch fetch from the Mines in Japan, sooner or later, goes to Indostan; and the goods carry'd hence into Europe, whether to France, England, or Portugal, are all purchas'd for ready Mony, which remains there. (32.1) How did silver and gold from America reach India ? (32.2) How did ships contribute to the flow of silver and gold to India ? (32.3) How did India benefit from global trade networks in the 17$^{th}$ century ?

answer.text:
32.1 Silver and gold from America reached India by passing through several kingdoms of Europe, Turkey and Persia for trade.
32.2 Indian, Dutch, English and Portuguese ships carried goods to different countries in exchange for goods, contributing to the flow of silver and gold to India.
32.3 India received enormous gold and silver, which enriched the Mughal Empire and strengthened the Mughal economy; it brought stability in the availability of metal currency, expansion of minting of coins, circulation of money in the economy, and improved the ability of the Mughal state to extract taxes and revenue in cash.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: ‘Kabir is known as one of the saints whose philosophy has greatly influenced the Bhakti Movement.’ Justify the statement with suitable points.

answer.text: Kabir's philosophy greatly influenced the Bhakti movement: his mystical verses describe the Ultimate Reality in many ways — as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir, as well as through terms drawn from Vedantic traditions such as Alakh (the unseen), Nirakar (formless), Brahman and Atman, and mystical terms from yogic traditions such as Shabda (sound) or Shunya (emptiness); diverse, sometimes conflicting ideas are expressed in his poems — some draw on Islamic monotheism, while he also used the Sufi concept of love to express the Hindu practice of Nam-simaran (remembrance of God's name); he remains, to the present day, a source of inspiration for those who question entrenched religious and social institutions in their search for the Divine; verses ascribed to him have been compiled in three overlapping traditions — the Kabir Bijak preserved by the Kabir panth in Varanasi and Uttar Pradesh, the Kabir Granthavali associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan, and compositions found in the Adi Granth Sahib; his poems have survived in several languages and dialects, including the special sant bhasha and the inverted-meaning ulatbansi (upside-down sayings) style.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (a) Describe the philosophy and teachings of Kabir.

answer.text: Philosophy and teachings of Kabir: he was a nirguna poet-saint whose mystical experiences were many, used to describe the Ultimate Reality, which he described as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir; he also used terms drawn from Vedantic traditions such as Alakh (the unseen), Nirakar (formless), Brahman and Atman, and mystical terms such as Shabda (sound) or Shunya (emptiness) drawn from yogic traditions; diverse and sometimes conflicting ideas are expressed in his poems, including the Ulat Bansi (upside-down sayings) style; some poems draw on Islamic monotheism, and he used the Sufi concept of love to express the Hindu practice of Nam-simaran (remembrance of God's name); he remains, even today, a source of inspiration for those who question entrenched religious and social institutions in their search for the Divine; verses attributed to him use the words Guru and Satguru, and he argued against distinctions made between the gods of different communities.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) Describe the teachings and philosophy of Islam.

answer.text: Teachings and philosophy of Islam: all those who adopted Islam accepted, in principle, the five 'pillars' of the faith — that there is one God, Allah, and Prophet Muhammad is His messenger; offering prayers five times a day; giving alms; fasting during the month of Ramzan; and performing the pilgrimage to Mecca. However, these universal features were often overlaid with diversities in practice derived from local customary practices of converts from different social milieus, and Islam came to be divided into Shias and Sunnis — for example the Khojahs, a branch of the Shi'a sect, composed devotional poems in Punjabi, Multani, Sindhi, Kachchi, Hindi and Gujarati, and sang them in special ragas during daily prayer meetings; the Sharia is the law governing the Muslim community, based on the Quran and the Hadith; and mosques developed their own distinctive architecture.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (a) Explain the philosophy and teachings of Guru Nanak Dev.

answer.text: Philosophy and teachings of Guru Nanak Dev: he advocated Nirguna Bhakti and rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims; for him the Absolute, or Rab, had no gender or form, and he proposed a simple way to connect to the divine by remembering and repeating the name of Rab; he set up rules for congregational worship (sangat) and expressed his ideas through hymns called shabad, which Baba Guru Nanak would sing in various ragas while his attendant Mardana played the rabab; his hymns are compiled in the Adi Granth Sahib; Baba Guru Nanak did not wish to establish a new religion, but after his death his followers consolidated his practices and distinguished themselves from both Hindus and Muslims.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) Explain the beliefs and practices of Sufism.

answer.text: Beliefs and practices of Sufism: religious-minded people who were against the growing materialism of the caliphate were called Sufis, and were critical of dogmatic traditions; they laid emphasis on seeking salvation through intense devotion and sought the interpretation of the Quran based on their personal experience; they organised communities around the hospice or khanqah, and the Sufi silsila represented a chain between the master and the disciple; special rituals were initiated, including a path of allegiance, patched garments and shaving of the head; the practice of pilgrimage (ziyarat) to a tomb (dargah) was encouraged, and mystical chants (qawwali) were performed; the Sufis generally maintained good relations with the rulers, who also wanted legitimacy — the Sufis solicited and accepted grants from rulers, who set up charitable trusts and endowments for hospices and gave tax-free lands to Sufis; the Chishtis accepted donations in cash as well as kind, and Sufis were often called upon to interpret the Sharia, though some instances of conflict did take place between Sultans and Sufis.

God was worshipped with attributes in the Nirguna bhakti.

answer.text: I, II and III

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (a) ‘Kabir Das is one of the most outstanding examples of a Poet-saint who has given extensive views on social situation, institutions and on ultimate reality.’ Explain the statement.

answer.text: Kabir Das is one of the most outstanding examples of a poet-saint who gave extensive views on social situations, institutions and the Ultimate Reality: according to tradition he was born a Hindu and raised in a family of Muslim weavers; he was a nirguna saint, influenced by both Bhakti and Sufi ideals, and his verses are compiled in the Kabir Bijak, the Kabir Granthavali and the Adi Granth Sahib; his poems are found in several languages and dialects, including the sant bhasha of nirguna poets and the ulatbansi (upside-down sayings) style, and his mystical experiences describe the Ultimate Reality on the basis of Islamic, Vedantic and yogic traditions, expressing diverse and sometimes conflicting ideas; his poems draw on Islamic ideas such as monotheism and iconoclasm, and he used the concepts of zikr and ishq along with the Hindu practice of Nam-simaran; he was against the caste system, critical of rituals and idol worship, and equally critical of both Hinduism and Islam; Kabir remains a source of inspiration for many people today, and the verses attributed to him use the words guru and satguru.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) ‘The Chistis became the most influential Sufi devotional tradition in the late twelfth century.’ Explain the statement.

answer.text: The Chishtis became the most influential Sufi devotional tradition in the late twelfth century: they adapted and adopted features of Indian traditions, turning to asceticism and mysticism with an emphasis on intense devotion and love for God; they organised communities around a hospice (khanqah) under a teaching master known as Shaikh, Pir or Murshid, who enrolled disciples (murids) and appointed a successor (khalifa), establishing rules for spiritual conduct between inmates as well as between laypersons and the master; Sufi silsilas represented a genealogy stretching back to the Prophet Muhammad, and the tomb-shrine (dargah) of a Sufi saint became the centre of devotion, with ziyarat (pilgrimage) to such dargahs, along with the use of music and dance - sama and qawwali - to recite the Divine Name (zikr); a cult of the Shaikh revered as a wali evolved, an open kitchen (langar) was run on charity (futuh), and day-to-day practices represented attempts to assimilate local traditions; some Sufis, known as Qalandars, Madaris and Haidaris, took to mendicancy and celibacy and were called be-shari'a, in contrast to the ba-shari'a who complied with the Sharia; the Chishtis kept their distance from worldly power even as they accepted donations in cash and kind for their daily requirements, and people believed in the saints' miraculous powers, with kings too seeking their support.

(Any four to be explained) Relations with state – they developed their own literature and practices; a major feature of the Chishti tradition was austerity, including distance from worldly power; Sufis accepted unsolicited grants and donations from political elites; Sultans set up charitable trusts, gave endowments for hospices and granted tax-free land; kings demonstrated their association with Sufis and required legitimation from them; the Delhi Sultans resisted the ulema's insistence on imposing shariat as state law; Sultans sought out Sufis who derived authority directly from God; kings often wanted their tombs near Sufi shrines and hospices; there were instances of conflict between sultans and Sufis; Sufi Shaikhs were addressed with high-sounding titles like sultan-ul-mashaikh; both sultans and Sufis expected certain rituals such as prostration and kissing of the feet. (Any four to be explained)

Distinctions are only words we invent…” 32.1 How did Kabir describe the ultimate reality ? 32.2 How does Kabir's philosophy contribute to a broader understanding of spiritualism ? 32.3 How has Kabir advocated an inclusive and compassionate view of humanity ?

questions.text: (a) Explain the main beliefs and teachings of Guru Nanak Dev.

answer.text:
Main beliefs and teachings of Guru Nanak Dev:
His message is spelt out in his hymns and teachings; he advocated a form of nirguna bhakti.
He repudiated the external practices of religions, rejecting sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims.
The Absolute or 'rab' had no gender or form.
He proposed a simple way to connect to the Divine by remembering and repeating the Divine Name, and expressed his ideas through hymns called 'shabad'.
He organised his followers into a community and set up rules for congregational worship (sangat) involving collective recitation.
He appointed one of his disciples, Angad, to succeed him as the preceptor (guru).

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) Explain the major beliefs and teachings of Chishtis during medieval India.

answer.text:
Major beliefs and teachings of the Chistis during medieval India:
The Chistis were a group of Sufis who migrated to India in the late 12th century and successfully adapted to the Indian environment and traditions.
The khanqah was the centre of their social life; Shaikh Nizamuddin appointed several spiritual successors and deputed them to set up hospices.
Pilgrimage to the tombs of Sufi saints (Ziyarat) is prevalent all over the Muslim world; most Chistis visit the tomb of Khwaja Moinuddin at Ajmer, which Sultan Ghiyasuddin Khalji and Akbar visited several times.
A part of the Ziyarat is the use of music or Qawwali at the tomb.
In the khanqah there was an open kitchen (langar), run on futuh (unasked-for charity), and people from all walks of life were welcome.
Chistis practiced bowing before the Shaikh, offering water to visitors, shaving the heads of initiates, and practicing yogic exercises.
The Sufis remembered God by reciting the zikr (the Divine Names) and evoked His Presence through sama.

answer.text:
Teachings of Guru Nanak:
He advocated a form of nirguna bhakti and rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims.
For him, the Absolute or 'rab' had no gender or form.
His ideas were expressed through hymns called 'Shabad', composed in regional language and called Gurbani; these were later compiled by Guru Arjan into the Adi Granth Sahib.
He set up rules for congregational worship (sangat) involving collective recitation, and would sing his compositions in various ragas.
He proposed a simple way to connect to the Divine by remembering and repeating the Divine Name.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (a) How has the legacy of Guru Nanak Dev's teachings influenced the principles of Sikhism ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How the legacy of Guru Nanak Dev's teachings influenced the principles of Sikhism:
Guru Nanak's message is spelt out in his hymns and teachings; he advocated a form of nirguna bhakti, rejecting external practices - sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities, and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims.
According to him, 'Rab' has no gender or form; he proposed a simple way to connect to the Divine by remembering and repeating the Divine Name (Nam simran), expressing his ideas through hymns called 'shabad' in Punjabi.
He organised his followers into a community and set up rules for congregational worship (sangat) involving collective recitation; he appointed Angad to succeed him as preceptor (guru), a practice followed for nearly 200 years.
This led to compilation of the Adi Granth Sahib - hymns/Gurbani composed by religious poets in various languages; Guru Gobind Singh included the compositions of the ninth guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and this scripture came to be called the Guru Granth Sahib.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) How do Kabir Das's poems serve as a medium for fostering a sense of unity and spirituality among the diverse communities ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
How Kabir Das's poems served as a medium for fostering unity and spirituality among diverse communities:
Kabir was a 'nirguna' poet-saint of the fourteenth-fifteenth centuries; his life can be studied through compositions attributed to him, compiled in three distinct but overlapping traditions - the Kabir Bijak, the Kabir Granthavali, and the Adi Granth Sahib. His poems survive in several languages and dialects, including the special sant bhasha of nirguna poets.
Ulatbansis (upside-down sayings) are written in a form where everyday meanings are inverted; expressions like 'the lotus which blooms without flower' or the 'fire raging in the ocean' convey his mystical experiences, capturing the nature of the Ultimate Reality in words.
Kabir drew on a range of traditions including Islam, describing the Ultimate Reality as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir, while also using terms from Vedantic traditions - alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman, Atman, etc.; diverse and sometimes conflicting ideas are expressed in his poems.
Some poems draw on Islamic monotheism and iconoclasm to attack Hindu polytheism and idol worship; he used the Sufi concepts of zikr and ishq (love) to express the Hindu practice of remembering God's name.
Kabir remains a source of inspiration for those who question religious and social institutions, ideas and practices in their search for the Divine; his ideas were crystallised through dialogue and debate with Sufi and yogi traditions in the region of Awadh.

questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Declining a royal gift” — This excerpt from a sufi text describes the proceedings at Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya's hospice in 1313 : “I (the author, Amir Hasan Sijzi) had the good fortune of kissing his (Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya's) feet … At this time a local ruler had sent him the deed of ownership to two gardens and much land, along with the provisions and tools for their maintenance. The ruler had also made it clear that he was relinquishing all his rights to both the gardens and land. The master … had not accepted that gift. Instead, he had lamented: “What have I to do with gardens and fields and lands ? … None of … our spiritual masters had engaged in such activity.” Then he told an appropriate story: “… Sultan Ghiyasuddin, who at that time was still known as Ulugh Khan, came to visit Shaikh Fariduddin (and) offered some money and ownership deeds for four villages to the Shaikh, the money being for the benefit of the dervishes (sufis), and the land for his use. Smiling, Shaikh al Islam (Fariduddin) said: ‘Give me the money. I will dispense it to the dervishes. But as for those land deeds, keep them. There are many who long for them. Give them away to such persons.’” (32.1) What did the ruler offer Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya ? (32.2) What reason did the Shaikh give for refusing the land deeds ? (32.3) How does the response of the Shaikh reflect the Sufi values ?

answer.text:
32.1: The local ruler offered Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya ownership of two gardens and land, along with provisions and tools for their maintenance, giving up his own rights to the gardens and land.
32.2: The Shaikh refused the land deeds, saying they were of no use to him/mendicants like him, that spiritual masters had never engaged in such activities, and suggesting the land instead be given to the needy.
32.3: The Shaikh's response reflects Sufi values of asceticism, detachment from material possessions, spiritualism, and generosity/compassion.

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (a) “Kabir is one of the most outstanding examples of poet-saints of Nirguna Bhakti.” Explain the statement.

answer.text:
Kabir described the ultimate Reality using terms drawn from Vedantic traditions - alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman, Atman etc.
He also described the Ultimate Reality as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir, taken from Islamic tradition.
He used mystical connotations - terms like shabda (sound) or shunya (emptiness), drawn from yogic tradition.
Some of his poems draw on Islamic ideas; they use monotheism and iconoclasm to attack Hindu polytheism and idol worship.
Some others use the Sufi concept of zikr and ishq (love) to express the Hindu practice of nam-simaran (remembrance of God's name).

questions.chapter: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts
questions.text: (b) “Alvars of the sixth century created a rich cultural legacy.” Explain the statement.

answer.text:
Alvars were devotees of Vishnu who travelled from place to place singing hymns in Tamil in praise of their gods.
During their travels the Alvars identified certain shrines as abodes of their chosen deities; large temples were later built at these sacred places, which developed as centres of pilgrimage.
Singing compositions of these poet-saints became part of temple rituals.
Alvars initiated a movement of protest against the caste system and the dominance of Brahmanas, attempting to reform the system; bhaktas hailed from diverse social backgrounds ranging from Brahmanas to artisans and cultivators, and even from castes considered 'untouchable'.
The compositions of the Alvars were considered as important as the Vedas - the Nalayira Divyaprabandham is often described as the Tamil Veda.
The presence of women was also an important part of the tradition, for instance Andal, a woman Alvar saint.

Kabir's poems have survived in several languages and dialects; some are composed in the special language of nirguna poets, the sant bhasha, and others known as ulatbansi.
He described the nature of the Ultimate Reality in words: expressions such as 'the lotus which blooms without flower' or 'the fire raging in the ocean' convey a sense of Kabir's mystical experiences.
He described the Ultimate Reality as Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir; he also used terms drawn from Vedantic traditions - alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman, Atman, etc.
Mystical connotations such as shabda (sound) or shunya (emptiness) were drawn from yogic traditions.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Explain the reasons of apogee and fall of the Vijayanagara Empire.

answer.text: Reasons for the apogee and fall of the Vijayanagara Empire: Krishnadeva Raya was a powerful ruler who expanded and consolidated the empire; he acquired the Raichur Doab and defeated the rulers of Orissa and the Sultans of Bijapur; the Amara-Nayaka system also helped consolidate the empire; in times of peace many temples and impressive gopurams were built. After the death of Krishnadeva Raya, strain began to show within the imperial structure; Nayakas or military chiefs started troubling his successors; Rama Raya became very ambitious and played one Sultan against another; the Sultans saw through his tricks and combined their forces; Rama Raya led his army against the combined Sultans in a battle where his army was routed; in this way the Sultans ruined Vijayanagara.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Explain the distinctive features of the Royal Centre of Vijayanagara Empire.

answer.text: Distinctive features of the Royal Centre of the Vijayanagara Empire (which had more than 60 temples and about 30 buildings): (a) The Mahanavami Dibba is located on the highest point, with a base of 11,000 sq. feet and 40 feet in height; Dusehra and Durga Puja were celebrated here; Vijayanagara kings displayed power and prestige here; wrestling matches and processions were held here. (b) The Hazara Rama Temple is a spectacular temple probably meant for the use of the king and his family; the images in the central shrine are missing, but sculpted panels survive on the walls depicting scenes from the Ramayana. (c) The Lotus Mahal is the most beautiful building in the Royal Centre; it may have been used as a council chamber where the king met his advisors; it was so named by British travellers in the 19th century. (d) A building called the 'Elephants' Stables' was located close to the Lotus Mahal.

questions.text: Why was Vijayanagar named as Hampi ? Select the appropriate option from the following :
options: This name was given by Krishnadeva Raya to Vijaynagar.
This name was derived by Colin Meckenzie, an antiquarian.
This name was derived from the local goddess named Pampadevi.
This name was devoted to Vithhla and Virupaksha deities.

answer.text: This name was derived from the local goddess named Pampadevi.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Analyse the features of the sacred centre of ‘Vijaynagar Empire’.

answer.text: Features of the sacred centre of the Vijayanagara Empire: it was dedicated to the principal deity Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra; the temple complex was designed as a chariot, with structures of immense scale such as gopurams (royal gateways) that often dwarfed the towers of the central shrines and signalled the temple's presence from a great distance, and it had mandapas or pavilions; chariot streets extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line, paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions where merchants set up shops. Features of the Virupaksha temple: Virupaksha, a form of Shiva, was the guardian deity of Vijayanagara, and shrines of Virupaksha and Pampadevi existed there; Vijayanagara rulers claimed to rule on behalf of Virupaksha and signed all royal orders as 'Shri Virupaksha', indicating their close link with the god; a royal visit to the temples was treated as a grand occasion; the temple was a centre of learning, and rulers granted land and resources for the maintenance of temples; sculptures of the rulers were displayed in the temples, along with raya gopurams, mandapas with carved pillars and gateways; programmes of music, dance and drama were organised, and the marriage of deities was celebrated there.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Examine the architectural and ritual features of ‘Mahanavmi Dibba’.

answer.text: Architectural features of the Mahanavami Dibba: it was a distinctive, impressive platform in the royal centre, the entire complex surrounded by high double walls with a street running between them; nearby an audience hall stood on a high platform with slots for wooden pillars at close, regular intervals and a staircase going up to a second floor (though it is not clear what the hall was used for); the Mahanavami Dibba itself was a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft, with evidence that it supported a wooden structure, and the base of the platform is covered with relief carvings. Ritual features associated with the Mahanavami Dibba: the rituals probably coincided with the day Mahanavami-Dussehra, when the kings of Vijayanagara displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty; ceremonies on this occasion included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, and the sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals; dances, wrestling matches and processions of caparisoned horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers took place; the king and his guests received ritual presentations from the chief nayakas and subordinate kings; the ceremonies were imbued with deep symbolic meaning.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) “Virupaksha Temple was significant in Vijayanagara Empire.” Substantiate the statement.

answer.text: The Virupaksha Temple was significant in the Vijayanagara Empire: the Vijayanagara kings claimed to rule on behalf of the god Virupaksha, and all royal orders were signed 'Shri Virupaksha', usually in the Kannada script; rulers also indicated their close links with the gods by using the title 'Hindu Suratrana', meaning Hindu Sultan; the temple had raya gopurams or royal gateways that often dwarfed the towers on the gateways, signalling the temple's presence from a great distance; it had mandapas or pavilions and long pillared corridors running around the shrines; the hall in front of the main shrine was built by Krishnadeva Raya to mark his accession; the halls in the temple were used for a variety of purposes — some were spaces where images of gods were placed to witness special programmes of music, dance and drama, others were used to celebrate the marriages of deities, and yet others were meant for deities to swing in.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) “The architecture of Vitthala temple was unique.” Substantiate the statement.

answer.text: The architecture of the Vitthala Temple was unique: its principal deity was Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra, and worship of the deity was part of an imperial culture; the temple complex was designed as a chariot, and its streets were paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions in which merchants set up their shops; it has several halls and a unique shrine designed as a chariot, with mandapas or pavilions and long, pillared corridors running around the shrines within the temple complex, a characteristic feature of Vijayanagara temple complexes; its chariot streets extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line; the temples were a mark of imperial authority, decorated with delicately carved pillars, and had a garbhagriha (sanctum).

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: “The very choice of the site of Vijayanagara was inspired by the existence of the shrines of Virupaksha and Pampadevi.” Justify the statement.

answer.text: The very choice of the site of Vijayanagara was inspired by the existence of the shrines of Virupaksha and Pampadevi: temple building in this region had a long history, and building temples meant associating oneself with the temple deities — Virupaksha as Lord Shiva and Pampadevi as Goddess Parvati; temples also functioned as centres of learning, and rulers gave grants for their maintenance; the temples of Virupaksha and Pampadevi were perhaps the main reason the city developed here, since from the rulers' point of view, constructing, repairing and maintaining temples were important means of winning support and recognition for their power, wealth and piety; according to local tradition, these hills sheltered the monkey kingdom of Vali and Sugriva mentioned in the Ramayana, and among these hills are found Jaina temples of the pre-Vijayanagara period; the Vijayanagara kings claimed to rule on behalf of the god Virupaksha, and all royal orders were signed 'Shri Virupaksha'.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Why was Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq greatly impressed by the fortifications of Vijayanagara empire ? Explain.

answer.text: The Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq was greatly impressed by the fortifications of the Vijayanagara Empire: he mentioned seven lines of fortification, with walls encircling not only the city but also its agricultural land and forests; the outermost wall linked the hills surrounding the city, and the massive masonry construction was slightly tapered, with no mortar or cementing agent used - the stone blocks used were wedge-shaped, while the inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble, with square or rectangular bastions projecting outwards; the fortification enclosed agricultural tracts, and between the first, second and third walls there were fields, gardens and houses, with evidence of an agricultural tract between the sacred centre and the urban core, serviced by an elaborate canal system; large granaries were located within the fortified areas as part of an elaborate strategy of protecting the agricultural belt itself.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Why was the ‘Mahanavami Dibba’ a centre of main Vijayanagara rituals ? Explain.

answer.text: The Mahanavami Dibba was the centre of the main Vijayanagara rituals: it was located on one of the highest points in the city and was a massive platform, rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft, which supported a wooden structure, with the base of the platform covered in relief carvings; the rituals associated with it coincided with the Mahanavami festival, the ninth day of the ten-day Hindu festival, during which the Vijayanagara rulers displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty; ceremonies performed on this occasion included worship of the image and of the state horse, the sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals, dances and wrestling matches, and processions of caparisoned horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers, along with ritual presentations before the king and his guests by the chief nayakas and subordinate kings.

questions.text: Which one of the following was the main factor that led to the decline of the Vijayanagara empire ?
options: Internal conflicts and alliance with the Sultanates against Vijayanagara.

questions.text: (a) Examine the main reasons for the rise and decline of the Vijaynagar empire.

answer.text: (a) Main reasons for the rise and decline of the Vijayanagara empire: Rise – there were too many claimants to power; the first dynasty, the Sangamas, exercised control till 1485; they were succeeded by the Saluvas, who ruled till 1503; they were replaced by the Tuluvas, to which Krishnadeva Raya belonged; his rule was characterised by expansion and consolidation; he acquired land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers; the rulers of Orissa were subdued and he defeated the Sultan of Bijapur; the kingdom remained in a constant state of military preparedness; the empire saw peace and prosperity during his reign; he built beautiful temples and added gopurams to many south Indian temples; he founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara called Nagalapuram. (Any four to be explained) Decline – after Krishnadeva Raya's death his successors were troubled by rebellious nayakas or military chiefs; by 1542 control shifted to the Aravidu dynasty; clashes between the rulers of Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates resulted in shifting alignments; the Sultanates formed an alliance against Vijayanagara and defeated Rama Raya at the Battle of Talikota; the city was destroyed and abandoned within a few years. (iv) The massive masonry construction was slightly tapered; no mortar or cementing agent was used. (v) Stone blocks were wedge-shaped, which held them in place. (vi) The inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble. (vii) Square or rectangular bastions projected outwards. (viii) Between the first, second and third walls there were cultivated fields, gardens and houses. (ix) Fortification was useful during sieges, allowing agriculture to continue and crops to be grown, saving people from starvation. (x) The second line of fortification went round the inner core of the urban complex, and a third line surrounded the royal centre. (xi) The fort was entered through well-guarded gates, showing the influence of Indo-Islamic architecture. (xii) Roads connected various parts of the city. (Any eight to be explained)

His successors were troubled by rebellious Nayaka (military) chiefs.
The military ambitions of the Vijayanagara rulers and the Deccan Sultanates resulted in shifting alignments.
