questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Analyse the role of Amara-nayakas in the Vijayanagara empire.

answer.text:
Role of Amara-nayakas in the Vijayanagara empire:
Amara-nayakas were military commanders given territories to govern by the Raya.
They collected taxes from peasants, craftsmen and traders, and retained part of the revenue for personal use.
They maintained stipulated contingents of horses and elephants, and provided contingents to the king as needed.
They used part of the revenue for the maintenance of temples and irrigation works.
This was a major political innovation derived from the Iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate.
They sent tribute to the king annually and personally appeared at court with gifts, though they were occasionally transferred; many later established independent kingdoms in the 17th century.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Analyse the factors that led the rulers of the Vijayanagara empire to choose the site of Vijayanagara as their capital.

answer.text:
Factors that led the rulers of the Vijayanagara empire to choose the site of Vijayanagara as their capital:
The choice of the site was inspired by the existence of the shrines of Virupaksha and Pampadevi.
Vijayanagara kings ruled on behalf of the god Virupaksha, and all royal orders were signed as 'Shri Virupaksha'.
The area was associated with several sacred traditions, e.g. Jaina temples and associations with the Ramayana.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Imagine studying the water management system of the Vijayanagara empire. How did the empire's water resources support its agriculture and urban development ? Explain.

answer.text:
The Vijayanagara empire's water management system supported its agriculture and urban development:
Vijayanagara was located in the natural basin formed by the river Tungabhadra, which flows in a north-easterly direction; embankments were built along streams to create reservoirs of varying sizes, since this was one of the most arid zones of the peninsula.
The most important such tank, the Kamalapuram tank, was built in the early 15th century; water from it irrigated nearby fields and was conducted through a channel to the royal centre.
The most prominent waterwork among the ruins is the Hiriya canal, built by the Sangama dynasty, which drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra and irrigated the cultivated valley separating the 'sacred centre' from the 'urban core'.
Domingo Paes' description of Vijayanagara mentions lakes, and field surveys indicate that wells, aqueducts, rainwater tanks and temple tanks may have served as sources of water for ordinary town dwellers.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Imagine studying Vijayanagara's trade records. What information do they reveal about the goods traded and the empire's economic connections ? Explain.

answer.text:
Vijayanagara's trade records reveal information about goods traded and the empire's economic connections:
Trade was initially controlled by Arab traders; local communities of merchants known as kudirai chettis (horse merchants) also participated in trade, and the Portuguese later arrived on the west coast and attempted to establish trading relations.
Vijayanagara was noted for its markets dealing in spices, textiles and precious stones; trade was regarded as a status symbol, and the city's wealthy population demanded high-value exotic goods, especially precious stones and jewellery.
Trade in turn contributed significantly to the prosperity of the state.
Records of travellers highlight this trade, e.g. Nicolo de Conti, the ambassador Abdur Razzaq sent by the ruler of Persia, and the merchant Afanasii Nikitin.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Imagine yourself as a historian reconstructing the events that took place on the \textit{Mahanavami Dibba}. How would the architecture of the platform help you to understand the royal ceremonies ? Explain.

answer.text:
How the architecture of the Mahanavami Dibba platform helps understand royal ceremonies at Vijayanagara:
The Mahanavami Dibba is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft, with evidence that it supported a wooden structure; its base is covered with relief carvings.
Rituals associated with the structure probably coincided with Mahanavami (the 'great ninth day') of the ten-day Hindu festival during the autumn months of September-October; on the last day the king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas, and the Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty on this occasion.
Ceremonies performed on the occasion included worship of the image and of the state horse, sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals, dances, wrestling matches, processions of caparisoned horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers, and ritual presentations before the king and his guests by chief nayakas and subordinate kings, who brought rich gifts and the stipulated tribute.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Imagine exploring the roles of the Rayas and the Nayakas in the Vijayanagara Empire. How did their administrative roles influence the empire's stability ? Explain.

answer.text:
Roles of the Rayas and the Nayakas in the Vijayanagara Empire and their influence on the empire's stability:
The rulers of Vijayanagara called themselves rayas; nayakas were appointed by the king as military chiefs, controlled forts, and had armed supporters, though they often moved from one area to another and submitted to the authority of the king.
The amara-nayaka system was a military innovation inspired by the Iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate - amara-nayakas were military commanders given territories to govern by the king, maintained contingents (providing the Vijayanagara kings an effective fighting force), and collected taxes from peasants, craftspersons and traders in the area, retaining part of the revenue for personal use and using some for maintenance of temples and irrigation works.
They sent tribute to the king annually and personally appeared at court with gifts to express loyalty, though they were occasionally transferred.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: “The Vitthala temple of Vijayanagara was known for its unique architecture.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
The Vitthala temple of Vijayanagara was known for its unique architecture:
The principal deity was Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra; worship of the deity was part of an imperial culture.
The temple has several halls and a unique shrine designed as a chariot.
Streets were paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions in which merchants set up their shops; mandapas/pavilions and long pillared corridors running around the shrines within the temple complex were a characteristic feature.
The chariot streets extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line; temples were a mark of imperial authority and were decorated with delicately carved pillars.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) The Virupaksha Temple is a historic temple located in Hampi. What features make it a key architectural and cultural landmark of the Vijayanagara Empire ? Explain.

answer.text:
The Virupaksha temple of the Vijayanagara empire was known for its unique architecture:
The temple was built over centuries; the earliest shrine dated to the ninth-tenth centuries and was substantially enlarged with the establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire.
The hall in front of the main shrine was built by Krishnadeva Raya to mark his accession, decorated with delicately carved pillars; he is also credited with the construction of the eastern gopuram.
These additions meant the central shrine came to occupy a relatively small part of the complex; the halls were used for a variety of purposes - some were spaces where images of gods were placed to witness special programmes of music, dance and drama, some were used to celebrate the marriages of deities, and others were meant for the deities to swing in, with special images (distinct from those kept in the small central shrine) used on special occasions.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) The Royal Centre in Vijayanagara was significant. Which architectural features make it an important cultural landmark ? Explain.

answer.text:
The Royal Centre in Vijayanagara was significant, with important architectural features as a cultural landmark:
The Royal Centre was located in the western part of the settlement and included over 60 temples; rulers legitimised their authority through association with the divinities housed in the shrines. Thirty building complexes were identified as palaces.
The Mahanavami Dibba was a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft, its base covered with relief carvings; the audience hall was a high platform with slots for wooden pillars at close, regular intervals, with a staircase going up to the second floor resting on these pillars.
The Lotus Mahal is considered the most beautiful building in the Royal Centre - according to Mackenzie it may have been a council chamber where the king met his advisors; it had nine towers, a high central one and eight along the sides. Elephant stables were located close to the Lotus Mahal, probably to keep elephants.
The Hazara Rama temple was used by the king and his family, its walls including scenes from the Ramayana sculpted on the inner walls of the shrine.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Describe the significance of Kamalpuram tank and Hiriya Canal as sources of water for the Vijayanagara.

answer.text:
Vijayanagara, situated in one of the most arid zones of the peninsula, required elaborate arrangements to store rainwater and conduct it to the city.
The Kamalpuram tank was built in the early years of the 15th century; water from it was used for the royal centre and also for irrigation, as it stored rain water.
The Hiriya canal was another important source of water supply; it drew water from a dam across the Tungabhadra river and was used for irrigating the cultivated valley.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Describe the views of Dominingo Paes on the city of Vijaynagara.

answer.text:
Domingo Paes saw Vijayanagara as a sprawling city spread between several ranges of hills.
It was as large as Rome and very beautiful to the sight.
There were many groves of trees within it; the houses had gardens, and there were many conduits of water which flowed into the midst of it.
In places there were lakes, and the king's palace had a palm-grove and other rich fruit-bearing trees close by.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) “Vijayanagara Kingdom flourished under conditions of unparalleled peace and prosperity during the rule of Krishandeva Raya but after his death Vijayanagara declined.” Substantiate the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Krishnadeva Raya was an able and strong ruler; his rule was characterised by expansion and consolidation - he captured the land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers (the Raichur doab) in 1512, subdued the rulers of Orissa in 1514, and inflicted severe defeats on the Sultan of Bijapur in 1520.
He is credited with building fine temples and adding impressive gopurams to many important south Indian temples, and founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara called Nagalapuram after his mother.
His descendants were not able and strong; his successors were troubled by rebellious nayakas, and by 1542 control at the centre had shifted to the Aravidu dynasty.
Rama Raya, chief minister of Vijayanagara, led the army into the battle at Rakshasi Tangadi (Talikota) in 1565 against the combined armies of the Sultans of Bijapur, Golconda and Ahmadnagar; the combined armies were victorious and sacked the city of Vijayanagara, which was totally abandoned within a few years.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) “The fortification of Vijaynagara was impressive in the medieval India.” Substantiate the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Abdur Razzaq was impressed by the fortification of the city; he mentioned seven lines of forts, which encircled agricultural tracts and forests.
It was a massive masonry construction; no mortar or cementing agent was employed anywhere - the stone blocks were wedge-shaped, which held them in place, and the inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble.
The agricultural tracts where rice was grown were irrigated by a canal drawing water from the Tungabhadra; the objective of fortifying agricultural land was to save people from starvation during medieval sieges.
The second line of fortification was round the inner core of the urban complex; the fort was entered through well-guarded gates, and roads generally wound around through the valleys, avoiding rocky terrain.

questions.text: Which of the following battles in 1565 led to the decline of the Vijayanagara empire ?

answer.text: Battle of Talikota

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) Examine the structural and ceremonial features of the Mahanavami Dibba of the Vijayanagara Empire.

answer.text:
Structural features: the entire complex is surrounded by high double walls with a street running between them; the Mahanavami Dibba is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft; there is evidence that it supported a wooden structure, and the base of the platform is covered with relief carvings.
Ceremonial features: rituals associated with the structure probably coincided with Mahanavami of the ten-day Hindu festival known variously as Dusehra (northern India), Durga Puja (Bengal) and Navaratri or Mahanavami (peninsular India); the Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty on this occasion.
Ceremonies included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, and sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals; there were dances, wrestling matches, and processions of caparisoned horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers; ritual presentations were made before the king and his guests.
The king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas in a grand ceremony in an open field, and the nayakas brought rich gifts for the king as well as the stipulated tribute.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Examine the distinctive features of the Vijayanagara fortifications that reflected the strength of the empire.

answer.text:
Abdur Razzaq, in the fifteenth century, was greatly impressed by the fortifications; he mentioned seven lines of forts, which encircled not only the city but also its agricultural hinterland and forests, with the outermost wall linking the surrounding hills.
The massive masonry construction was slightly tapered; no mortar or cementing agent was employed anywhere, the stone blocks were wedge-shaped which held them in place, and the inner portion of the walls was of earth packed with rubble; square or rectangular bastions projected outwards.
Abdur Razzaq noted cultivated fields, gardens and houses between the first, second and third walls; Paes observed rice fields, gardens and abundant water from two lakes between the first circuit and the city - statements corroborated by present-day archaeologists, who found an agricultural tract between the sacred centre and the urban core, serviced by a canal system drawing water from the Tungabhadra.
A second line of fortification went round the inner core of the urban complex, and a third line surrounded the royal centre, within which each set of major buildings was surrounded by its own high walls; the fort was entered through well-guarded gates linking the city to major roads.
Gateways were distinctive architectural features in the Indo-Islamic style; roads generally wound through the valleys avoiding rocky terrain, and some of the most important roads extended from temple gateways and were lined by bazaars.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: Which of the following regions was known as the ‘Raichur Doab’ that was captured by the Vijayanagara Empire in 1512 ?
options: The region between Narmada and Kaveri rivers
The region between Godavari and Krishna rivers

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (a) “The temple architecture of the Vijayanagara empire was distinctive and unique.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
The raya gopurams or royal gateways often dwarfed the towers on the central shrines, signalling the presence of the temple from a great distance, and were also probably meant as reminders of the power of kings able to command the resources needed to construct them.
Other distinctive features include mandapas or pavilions and long, pillared corridors that often ran around the shrines within the temple complex.
The Virupaksha temple was built over centuries: while inscriptions suggest the earliest shrine dated to the ninth-tenth centuries, it was substantially enlarged with the establishment of the Vijayanagara Empire; the hall in front of the main shrine was built by Krishnadeva Raya to mark his accession, decorated with delicately carved pillars, and he is also credited with the eastern gopuram.
The halls in the temple were used for a variety of purposes: some were spaces where images of gods were placed to witness music, dance and drama; others were used to celebrate the marriages of deities, or for deities to swing in, using special images distinct from those in the central shrine.
The Vitthala temple had Vitthala, a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra, as its principal deity, and had several halls and a unique shrine designed as a chariot.
A characteristic feature of the temple complexes is the chariot streets that extended from the temple gopuram in a straight line, paved with stone slabs and lined with pillared pavilions where merchants set up shops.
The Hazara Rama temple, one of the most spectacular, was located in the royal centre and probably meant to be used only by the king and his family; the images in the central shrine are missing, but sculpted panels survive, including scenes from the Ramayana sculpted on the inner walls.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) “The Royal Centre of Vijayanagara comprised a variety of buildings that reflected the prestige of the empire.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
The royal centre was located in the south-western part of the settlement and included over 60 temples; nearly thirty building complexes have been identified as palaces - relatively large structures not associated with ritual functions, whose superstructure (unlike temples, built entirely of masonry) was made of perishable materials.
The 'king's palace' is the largest of the enclosures but has not yielded definitive evidence of being a royal residence; it has two of the most impressive platforms, the 'audience hall' and the 'mahanavami dibba', and the entire complex is surrounded by high double walls with a street running between them.
The audience hall is a high platform with slots for wooden pillars at close, regular intervals, with a staircase leading to a second floor resting on these pillars; the pillars being closely spaced would have left little free space, so it is not clear what the hall was used for.
The mahanavami dibba is a massive platform rising from a base of about 11,000 sq. ft to a height of 40 ft, which supported a wooden structure, with its base covered in relief carvings; rituals associated with it probably coincided with Mahanavami of the ten-day Hindu festival, when the Vijayanagara kings displayed their prestige, power and suzerainty.
Ceremonies included worship of the image, worship of the state horse, sacrifice of buffaloes and other animals, dances, wrestling matches, and processions of caparisoned horses, elephants, chariots and soldiers, with ritual presentations before the king and his guests by the chief nayakas and subordinate kings; on the last day the king inspected his army and the armies of the nayakas in a grand ceremony in an open field, and the nayakas brought rich gifts and tribute.
One of the most beautiful buildings in the royal centre is the Lotus Mahal, which may have been a council chamber where the king met his advisers; the Hazara Rama temple, one of the most spectacular buildings, was also located in the royal centre and probably meant to be used only by the king and his family.

questions.chapter: An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara
questions.text: (b) Why was the Amara-Nayaka system considered a major political innovation of the Vijayanagara Empire ? Explain.

answer.text:
The Amara Nayakas were military commanders who governed territory given by the Rayas; they collected taxes and dues from peasants, craftspersons and traders.
They retained part of the revenue for personal use and for maintaining a contingent of horses and elephants; some of the revenue was used for maintaining temples and irrigation works.
They sent tribute to the king annually and personally appeared in the royal court with gifts to express their loyalty.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Cash or Kind ?” — The Ain on land revenue collection : “Let him (the amil-guzar) not make it a practice of taking only in cash but also in kind. The latter is effected in several ways. First, kankut: in the Hindi language kan signifies grain, and kut, estimates … If any doubts arise, the crops should be cut and estimated in three lots, the good, the middling, and the inferior, and the hesitation removed. Often, too, the land taken by appraisement, gives a sufficiently accurate return. Secondly, batai, also called bhaoli, the crops are reaped and stacked and divided by agreement in the presence of the parties. But in this case several intelligent inspectors are required; otherwise, the evil-minded and false are given to deception. Thirdly, khet-batai, when they divide the fields after they are sown. Fourthly, lang batai, after cutting the grain, they form it in heaps and divide it among themselves, and each takes his share home and turns it to profit.” (32.1) Explain the meaning of cash. (32.2) Explain the role of Amil-Guzar. (32.3) Explain the system of lang batai.

answer.text:
(32.1) Cash means money, i.e. metal currency in the form of Rupya/Rupee.
(32.2) The role of the Amil-Guzar was to assess the land revenue and then collect it from the peasants, either in cash or in kind.
(32.3) Under the system of lang batai, after cutting the grain the heaps were formed and divided among themselves, and each person took his share home and turned it to profit.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) How revenue from the land was the economic mainstay of the Mughal Empire ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: Revenue from the land was the economic mainstay of the Mughal Empire: the Mughal State maintained an administrative apparatus to control agricultural production and to fix and collect revenue from its rapidly expanding empire; the office of the diwan supervised the fiscal system, with revenue collectors called amil-guzar; the State first tried to acquire specific information about the extent of agricultural lands and their produce before fixing the burden of taxes; the land revenue arrangements had two stages — the Jama (amount assessed) and the Hasil (amount collected); generally one-third of the produce was collected as revenue; cultivated and cultivable lands were measured in each province and classified as good, middling and bad, and the produce of these was averaged to fix the royal dues; Akbar ordered that while amil-guzars should try to make cultivators pay in cash, the option of payment in kind was to be kept open, and methods such as kankut, batai/bhaoli and khet-batai were devised for this; the Mughal State encouraged peasants to cultivate jins-i-kamil ('perfect crops') such as cotton and sugarcane, as these brought in more revenue.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) Explain the role of village panchayats in the Mughal rural society.

answer.text: Role of village panchayats in Mughal rural society: the village panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually important people with hereditary rights over their property; in mixed-caste villages it was usually a heterogeneous, oligarchic body representing various castes and communities (though the village menial-cum-agricultural worker was unlikely to be represented), and its decisions were binding on members; the headman (muqaddam) held office as long as he enjoyed the confidence of the village elders and could be dismissed by them, his chief function being to supervise preparation of village accounts, assisted by the accountant or patwari; the panchayat derived its funds from contributions to a common financial pool, used for community welfare such as tiding over natural calamities, or for constructing a bund or digging a canal that peasants could not afford individually; an important function was to ensure caste boundaries among various communities were upheld, and panchayats had authority to levy fines and inflict punishments including expulsion from the community (usually for a limited period); in addition to the village panchayat, each caste or jati in the village had its own jati panchayat which wielded considerable power in rural society; archival records from western India, notably Rajasthan and Maharashtra, contain petitions presented to panchayats by villagers from the lowest rungs of rural society, complaining about extortionate taxation or unpaid labour (begar) imposed by superior castes or state officials.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Irrigating trees and fields” — This is an excerpt from the Babur Nama that describes the irrigation devices the emperor observed in northern India : The greater part of Hindustan country is situated on level land. Many though its towns and cultivated lands are, it nowhere has running waters ... For ... water is not at all a necessity in cultivating crops and orchards. Autumn crops grow by the downpour of the rains themselves; and strange it is that spring crops grow even when no rains fall. (However) to young trees water is made to flow by means of buckets or wheels ... In Lahore, Dipalpur (both in present-day Pakistan) and those other parts, people water by means of a wheel. They make two circles of rope long enough to suit the depths of the well, fix strips of wood between them, and on these fasten pitchers. The ropes with the wood and attached pitchers are put over the wheel-well. At one end of the wheel-axle a second wheel is fixed, and close to it another on an upright axle. The last wheel the bullock turns; its teeth catch in the teeth of the second (wheel), and thus the wheel with the pitchers is turned. A trough is set where the water empties from the pitchers and from this the water is conveyed everywhere. In Agra, Chandwar, Bayana (all in present-day Uttar Pradesh) and those parts again, people water with a bucket ... At the well-edge they set up a fork of wood, having a roller adjusted between the forks, tie a rope to a large bucket, put the rope over a roller, and tie its other end to the bullock. One person must drive the bullock, another empty the bucket. (32.1) Examine the factor that accounted for the expansion of agriculture in Mughal Period. (32.2) How did the expansion of irrigation facilities increase the participation of farmers ? (32.3) Examine the irrigation devices used in agrarian culture.

answer.text:
(32.1) The expansion of agriculture in the Mughal period was accounted for by irrigation and technology, the abundance of land, and the availability of labour along with the mobility of peasants.
(32.2) The expansion of irrigation facilities increased the participation of farmers because the Mughal State encouraged peasants to cultivate crops such as cotton and sugarcane, which were jins-i-kamil ('perfect crops') bringing in more revenue; both khud-kashta (resident) and pahi-kashta (non-resident) cultivators became involved, more varieties of crops were grown, and the use of drilling, hoeing and weeding helped farmers grow more; a continuous supply of water resulted in three crops a year, enhancing commercial production.
(32.3) Irrigation devices used in agrarian culture included a reconstructed Persian wheel; wells and tanks were the main sources of irrigation, with different devices used for lifting water from wells into field-channels; the state also undertook the digging of new canals (nahr, nala) and repaired old ones, such as the Shahnahr.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Peasants on the move” — This was a feature of agrarian society which struck a keen observer like Babur, the first Mughal emperor, forcefully enough for him to write about it in the Babur Nama, his memoirs: In Hindustan hamlets and villages, towns indeed, are depopulated and set up in a moment! If the people of a large town, one inhabited for years even, flee from it, they do it in such a way that not a sign or trace of them remains in a day and a half. On the other hand, if they fix their eyes on a place to settle, they need not dig water courses because their crops are all rain-grown, and as the population of Hindustan is unlimited it swarms in. They make a tank or a well; they need not build houses or set up walls ... khas-grass abounds, wood is unlimited, huts are made, and straightaway there is a village or a town! (32.1) What is Babur Nama ? (32.2) How did the peasants meet the needs of water ? (32.3) Explain the distinctive features of agrarian society.

answer.text:
(32.1) The Baburnama is the memoir of Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur, written in the Chagtai/Turkish language; it covers the history, geography and politics of that time.
(32.2) Peasants met the needs of water by digging tanks to collect rainwater or sinking wells to get water; they also repaired old canals, such as the Shahnahr in Punjab during Shah Jahan's reign, and irrigation projects received support from the state.
(32.3) Distinctive features of agrarian society: the peasants were highly mobile and would start cultivating land quickly; they could move and settle in new places immediately, and their crops were rainfed.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: Examine the position of Zamindars in the Mughal Village Society.

answer.text: Position of Zamindars in the Mughal countryside: zamindars were landlords who enjoyed certain social and economic privileges, with caste being one factor for their elevated status; they performed certain services (khidmat) on behalf of the State, collecting taxes from the peasants and thereby wielding considerable power; the zamindars held extensive personal lands termed milkiyat (property), cultivated for their private use often with hired labour, which they could sell or donate at will; they had control over military resources, and most zamindars had fortresses as well as an armed contingent; zamindars came from both upper castes and so-called intermediate castes, and contemporary documents suggest conquest and the dispossession of weaker people were sometimes sources of the origin and expansion of zamindaris; zamindars spearheaded the colonisation of agricultural land and helped settle cultivators, sold the produce from their milkiyat lands, and often established markets (haats) to which peasants also came to sell their produce; the relationship between zamindar and peasant had an element of reciprocity, paternalism and patronage, with zamindars often receiving the support of the peasantry in their struggles against the State and being seen as not exploitative according to the bhakti saints; they were also part of the village panchayats and helped peasants in times of distress.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: “Ain-i-Akbari is considered a major source for the agrarian history of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.” Examine the statement.

answer.text: Ain-i-Akbari as a major source for agrarian history of the 16th-17th centuries: (i) Ain-i Akbari, an important chronicle, was written by Akbar's court historian Abu'l Fazl. (ii) It gives information on measures adopted by the state to ensure cultivation. (iii) It gives information on revenue collection by state officers. (iv) It explains the relationship between the state and local zamindars. (v) It mentions terms used for peasants – raiyat or muzarian, kisan or asami. (vi) It mentions two types of peasants – khud-kashta and pahi-kashta. (vii) It mentions that agriculture expanded because of abundant land, labour and mobility of peasants. (viii) It mentions crops grown – rice, wheat or millets. (ix) Cultivation was based on the principle of individual ownership. (x) It tells us agriculture was rain-fed; artificial systems of irrigation were used and received state support. (xi) Agriculture was labour-intensive; peasants used technologies like cattle harness, wooden plough etc. (xii) There were two cycles of crops – kharif (autumn) and rabi (spring); arid terrains produced two crops a year (do-fasla), while rainfed/irrigated areas gave three crops. (xiii) The province of Agra produced 39 varieties of crops, Delhi 43 varieties, and Bengal 50 varieties of rice. (xiv) Agriculture was not just for subsistence; the state encouraged peasants to cultivate cash crops (jins-i-kamil). (xv) During the seventeenth century new crops from different parts of the world were introduced. (Any three to be explained)

answer.text:
Role of the Panchayat in advocating for the rights of common people during the Mughal era:
Panchayats were an assembly of elders and a heterogeneous body.
Decisions made by the Panchayat were binding on the members.
Funds collected as contributions from individuals were used for community welfare activities.
The Panchayat ensured that caste boundaries among the various communities were upheld, and marriages were held in the presence of the mandal/headman.
Panchayats had the authority to levy fines and could inflict more serious punishments such as expulsion.
Gram and jati panchayats settled disputes over land.
Panchayats received petitions from common people, including women, and their decisions were respected by the state.

questions.text: Describe the role of Panchayats in the Mughal era.

answer.text:
Role of Panchayats in the Mughal era:
The Panchayat was an assembly of elders, a heterogeneous body whose decisions were binding on members.
Funds collected were used for community welfare activities, and the Panchayat ensured caste boundaries among communities were maintained.
It had the authority to levy fines and inflict punishments.
It received petitions, including from women, mediated on social functions like marriage and on claims of land.
Decisions of the jati panchayat were respected by the state, and it played a role in village governance.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) Imagine if you were developing an educational programme on forest life during the Mughal era. What key aspects of the life of forest-dwellers during that time would you explain ? Substantiate.

answer.text:
Key aspects of the life of forest-dwellers during the Mughal era:
The term 'forest dwellers' described those whose livelihood came from gathering forest produce, hunting and shifting agriculture; these activities were season-specific, which perpetuated mobility.
For the state, the forest was a place of refuge for troublemakers; external forces entered the forest in different ways - the peshkash levied from forest people often included a supply of elephants, and the hunt symbolised the state's concern to ensure justice to all its subjects.
The spread of commercial agriculture was an important external factor affecting forest dwellers - forest products like honey, beeswax and gum lac were in great demand and became major items of overseas export from India; elephants were captured and sold, and trade involved barter.
The Lohanis tribe from Punjab were involved in overland trade between India and Afghanistan; tribes from the Sind region had armies with cavalry and infantry, and in Assam the Ahom kings had their paiks.
Social factors too affected forest dwellers' lives, such as the protection of springs by tribes like the Bhils.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) Imagine if you were tasked with researching the contributions of women in Mughal rural society. How would you analyse their roles in agriculture and society ? Explain.

answer.text:
Contributions of women in Mughal rural society - their roles in agriculture and society:
Women worked shoulder to shoulder with men in the fields; men tilled and ploughed, while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.
Artisanal tasks such as spinning yarn, sifting and kneading clay for pottery, and embroidery, depended heavily on female labour; women also went to the houses of employers or to markets when necessary, and were child bearers in a labour-dependent society.
Marriages in many rural communities required payment of bride-price rather than dowry to the bride's family; remarriage was considered legitimate, though women were kept under strict control by family and community.
Women sent petitions to village panchayats seeking redress and justice, including protesting against infidelity; the woman petitioner was referred to as the mother, sister or wife of the male head of the household.
Women had the right to inherit property; in Punjab, women including widows actively participated in the rural land market as sellers of inherited property, and both Hindu and Muslim women inherited zamindaris which they were free to sell or mortgage.
Women zamindars were known in 18th century Bengal - one of the biggest and most famous zamindaris, that of Rajshahi, had a woman at its helm.

Parauti - land left out of cultivation for a time so that it may recover its strength.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) “The role of women in the Mughal agrarian society was significant.” Explain the statement giving examples.

answer.text:
The role of women in Mughal agrarian society was significant:
Men and women worked shoulder to shoulder - men tilled and ploughed, while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest; the basis of production was the labour and resources of the entire household, though menstruating women were not allowed to touch the plough or the potter's wheel.
Women spun yarn, kneaded clay for pottery, and undertook tasks like embroidery that were dependent on female labour; commercialised tasks also required women's labour, and peasant and artisan women worked in the houses of their employers and went to markets.
Women were considered an important resource in agrarian society as they were child bearers; high mortality rates among women meant a shortage of wives, leading to the emergence of social customs in peasant and artisan communities distinct from those among elite groups - marriages in many rural communities required payment of bride-price, and remarriage of women was allowed, though women were kept under strict control by male family members and the community.
Women inherited zamindaris, filed petitions to panchayats, and could sell or mortgage their land; widows actively participated in the rural land market as sellers of property inherited by them.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) “The \textit{Ain-i-Akbari} is an extraordinary document of the Mughal Empire.” Explain the statement giving examples.

answer.text:
The Ain-i-Akbari is an extraordinary document of the Mughal Empire:
It was part of a larger, officially sponsored project of history writing - the culmination of a large historical, administrative project of classification undertaken by Abu'l Fazl; the Ain is a view of society from its apex, made up of five books consisting of imperial regulations.
It gives a detailed account of the organisation of the court, army and administration, and explains the sources of revenue; it lays out literary, cultural and religious traditions, and gives an elaborate description of the various provinces of the empire.
It provides fascinating glimpses into the structure and organisation of the Mughal Empire and gives quantitative information about it; Abu'l Fazl also wrote about remarkable political events, recording information about the empire and its people.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) “Panchayats played a crucial role in the Mughal rural society.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text:
The Panchayat played a crucial role in Mughal rural society:
The village panchayat was an assembly of elders, headed by a headman known as muqaddam or mandal; the decision of the panchayat was binding on the members.
The headman supervised the preparation of village accounts, assisted by the accountant or patwari; the panchayat derived its funds from a common financial pool.
The panchayat had the authority to levy fines and could inflict more serious forms of punishment such as expulsion; it ensured that caste boundaries among the various communities of the village were upheld, to prevent any offence against caste norms.
Caste and jati panchayats settled disputes over land; in Rajasthan, jati panchayats ensured that marriages were performed according to caste norms.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) “Many forest-dwelling communities maintained a significant level of political independence.” Examine the statement in the context of Mughal empire.

answer.text:
Many forest-dwelling communities maintained a significant level of political independence, in the context of the Mughal empire:
The term 'forest dwellers' described those whose livelihood came from gathering forest produce, hunting, and shifting agriculture; these activities were season-specific. For the state, the forest was a place of refuge for troublemakers, and external forces entered the forest in different ways - the peshkash levied from forest people often included a supply of elephants, and the hunt symbolised the state's concern to ensure justice to all its subjects, a theme also depicted in paintings.
The spread of commercial agriculture was an important external factor that impinged on the life of forest dwellers; the Lohani tribe from Punjab was involved in overland trade between India and Afghanistan, tribes from the Sind region had armies consisting of cavalry and infantry, the Bhils followed their own system, and the Ahoms of Assam had their paiks.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) Explain the development of agriculture during Mughal period.

answer.text:
Agriculture was being constantly expanded, based on the principle of individual ownership.
The abundance of land, availability of labour, and mobility of peasants were three factors that accounted for the constant expansion of agriculture.
Basic staple foods such as rice, wheat, barley and millets were grown; monsoons were the backbone of Indian agriculture.
Artificial systems of irrigation were used and irrigation projects received state support.
Agriculture was labour intensive but peasants did use technologies that often harnessed cattle energy; rudimentary technology like the hoe, spade and ploughshare were used.
Agriculture was organised around two major seasonal cycles, the kharif (autumn) and the rabi (spring).
The Mughal state also encouraged peasants to cultivate commercial crops such as cotton, sugarcane and oilseeds, as they brought in more revenue.
During the seventeenth century several new crops from different parts of the world reached India, such as potatoes, tomatoes, maize and chillies.
In most regions a minimum of two crops a year (do-fasla) was produced; where rainfall or irrigation assured a continuous supply of water, three crops were grown.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) Explain the role of women in the Agrarian society during 16$^{th}$ and 17$^{th}$ centuries.

answer.text:
Women were performing certain specified roles in society: men tilled and ploughed while women sowed, weeded, threshed and winnowed the harvest.
Biases related to women's biological functions did continue: menstruating women, for instance, were not allowed to touch the plough or the potter's wheel in western India, or enter the groves where betel-leaves (paan) were grown in Bengal.
Artisanal tasks such as spinning yarn, kneading clay for pottery and embroidery were done by women; women's labour was in high demand and all household work was done by women.
Women were considered an important resource in agrarian society because they were child bearers, but were kept under strict control by the male members of the family and community, and could face draconian punishments if infidelity was suspected.
Amongst the landed gentry, women had the right to inherit property; Hindu and Muslim women inherited zamindaris, which they were free to sell or mortgage.

questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Trade between the hill tribes and the plains, c. 1595” — This is how Abu'l Fazl describes the transactions between the hill tribes and the plains in the \textit{suba} of Awadh (part of present-day Uttar Pradesh) : From the northern mountains quantities of goods are carried on the backs of men, of stout ponies and of goats, such as gold, copper, lead, musk, tails of the \textit{kutas} cow (the yak), honey, \textit{chuk} (an acid composed of orange juice and lemon boiled together), pomegranate seed, ginger, long pepper, \textit{majith} (a plant producing a red dye) root, borax, zedoary (a root resembling turmeric), wax, woollen stuffs, wooden ware, hawks, falcons, black falcons, merlins (a kind of bird), and other articles. In exchange they carry back white and coloured clothes, amber, salt, asafoetida, ornaments, glass and earthen ware. (32.1) Why was trade between the mountains and plains important for the Mughal economy ? (32.2) How did the people of the plains benefit from trade with the hill tribes ? (32.3) How did Abu'l Fazl describe the variety of goods carried by the hill tribes ?

answer.text:
32.1 Trade between the mountains and the plains was important for the Mughal economy as it ensured supply of goods within the empire and supported the spread of commercial agriculture.
32.2 The people of the plains benefited from trade with the hill tribes by receiving forest products for daily use; forest items were also exported overseas.
32.3 Abu'l Fazl described goods from the northern mountains being carried on the backs of men, on the backs of stout ponies, and on the backs of goats.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (a) Examine the economic and social position of Zamindars in the rural society during the Mughal rule.

answer.text:
Zamindars were landed proprietors who also enjoyed certain social and economic privileges by virtue of their superior status in rural society; caste was one factor that accounted for their elevated status, and they performed certain services (khidmat) for the state.
Zamindars held extensive personal lands termed milkiyat, cultivated for their private use, often with hired or servile labour; they often collected revenue on behalf of the state, for which they were compensated financially.
Most zamindars had fortresses (qilachas) as well as an armed contingent of cavalry, artillery and infantry; they spearheaded the colonisation of agricultural land, helping settle cultivators by providing means of cultivation, including cash loans.
Zamindars often established markets (haats) to which peasants also came to sell their produce; their relationship with the peasantry had an element of reciprocity, paternalism and patronage, and during agrarian uprisings, zamindars often received the support of the peasantry against the state.

questions.chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
questions.text: (b) Examine the role and responsibilities of the Panchayats in village administration during the Mughal period.

answer.text:
The village panchayat was an assembly of elders with hereditary rights over their property; in mixed-caste villages it was usually a heterogeneous body, an oligarchy representing various castes and communities.
The panchayat was headed by a headman known as muqaddam or mandal, chosen through the consensus of village elders and ratified by the zamindar; his chief function was to supervise the preparation of village accounts.
The panchayat derived its funds from contributions made by individuals to a common financial pool, used for defraying costs of entertaining revenue officials and for community welfare activities such as tiding over natural calamities, construction of a bund, or digging a canal.
The panchayat ensured that caste boundaries among the various communities in the village were upheld; it also had the authority to levy fines and inflict more serious punishments like expulsion from the community.
Each jati in the village had its own jati panchayat, which wielded considerable power in rural society; villagers considered the panchayat a court of appeal.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: Read the following source and answer the questions that follow : “From the Fifth Report” — Referring to the condition of zamindars and the auction of lands, the Fifth Report stated : The revenue was not realised with punctuality, and lands to a considerable extent were periodically exposed to sale by auction. In the native year 1203, corresponding with 1796-97, the land advertised for sale comprehended a jumma or assessment of sicca rupees 28,70,061, the extent of land actually sold bore a jumma or assessment of rupees 14,18,756 and the amount of purchase money sicca rupees 17,90,416. In 1204, corresponding with 1797-98, the land advertised was for sicca rupees 26,66,191, the quantity sold was for sicca rupees 22,74,076, and the purchase money sicca rupees 21,47,580. Among the defaulters were some of the oldest families of the country. Such were the rajahs of Nuddea, Rajeshaye, Bishenpore (all districts of Bengal), ... and others, the dismemberment of whose estates at the end of each succeeding year, threatened them with poverty and ruin, and in some instances presented difficulties to the revenue officers, in their efforts to preserve undiminished the amount of public assessment. (33.1) Examine the reason for calling it as a ‘Fifth Report’. (33.2) Why were activities of East India company closely debated in England ? (33.3) Analyse any two limitations of this report.

answer.text:
(33.1) It was called the Fifth Report because it was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India.
(33.2) The activities of the East India Company were closely watched and debated in England because groups in Britain opposed the Company's monopoly over trade with India and China and wanted the Royal Charter revoked; an increasing number of private traders wanted a share in Indian trade; British industrialists were keen to open up the Indian market for British manufactures and argued that the conquest of Bengal was benefiting only the Company, not the British nation as a whole; and information about Company misrule and maladministration, including incidents of greed and corruption among Company officials, was widely and hotly debated in the British press.
(33.3) Two limitations of the Fifth Report: it ran to 1002 pages, of which over 800 were appendices reproducing petitions of zamindars and ryots, collectors' reports, statistical tables and notes on revenue and judicial administration written by officials, making it unwieldy; and, being intent on criticising the Company's maladministration, the Report exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power and overestimated the scale on which zamindars were losing their land.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “The jotedars of Dinajpur” — Buchanan described the ways in which the jotedars of Dinajpur in North Bengal resisted being disciplined by the zamindar and undermined his power : Landlords do not like this class of men, but it is evident that they are absolutely necessary, unless the landlords themselves would advance money to their necessitous tenantry ... The jotedars who cultivate large portions of lands are very refractory, and know that the zamindars have no power over them. They pay only a few rupees on account of their revenue and then fall in balance almost every kist (instalment), they hold more lands than they are entitled to by their pottahs (deeds of contract). Should the zamindar’s officers, in consequence, summon them to the cutcherry, and detain them for one or two hours with a view to reprimand them, they immediately go and complain at the Fouzdarry Thanna (police station) for imprisonment and at the munsiff’s (a judicial officer at the lower court) cutcherry for being dishonoured and whilst the causes continue unsettled, they instigate the petty ryots not to pay their revenue consequently ... (33.1) Why did jotedars resist the Zamindars of Dinajpur ? (33.2) How did Jotedars instigate the ryots ? (33.3) How did jotedars gain power in the village ?

answer.text:
(33.1) The Jotedars resisted the Zamindars of Dinajpur because they opposed the Zamindars' moves to increase the jama (revenue assessment) of a village; the Jotedars lived in the villages themselves and so were in a better position to interact with and influence the peasants.
(33.2) The Jotedars instigated the ryots by mobilising the villagers who were dependent on them, and by deliberately delaying payment of revenue to the Zamindars.
(33.3) The Jotedars gained power in the village because they lived in the villages only and so were in a better position to interact with and influence the peasants; they were rich and owned large areas of land under cultivation; they deliberately delayed revenue payments to the Zamindars, and when the Zamindars' estates were auctioned off for failure to pay revenue, the Jotedars often bought up these estates themselves — this made the Jotedars the most powerful figures in the village.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: (a) Examine how jotedars became a powerful figure in rural areas of Bengal during the end of the 18$^{th}$ century.

answer.text: Jotedars became powerful figures in rural areas of Bengal towards the end of the 18th century: they had acquired vast areas of land and controlled local trade as well as money lending; in the villages the power of jotedars was more effective than that of the zamindars, since they lived in the villages and had direct control over the villagers; they deliberately delayed payment of rent to the zamindars, and as a result many zamindaris were auctioned, with jotedars themselves among the purchasers; they were most powerful in North Bengal, where in some places they were known as haoladars, gantidars or mandals.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: (b) Examine the causes for the failure of zamindars to pay the revenue demand during the last decades of the 18$^{th}$ century.

answer.text: Causes for the failure of zamindars to pay the revenue demand during the last decades of the 18th century: zamindars often defaulted on making revenue payments because the initial revenue demands were set very high; the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually — under the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari was auctioned; to minimise its own loss the Company pegged the revenue demand high, and high rates of revenue were imposed even as prices were depressed due to natural calamities, so zamindars could not collect rent from the ryots; the Permanent Settlement also delimited the power of the zamindars, who lost their power to organise local justice; company officers were often harsh at the time of revenue collection, and ryots at times deliberately delayed payment.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: Read the following source and answer the questions that follows : “A newspaper report” — The following report, titled ‘The ryot and the moneylender’, appeared in the Native Opinion (6 June, 1876), and was quoted in Report of the Native Newspapers of Bombay : They (the ryots) first place spies on the boundaries of their villages to see if any Government officers come, and to give timely intimation of their arrival to the offenders. They then assemble in a body and go to the houses of their creditors, and demand from them a surrender of their bonds and other documents, and threaten them in case of refusal with assault and plunder. If any Government officer happens to approach the villages where the above is taking place, the spies give intimation to the offenders and the latter disperse in time. (33.1) What does the given report of newspaper show about the Deccan Countryside ? (33.2) Examine the causes of revolt by the ryots against moneylender. (33.3) Examine the ways through which ryots spied the British.

answer.text:
(33.1) The newspaper report shows that in the Deccan countryside the ryot was exploited by the British, that there was conflict and distrust between the ryots and the sahukars/moneylenders and zamindars, that the ryot was unhappy with the moneylenders and found innovative ways to avoid paying their dues, and that the Deccan ryots were apprehensive about the arrival of government officials, maintaining a good spy network posted at the boundaries of their villages to give timely warning.
(33.2) The ryots revolted against the moneylenders because the moneylenders charged a high rate of interest and extracted dues, controlled the crop cultivation of the ryots, subjected them to oppression, suppression and inhuman treatment, used inflexible methods of tax collection, and threatened to take away the ryots' lands, causing them injustice and suffering.
(33.3) The ryots spied on the British by placing spies on the boundaries of their villages, who gave timely intimation of the arrival of government officers to the offenders so that if any government officer approached the village while illegal activity was taking place, the spies would alert them and they would disperse in time and seize any incriminating records.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: (a) Imagine you are leading a historical research team. How would you explain the role of Ryotwari System in fostering rural indebtness and its long-term consequences on Bombay-Deccan peasantry ? Explain.

answer.text:
Role of the Ryotwari System in fostering rural indebtedness and its long-term consequences on the Bombay-Deccan peasantry:
The Ryotwari settlement was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in the 1820s, with revenue directly settled with the ryot.
Land was resurveyed every 30 years and revenue rates increased; the revenue demand was no longer permanent, and due to high revenue rates peasants deserted their villages.
In case of failure of payment, a fine was imposed on the whole village.
The fall in prices of agricultural products after 1832 was severe, leading to a decline in peasants' income; moneylenders played a growing role as unpaid revenue balances mounted.
The revenue system was rigid, and the peasant economy was on the verge of collapse.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: (b) You are asked to prepare a report on how the end of the American Civil War affected the cotton boom in the Indian Deccan. How would you assess the changes ? Explain.

answer.text:
How the end of the American Civil War affected the cotton boom in the Indian Deccan:
When the American Civil War broke out, a wave of panic spread in cotton circles as it affected the supply of cotton to cotton mills in England; frantic messages were sent to India to increase the area under cotton.
Ryots in the Deccan were given credit for growing more cotton, and Shahukars were willing to extend long-term loans; these boom years brought prosperity, and acreage under cotton doubled.
Only rich peasants earned well, while marginal peasants ended up in indebtedness.
As the civil war ended in America, Indian cotton exports to Britain declined; credit dried up for peasants resulting in debt burden, as export merchants and Shahukars were no longer keen on extending long-term credit.
While credit dried up, revenue demand increased, and the ryots were pushed into poverty and indebtedness.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: Analyse the impact of the Ryotwari system on the ryots of Bombay.

answer.text:
Impact of the Ryotwari system on the ryots of Bombay:
The revenue system introduced in the Bombay Deccan in 1820 came to be known as ryotwari; it provided individual ownership and attempted to reduce exploitation by intermediaries, improving revenue collection.
However, the fixed revenue demand often led to financial burdens on cultivators, especially during drought or crop failure; assessment sometimes resulted in overvaluation, causing economic distress.
Revenue was not permanent and was resurveyed every 30 years with increased rates; where demand was too high, peasants deserted their villages.
Prices of agricultural products fell sharply after 1832 and did not recover for over a decade and a half, causing a further decline in peasants' income.
Revenue could rarely be paid without a loan from a moneylender; as debt mounted and loans remained unpaid, peasants' dependence on moneylenders increased, and they needed loans even for everyday needs and production expenditure.
Fines were imposed on the whole village if payment defaulted, though this was later moderated to encourage the peasants.

questions.text: Analyse the main objectives of the British government in implementing the Permanent Settlement in Bengal ?

answer.text:
Main objectives of the British government in implementing the Permanent Settlement in Bengal:
The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793; the East India Company fixed the revenue each zamindar had to pay, and the estates of those who failed to pay were to be auctioned to recover the revenue.
By the 1770s the rural economy in Bengal was in crisis, and officials felt that resources of the state could be developed by encouraging investment in agriculture; this could be done by securing rights of property and permanently fixing the rates of revenue demand.
The objectives were to ensure a regular flow of revenue for the Company, enhance agricultural output, enhance the profit of farmers since the state would not increase revenue, and create a class of loyal farmers and rich landowners.

answer.text:
Three features of the Ryotwari system:
It was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in 1820, with rent directly settled with the ryot.
The fertility of the soil was estimated and the revenue-paying capacity of the ryot was assessed, with a proportion of revenue fixed as the state's share.
Land was to be resurveyed after 30 years and reassessed; the revenue demand was not permanent, and it was often high - in case of failure of payment, a fine was imposed on the whole village and peasants' crops could be seized, leading many to desert their villages.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: Critically examine the varied aspects of the Fifth Report of 1813.

answer.text:
The Fifth Report, a fifth in the series of reports, was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813.
It highlighted the administration and activities of the East India Company in India; the Fifth Report had 1002 pages, of which over 800 pages were appendices.
It reproduced petitions of zamindars and ryots, reports of collectors from different districts, statistical tables on revenue returns, and notes on the revenue and judicial administration of Bengal and Madras.
Many groups in Britain opposed the monopoly of the East India Company over trade with India and China, and wanted revocation of the Royal Charter that gave the Company this monopoly.
Information about Company misrule and maladministration was hotly debated in Britain, and incidents of greed and corruption of Company officials were widely publicised in the press.
The British Parliament passed a series of Acts to regulate and control Company rule in India; it forced the Company to produce regular reports on the administration of India, and a number of committees were appointed to enquire into its affairs.
The Fifth Report was one such report, produced by a Select Committee, and became the basis of intense parliamentary debates on the nature of the East India Company's rule in India.
The Fifth Report helps us understand the situation in rural Bengal, and the evidence contained in it is invaluable, but official reports like this have to be read carefully - we need to know who wrote the reports and why they were written.
Recent research shows that the arguments and evidence offered by the Fifth Report cannot be accepted uncritically; it exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power and overestimated the scale on which zamindars were losing their land.

questions.chapter: Colonialism and the Countryside: Exploring Official Archives
questions.text: How did the British exploit the Paharias of Rajmahal hills during the 18$^{th}$ century ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
As settled agriculture expanded, the area under forests and pastures contracted, sharpening the conflict between hill folk and settled cultivators.
In the 1770s the British embarked on a brutal policy of extermination, hunting the Paharias down and killing them; by the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed a policy of pacification.
Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for the proper conduct of their men, expected to maintain order in their localities; many Paharia chiefs refused the allowances, and those who accepted mostly lost authority within the community, being perceived as subordinate employees or stipendiary chiefs of the colonial government.
As the pacification campaigns continued, the Paharias withdrew deep into the mountains, insulating themselves from hostile forces; every white man appeared to represent a power destroying their way of life and snatching away control over their forests and lands.
The colonial government encouraged Santhals to settle in the lower hills, which led the Paharias to recede deeper into the drier, rocky and barren terrain.

The revenue system introduced in the Bombay Deccan, known as the Ryotwari Settlement, was directly settled with the ryot and fixed without any consideration.
The revenue demand was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions; when rains failed, peasants found it impossible to pay the revenue.
Revenue could rarely be paid without a loan from a moneylender, increasing dependence on moneylenders; when someone failed to pay, his crops were seized and a fine was imposed on the whole village.

questions.text: How did the rebels of 1857 give emphasis on the vision of unity ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: The rebels of 1857 gave emphasis to the vision of unity: this vision was clearly visible in the proclamations and ishtahars, for example the Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857; the rebels tried to get the support of all sections of society irrespective of caste and creed, and presented memories of the pre-British Hindu-Muslim past; the proclamation issued by Bahadur Shah appealed to people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir; rebels declared that British policies had dispossessed landlords, peasants, weavers, artisans and Indian sepoys alike, and proclaimed rejection of everything associated with British rule; the proclamations expressed the widespread fear that the British were destroying their religion by converting people to Christianity; they condemned the British for the annexations and broken treaties, and wanted to restore the previous secure way of life.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: How did the British control the powers of Taluqdars in the 1850’s ? Explain.

answer.text: The British controlled the powers of Taluqdars in the 1850s: the taluqdars were disarmed and their forts destroyed; the British introduced a new revenue system known as the Summary Settlement in 1856, under which land was taken from the taluqdars because the British blamed them for having acquired the land by force and fraud; through this settlement the British claimed they would settle the land income directly with the owners of the land and reduce their exploitation, while also aiming to increase revenue returns to the State; but in actual practice this did not happen — although revenues increased, the burden on the peasants did not reduce, and officials soon found that revenue rates had increased from 30 to 70 percent, with large areas of Awadh heavily over-assessed.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: How did the Britishers suppress the Revolt of 1857 ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: The British suppressed the Revolt of 1857: they passed a series of laws to help quell the insurgency, and North India was put under martial law; military officers and the British were given the power to try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion, and the ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended; reinforcements were brought in from Britain, and the British mounted a two-pronged attack — one force moved from Calcutta into North India and the other from Punjab to reconquer Delhi; the British used military power on a gigantic scale, and tried to break up unity by promising to give back to big landholders their estates.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (a) ‘The Rebel proclamations of 1857 appealed to all the sections of the population for Unity.’ Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: The rebel proclamations of 1857 appealed to all sections of the population for unity irrespective of caste and creed: this vision of unity was clearly visible in the proclamations and ishtahars, with Muslim princes taking care to address the sentiments of Hindus, as the rebellion was seen as a war in which both Hindus and Muslims had equally to lose or gain; the ishtahars reminded people of Mughal times when different communities had coexisted and lived in peace - for example, the Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857 appealed to people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir, called upon the wealthy to stake their lives and property for the well-being of the public, and assured poor people who joined the common cause of their daily subsistence; rebels declared that British policies had dispossessed landlords, peasants, weavers, artisans and Indian sepoys alike, and rejected everything associated with British rule; there was widespread fear that the British wanted to destroy the religion of both Hindus and Muslims, as with the rifle cartridges, and the British were condemned for the annexations and broken treaties they had carried out; people were urged to come together and fight to save their livelihood, faith, honour and identity, and the Azamgarh Proclamation appealed to all sections of people to rise against British rule - British efforts to create divisions, for instance in Bareilly, failed.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (b) “Art and Literature as much as the writing of history have helped in keeping alive the memory of 1857.” Explain the statement in reference to Rani Lakshmibai.

answer.text: Art and literature, as much as the writing of history, have helped keep alive the memory of 1857 with reference to Rani Lakshmibai: the Rani of Jhansi was presented as a heroic figure leading the country into battle, rousing people to righteous indignation against oppressive imperial rule; heroic poems were written about the valour of the queen, showing her with a sword in one hand and the reins of her horse in the other, fighting for the freedom of her motherland; she was represented as a masculine figure chasing the enemy, shown slaying British soldiers and fighting valiantly till her last; Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem 'Khoob ladi mardani woh to Jhansi wali Rani thi' is dedicated to her, and children in India have grown up reading these lines; in popular prints, Rani Lakshmi Bai is seen as a symbol of the determination to resist injustice and alien rule, and such depictions continue to instil patriotism and respect towards national leaders, with the heroes of the revolt being portrayed as godlike figures.

(ii) Proclamations issued under the name of Bahadur Shah appealed to the people to join the standards of Mahavir and Muhammad. (iii) In Barailley the British incited the Hindus and Muslims, the attempt failed. (iv) According to the Azamgarh Proclamation, 25th August 1857, both Hindus and Muslims were being ruined under tyranny and oppression. (v) Many social groups joined the revolt and appealed for the unity of the country. (Any three to be assessed)

The chief has bidden adieu to his country and gone abroad.” (33.1) What was the immediate impact of the removal of the Nawab ? questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (a) How did the rumours play a role in moving the people to revolt against the British during 1857 ? Explain.

answer.text: (a) How rumours played a role in moving people to revolt against the British during 1857: (i) It was rumoured that cartridges were greased with pig or cow fat, which would corrupt their caste and religion. (ii) Rumours spread fast and at Meerut, sepoys moved to revolt. (iii) Rumours circulated that the British had put cow and pig bone dust in flour sold in the market; sepoys and townspeople refused to touch the atta. (iv) Chapatis were circulated in several communities throughout North India. (v) Fears and suspicions abounded that the British were attempting to convert Indians to Christianity. (vi) The prophecy that British control would end on the anniversary of the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1857) bolstered the response. (vii) It was believed the British Government had hatched a gigantic conspiracy to destroy the caste and religion of Hindus and Muslims. (Any three to be explained)

questions.text: (b) Why were the British so keen to acquire Awadh ? Explain.

answer.text: (b) Why the British were keen to acquire Awadh: (i) Awadh was a fertile land, rich in agricultural productivity. (ii) The soil was good for producing indigo and cotton. (iii) Awadh was coming up as a principal market in Upper India. (iv) Awadh was the heart of North India. (v) Control of Awadh could pave the way for further British success. (vi) Young men of Awadh could be taken as army personnel. (vii) So the British were keen to annex/acquire Awadh. (Any three to be explained)

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (a) Under what circumstances did Bahadur Shah Zafar bless the rebellion of 1857 ? Explain.

answer.text: (a) Circumstances under which Bahadur Shah Zafar blessed the rebellion of 1857: (i) Sepoys arrived at the Red Fort on the morning of 11 May. (ii) They told him they had come from Meerut after killing all the Englishmen there. (iii) The English were forcing them to use greased cartridges. (iv) The faith of Hindus and Muslims was being corrupted. (v) Another group of sepoys entered Delhi, and ordinary people of the city joined them. (vi) Some sepoys entered the Red Fort, ignoring court etiquette. (vii) They demanded that the emperor give them his blessings. (viii) The emperor was old and weak, and feared the crowd that entered the fort. (ix) Initially he was unwilling to support the sepoys. (x) Surrounded by the sepoys, Bahadur Shah had no option but to accept leadership of the revolt. (xi) The revolt became legitimate as it could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor. (Any three to be explained)

(iii) British records, which reveal the minds of officials. (iv) Charles Ball noted that panchayats were held at night. (v) Arzis/petitions/applications of rebel sepoys. (vi) Visual representations, both British and Indian. (vii) Films and posters. (viii) Art and literature, e.g. the poem by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan, 'Khoob ladi mardani...'. (ix) Regional records. (Any three to be explained)
