questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah” — Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was one of the many maulvis who played an important part in the revolt of 1857. Educated in Hyderabad, he became a preacher when young. In 1856, he was seen moving from village to village preaching jehad (religious war) against the British and urging people to rebel. He moved in a palanquin, with drumbeaters in front and followers at the rear. He was therefore popularly called Danka Shah – the maulvi with the drum (danka). British officials panicked as thousands began following the maulvi and many Muslims began seeing him as an inspired prophet. When he reached Lucknow in 1856, he was stopped by the police from preaching in the city. Subsequently, in 1857, he was jailed in Faizabad. When released, he was elected by the mutinous 22nd Native Infantry as their leader. He fought in the famous Battle of Chinhat in which the British forces under Henry Lawrence were defeated. He came to be known for his courage and power. Many people in fact believed that he was invincible, had magical powers, and could not be killed by the British. It was this belief that partly formed the basis of his authority. (33.1) Why was Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah called 'Danka Shah' ? (1) (33.2) How did British officials react to Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah's growing influence ? (1) (33.3) To what extent did Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah's action reflect the resistance against British rule in India ? (2)

answer.text:
33.1: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was called 'Danka Shah' because he moved in a palanquin with drumbeaters (danka) in front and followers at the rear.
33.2: British officials reacted to his growing influence with panic, as thousands began following him and many Muslims began seeing him as an inspired prophet; when he reached Lucknow in 1856, the police stopped him from preaching in the city.
33.3: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah's actions reflected resistance against British rule - in the Battle of Chinhat he defeated British forces under Henry Lawrence; he became known for his courage and power, with many believing he was invincible and had magical powers that could not be killed by the British, a belief that partly formed the basis of his authority and had a psychological influence over the British.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Two rebels of 1857 — Shah Mal” — Shah Mal lived in a large village in pargana Barout in Uttar Pradesh. He belonged to a clan of Jat cultivators whose kinship ties extended over \textit{chaurasee des} (eighty-four villages). The lands in the region were irrigated and fertile, with rich dark loam soil. Many of the villagers were prosperous and saw the British land revenue system as oppressive: the revenue demand was high and its collection inflexible. Consequently cultivators were losing land to outsiders, to traders and moneylenders who were coming into the area. Shah Mal mobilised the headmen and cultivators of \textit{chaurasee des}, moving at night from village to village, urging people to rebel against the British. As in many other places, the revolt against the British turned into a general rebellion against all signs of oppression and injustice. Cultivators left their fields and plundered the houses of moneylenders and traders. Displaced proprietors took possession of the lands they had lost. Shah Mal's men attacked government buildings, destroyed the bridge over the river, and dug up metalled roads – partly to prevent government forces from coming into the area, and partly because bridges and roads were seen as symbols of British rule. They sent supplies to the sepoys who had mutinied in Delhi and stopped all official communication between British headquarters and Meerut. Locally acknowledged as the Raja, Shah Mal took over the bungalow of an English officer, turned it into a “hall of justice”, settling disputes and dispensing judgments. He also set up an amazingly effective network of intelligence. For a period the people of the area felt that \textit{firangi raj} was over, and their \textit{raj} had come. Shah Mal was killed in battle in July 1857. (33.1) How did Shah Mal's leadership contribute to the spread of the rebellion ? (33.2) How did the rebellion led by Shah Mal challenge the authority of the British ? (33.3) How does Shah Mal's establishment of a “hall of justice” reflect his vision of governance ?

answer.text:
33.1: Shah Mal's leadership contributed to the spread of the rebellion through communication and inspiration to rebels - he mobilised the headmen and cultivators of the chaurasee des, moving at night from village to village urging people to rebel against the British.
33.2: The rebellion led by Shah Mal challenged British authority by attacking symbols of power and government buildings, destroying the bridge over the river, digging up metalled roads, sending supplies to the sepoys who had mutinied in Delhi, and stopping official communication between British headquarters and Meerut.
33.3: Shah Mal's establishment of a 'hall of justice' - by taking over the bungalow of an English officer and using it for settling disputes and dispensing judgments - reflected his vision of governance; he also set up an effective network of intelligence against British exploitation.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “What \textit{taluqdars} thought” — The attitude of the \textit{taluqdars} was best expressed by Hanwant Singh, the Raja of Kalakankar, near Rae Bareli. During the mutiny, Hanwant Singh had given shelter to a British officer, and conveyed him to safety. While taking leave of the officer, Hanwant Singh told him: “Sahib, your countrymen came into this country and drove out our King. You sent your officers round the districts to examine the titles to the estates. At one blow you took from me lands which from time immemorial had been in my family. I submitted. Suddenly misfortune fell upon you. The people of the land rose against you. You came to me whom you had despoiled. I have saved you. But now – now I march at the head of my retainers to Lucknow to try and drive you from the country.” (33.1) How did Hanwant Singh express his dissatisfaction towards the British ? (33.2) Who did Hanwant Singh refer to as “the people of the land” ? (33.3) How did Hanwant Singh's statement reflect the sentiments of the taluqdars ?

answer.text:
33.1: Hanwant Singh expressed dissatisfaction towards the British by stating that the British had driven out their king, taken away their land, and sent officers to examine the titles (to land).
33.2: Hanwant Singh referred to 'the people of the land' as the local population/natives of the region.
33.3: Hanwant Singh's statement reflected the sentiments of the taluqdars, who felt dispossessed of the region - they were disarmed and their forts destroyed, their position and authority undermined, and they lost a number of villages they had previously held, leading to a breakdown of the entire social order as ties of loyalty and patronage were disrupted.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the following questions : “What taluqdars thought” — The attitude of the \textit{taluqdars} was best expressed by Hanwant Singh, the Raja of Kalakankar, near Rae Bareli. During the mutiny, Hanwant Singh had given shelter to a British officer, and conveyed him to safety. While taking leave of the officer, Hanwant Singh told him : Sahib, your countrymen came into this country. You sent your officers round the districts to examine the titles to the estates. At one blow you took from me lands which from time immemorial had been in my family. I submitted. Suddenly misfortune fell upon you. The people of the land rose against you. You came to me whom you had despoiled. I have saved you. But now – now I march at the head of my retainers to Lucknow to try and drive you from the country. (33.1) Explain the anguish of Hanwant Singh for the British officer. (33.2) How were Taluqdars facilitated by the rulers ? (33.3) Explain any two causes of dissatisfaction of Taluqdars from British rule.

answer.text:
33.1 Hanwant Singh expressed anguish for the British officer because the British had subdued the Indians by taking away their land and driving away their king; the people of the land had risen against the British; Hanwant Singh, like a true Indian, had given shelter to the British officer and conveyed him to safety, but expressed his anguish that he would now have to lead his retainers to drive the British away.
33.2 The Taluqdars were facilitated by the rulers as they had been given control and power over land, maintained armed retainers, built forts, and enjoyed a degree of autonomy.
33.3 Causes of dissatisfaction of the Taluqdars from British rule: the British land revenue policy undermined the position and authority of the taluqdars; the British removed the taluqdars from their lands wherever possible; the taluqdars lost more than half of the total number of villages they had previously held.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (a) Explain the events that took place on the very first day (10$^{th}$ May) of the rebellion of 1857 at Meerut.

answer.text:
On 10th May 1857, the sepoys in the Meerut cantonment revolted.
The common men of the town and villages joined them.
The sepoys captured the bell of arms and ammunition.
They ransacked and burnt bungalows and other Government property.
They attacked the record office, jail, court, post office and treasury etc.
The telegraph line to Delhi was cut.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: (b) Explain the events that took place on 11$^{th}$ May of the rebellion of 1857 at Red Fort of Delhi.

answer.text:
On 11th May, early in the morning, a group of sepoys reached the Red Fort and gathered around the emperor.
They did not care for court etiquettes.
They told the emperor that they had killed a large number of Europeans.
They demanded that the emperor bless them for the struggle.
The emperor had no option but to comply.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: How did Indian art and literature depict the Revolt of 1857 as the First War of Independence ? Explain.

answer.text:
Art and literature have helped keep alive the memory of 1857.
The leaders of the revolt were presented as heroic figures leading the country into battle.
Heroic poems were written about Rani Laxmibai; the Rani of Jhansi was represented as a masculine figure.
Children in many parts of India grow up reading the lines of Subhadra Kumari Chauhan: 'Khoob lari mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi'.
In popular prints Rani Lakshmi Bai is portrayed in battle armour, with a sword in hand and riding a horse - a symbol of the determination to resist injustice and alien rule.
The images indicate how the painters who produced them perceived those events, what they felt, and what they sought to convey.
Through the paintings and cartoons we know about the public that looked at the paintings, appreciated or criticised the images, and bought copies and reproductions to put up in their homes.
These images reflected the emotions and feelings of the people; they shaped sensibilities, and nationalist imageries of the revolt shaped the nationalist imagination.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “What the sepoys thought” — This is one of the \textit{arzis} (petition or application) of rebel sepoys that have survived : A century ago the British arrived in Hindostan and gradually entertained troops in their service, and became masters of every state. Our forefathers have always served them, and we also entered their service … By the mercy of God and with our assistance the British also conquered every place they liked, in which thousands of us, Hindostani men were sacrificed, but we never made any excuses or pretences nor revolted … But in the year eighteen fifty seven the British issued an order that new cartridges and muskets which had arrived from England were to be issued; in the former of which the fats of cows and pigs were mixed; and also that \textit{attah} of wheat mixed with powdered bones was to be eaten; and even distributed them in every Regiment of infantry, cavalry and artillery … They gave these cartridges to the \textit{sowars} (mounted soldiers) of the 3$^{rd}$ Light Cavalry, and ordered them to bite them; the troopers objected to it, and said that they would never bite them, for if they did, their religion and faith would be destroyed … upon this the British officers paraded the men of the 3 Regiments and having prepared 1,400 English soldiers, and other Battalions of European troops and Horse Artillery, surrounded them, and placing six guns before each of the infantry regiments, loaded the guns with grape and made 84 new troopers prisoners, and put them in jail with irons on them … The reason that the \textit{sowars} of the Cantonment were put into jail was that we should be frightened into biting the new cartridges. On this account we and all our country-men having united together, have fought the British for the preservation of our faith … we have been compelled to make war for two years and the Rajahs and Chiefs who are with us in faith and religion, are still so, and have undergone all sorts of trouble; we have fought for two years in order that our faith and religion may not be polluted. If the religion of a Hindoo or Mussalman is lost, what remains in the world ? (33.1) How did the sepoys justify their rebellion in the ‘arzi’ ? (33.2) How did the British introduce the new cartridges ? (33.3) Why did the sepoys and Indian chiefs work together ?

answer.text:
33.1 In the 'arzi', sepoys justified their rebellion by saying they wanted to preserve their religion and faith.
33.2 In 1857 the British issued an order that new cartridges and muskets, which had arrived from England, were to be issued; the cartridges were made of the fats of cows and pigs, and were given to the sowars (mounted soldiers) of the 3rd Light Cavalry, who were ordered to bite them.
33.3 The sepoys and Indian chiefs worked together because they had a common enemy in the British colonial government, believed unity gives strength, and wanted to protect their religion and faith.

questions.chapter: Rebels and the Raj: 1857 Revolt and its Representations
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “The Revolt of 1857” — Late in the afternoon of 10 May 1857, the sepoys in the cantonment of Meerut broke out in mutiny. It began in the lines of the native infantry, spread very swiftly to the cavalry and then to the city. The ordinary people of the town and surrounding villages joined the sepoys. The sepoys captured the bell of arms where the arms and ammunition were kept and proceeded to attack white people, and to ransack and burn their bungalows and property. Government buildings — the record office, jail, court, post office, treasury, etc. — were destroyed and plundered. The telegraph line to Delhi was cut. As darkness descended, a group of sepoys rode off towards Delhi. The sepoys arrived at the gates of the Red Fort early in the morning on 11 May. It was the month of Ramzan, the Muslim holy month of prayer and fasting. The old Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah, had just finished his prayers and meal before the sun rose and the fast began. He heard the commotion at the gates. The sepoys who had gathered under his window told him: “We have come from Meerut after killing all the Englishmen there, because they asked us to bite bullets that were coated with the fat of cows and pigs with our teeth. This has corrupted the faith of Hindus and Muslims alike.” Another group of sepoys also entered Delhi, and the ordinary people of the city joined them. Europeans were killed in large numbers; the rich of Delhi were attacked and looted. It was clear that Delhi had gone out of British control. Some sepoys rode into the Red Fort, without observing the elaborate court etiquette expected of them. They demanded that the emperor give them his blessings. Surrounded by the sepoys, Bahadur Shah had no other option but to comply. The revolt thus acquired a kind of legitimacy because it could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor. (33.1) Why was Bahadur Shah's involvement important for the rebels ? (33.2) How did the actions of the rebels in Delhi indicate a breakdown of British control ? (33.3) How did the sepoys and religious sentiments play an important role in this uprising ? Explain.

answer.text:
33.1 Bahadur Shah's involvement was important for the rebels because he was a Mughal emperor and political legitimacy was important; the revolt could now be carried on in the name of the Mughal emperor.
33.2 The actions of the rebels in Delhi indicated a breakdown of British control: Britishers were killed and rebels entered the Red Fort, Europeans were killed in large numbers, and the rich of Delhi were attacked and looted.
33.3 Bullets coated with cow and pig fat caused unrest among the sepoys; Hindus and Muslims felt offended as their religious sentiments were badly hurt, since the sepoys were asked to bite bullets coated with the fat of cows and pigs with their teeth, which corrupted the faith of Hindus and Muslims alike.

chapters.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Examine the reasons and outcomes of the Salt Satyagraha.

answer.text: Reasons for the Salt Satyagraha: the salt law was one of the most disliked laws in British India; salt manufacturing was a State monopoly; every household needed salt, yet people were forbidden from making it themselves and were compelled to buy it from shops at a high price; this state monopoly over salt was deeply unpopular, and because of the wide discontentment against British rule the Salt Satyagraha was launched. Outcomes: salt manufacture was allowed along the coast; Gandhi's name came to world attention as the march was widely covered by the European and American press; it was a national activity that shook British rule and showed that British rule was not going to last long.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) Examine the causes and events of Quit India Movement.

answer.text: Causes of the Quit India Movement: refusal of the proposal of Independence after the Second World War; in the meeting of Congress with Lord Linlithgow the nature of India's involvement in the war was discussed, but negotiations with the Viceroy broke down and the Congress Ministries resigned; the failure of the Cripps Mission; the political landscape became complicated as it turned into a three-way struggle between the Congress, the Muslim League and the British; there was unrest among the masses due to the Second World War. Events: it was, in fact, a mass movement; even common people rose in revolt against British rule, and it energised the youth in large numbers; in 1945 a Labour government came to power in Britain and was committed to freeing India; Gandhi urged people to follow the mantra of 'Do or Die'; the British arrested thousands of people and put them in jail, and civil rights and freedom of speech were suppressed; the British eventually realised that they had to leave India for good.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) How did ‘Salt Satyagraha’ of Gandhiji become the All-India campaign in opposition to the British ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: The Salt Satyagraha became an all-India campaign in opposition to the British: in 1930 Mahatma Gandhi announced he would lead a march to break one of the most unpopular laws in British India, which gave the State a monopoly over the manufacture and sale of salt; it was Gandhiji's tactical wisdom, since salt was used in every household yet people were forbidden from making it even for domestic use, and were compelled to buy it from shops at a high price — by making the Salt Law his target, Gandhiji mobilised wider discontent against British rule; on 12 March 1930 Gandhiji started his march from Sabarmati and reached Dandi three weeks later, giving speeches at villages en route calling on local officials to leave government jobs and join the freedom struggle, and appealing for the abolition of untouchability and the union of Hindus, Muslims, Parsees and Sikhs for real Swaraj; parallel salt marches were conducted in other parts of the country; across large parts of India peasants breached forest laws, factory workers went on strike, lawyers boycotted British courts, and students refused to attend government-run institutions while many officials resigned for the nationalist cause; the march was widely covered by the European and American press, and it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) “As a consequence of the Non-cooperation Movement the British Raj was shaken to its foundation for the first time since the Revolt of 1857.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: As a consequence of the Non-Cooperation Movement, the British Raj was shaken to its foundations for the first time since the Revolt of 1857 because: Gandhiji coupled Non-Cooperation with the Khilafat issue and joined Hindus and Muslims together to end colonial rule; these movements unleashed a surge of popular action altogether unprecedented in colonial India — Indians did not cooperate with the government at any level, boycotting schools, colleges and law courts (while national schools and colleges were opened instead), refusing to pay taxes, and renouncing titles and voluntary association with the government; the movement changed the course of Indian history as poor peasants, workers, students, lawyers and industrialists all joined it; Hindus, Muslims, Parsees and Sikhs were told to unite, thousands of volunteers joined the cause, many officials resigned from their posts, meetings were attended by all sections of people, and women participated in large numbers; it served as training for self-rule.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Analyze Gandhi’s activities in India during 1930 – 34.

answer.text: Gandhiji's activities in India during 1930-34: at the Lahore Congress session he demanded 'Purna Swaraj' and the observance of 26 January 1930 as Independence Day; soon after, he decided to launch a Salt Satyagraha, and in March 1930 began his famous Salt March, officially launching the Dandi Satyagraha; he chose the issue of salt as it was indispensable for every household; across large parts of India peasants breached forest laws, factory workers went on strike, lawyers boycotted courts and students refused to attend government-run institutions, while parallel salt marches were organised in other parts of the country; many Indians were arrested; Gandhiji made a plea to the upper castes to serve untouchables and called for Hindus, Muslims, Parsees and Sikhs to unite; thousands of volunteers joined the cause, many officials resigned, and women participated in large numbers; the Salt March made the British realise they would have to devolve some powers to Indians; the First Round Table Conference was held in November 1930, which Gandhiji did not attend; in 1931 the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed, under which Civil Disobedience was called off and prisoners released; the Second Round Table Conference was held in London in 1931, with Gandhiji representing the Congress, but it proved inconclusive; Gandhiji then returned to India and relaunched Civil Disobedience.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) ‘By 1922, Gandhi had transformed Indian nationalism’. Examine the statement.

answer.text: By 1922, Gandhiji had transformed Indian nationalism: his early contributions were the Kheda, Champaran and Ahmedabad movements; he coupled Non-Cooperation with the Khilafat issue and joined Hindus and Muslims together to end colonial rule; these movements unleashed a surge of popular action altogether unprecedented in colonial India; Indians did not cooperate with the government at any level, boycotting schools, colleges and law courts (while national schools and colleges were opened instead), refusing to pay taxes, and renouncing titles and voluntary association with the government; this movement changed the course of Indian history as poor peasants, workers, students, lawyers and industrialists all joined it; Hindus, Muslims, Parsis and Sikhs were told to unite; thousands of volunteers joined the cause, many officials resigned from their posts, meetings were attended by all sections of people, women participated in large numbers, and it served as training for self-rule.

answer.text: The Salt March was a notable event in the Indian freedom movement: it was really important as it became a mass movement, and people gave vehement support to it since salt was an important commodity used by all classes; forest laws were violated, workers went on strike, lawyers boycotted British courts, and students boycotted government schools and colleges; the British monopoly over salt broke down, as Gandhiji used the salt issue to mobilise wider discontent against the British; women participated in this movement for the first time, and the British realised that their days in India were numbered; it was this event that first brought Mahatma Gandhi to the world's attention.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Describe the causes and events of the Quit India Movement.

answer.text: Causes and events of the Quit India Movement: causes included dissatisfaction with the Government of India Act of 1935; the Congress did not accept the offer to participate in the Second World War as the British refused to meet its demands, and the Congress ministries resigned in October 1939; between 1940-41 the Congress organised individual satyagrahas to pressurise the British into promising freedom once the war was over; the Cripps Mission failed in 1942, and on 9 August 1942 Gandhiji launched the Quit India Movement with the slogan 'Do or Die', following which he was arrested. Events: after the failure of the Cripps Mission, a large number of people protested - liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth boycotted and burnt, people organised strikes and acts of sabotage, and in places such as Satara and Medinipur independent (parallel) governments were proclaimed; underground resistance was organised by socialist members such as Jayaprakash Narayan, and the British responded with force; many ordinary Indians, including students who left college to go to jail, joined the movement and followed Gandhi's call to lay down their lives for the nation, while the Muslim League expanded its influence during this period; Gandhiji was released from prison in 1944 and held meetings with Jinnah to try to bridge the gap between the Congress and the League; a Labour government came to power in Britain and resolved to leave India, and in August 1947 the British finally quit India.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) Describe the role of Gandhiji in the Indian freedom struggle from 1922 till 1931.

answer.text: Role of Gandhiji from 1922 till 1931: Gandhiji called off the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri-Chaura incident, but by 1922 he had already transformed Indian nationalism, with thousands of peasants, workers and artisans having participated in it; Gandhiji gained popularity among Indians as he dressed like them, lived like them and spoke their language, and rumours spread of his having miraculous powers; his success in broadening the base of nationalism rested on careful organisation - new branches of Congress were set up across India, 'Praja Mandals' were established, and provincial Congress committees were based on linguistic regions (mother tongue); he built a large following that included Mahadev Desai, Vallabhbhai Patel, J.B. Kripalani, Subhas Chandra Bose, Abul Kalam Azad and Jawaharlal Nehru; Gandhiji was released from prison in February 1924 and devoted himself to promoting khadi, the abolition of untouchability, and Hindu-Muslim unity, acting as both a social reformer and a politician; in 1928 he began to think of re-entering politics, giving his blessing to a movement against the Simon Commission and to the satyagraha at Bardoli; at the Lahore session the Congress demanded Purna Swaraj and decided to observe 26 January 1930 as Independence Day, and in March 1930 Gandhiji began his famous Salt March and officially launched the Dandi Satyagraha, choosing salt as a medium of protest since it was used by everyone; he broke the Salt Law by making a fistful of salt, parallel salt marches were organised elsewhere, peasants breached colonial forest laws, factory owners went on strike, lawyers boycotted British courts and students refused to attend schools and colleges; Gandhiji pleaded with upper castes to serve untouchables, called on Hindus, Muslims, Parsees and Sikhs to unite, and thousands of volunteers joined the cause while many officials resigned; the first Round Table Conference was not attended by the Congress or Gandhiji, but in 1931 the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed, calling off Civil Disobedience and releasing all prisoners; the Second Round Table Conference, held in London in 1931 with Gandhiji representing the Congress, proved inconclusive, and Gandhiji returned to India to relaunch Civil Disobedience, though it could not gain enough momentum thereafter.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) “Quit India Movement challenged the British rule and shaped the course of Indian Independence.” Justify the statement.

answer.text: Quit India Movement challenged British rule: (i) It gained momentum as it was against the Cripps Mission, Government of India Act 1935, threat of Japanese aggression, and inclusion of India in the Second World War. (ii) Younger activists organized strikes and acts of sabotage all over the country. (iii) Underground resistance by socialist members of the Congress like Jai Prakash Narayan. (iv) Establishment of independent government in several districts like Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east. (v) Unity among Indian masses. (vi) Active participation of all states. (vii) It was generally a mass movement. (viii) It disrupted the functioning of the British colonial government. (ix) It brought political awakening and empowerment in India. It uses machinery for the service of the poorest in their own cottages. questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Analyse the impact of national movement in India from 1915 to 1931 on the Indian masses.

answer.text:
Impact of the national movement in India from 1915 to 1931 on the Indian masses:
Gandhiji became the undisputed leader of the masses.
Major Satyagraha movements took place - Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad - and the idea of Satyagraha gained momentum.
There was mass participation in the Rowlatt Satyagraha, followed by the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Participation increased among people from different regions and religious traditions, including large-scale participation of women.
The movement promoted indigenous handicraft industries; Khadi and Charkha became symbols of the national movement among the masses.
Ideas of self-reliance and Swadeshi gained strength, with boycott of British goods and institutions.
The movement promoted Hindu-Muslim unity, and there was mass resignation from British offices and institutions and nonpayment of taxes.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) Analyse the role of Gandhiji after independence of India.

answer.text:
Role of Gandhiji after the Independence of India:
Gandhiji was not present at the festivities in the capital on 15 August 1947; he was in Kolkata on that day.
He spent the day fasting for 24 hours and did not attend any national function.
Gandhiji visited hospitals and refugee camps and consoled the distressed people.
He appealed to the Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims to forget the past and live in harmony.
After bringing peace in Bengal, he shifted to Delhi, where he appealed to all to live peacefully.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: Read the following source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Why the Salt Satyagraha ?” — Why was salt the symbol of protest ? This is what Mahatma Gandhi wrote : The volume of information being gained daily shows how wickedly the salt tax has been designed. In order to prevent the use of salt that has not paid the tax which is at times even fourteen times its value, the Government destroys the salt it cannot sell profitably. Thus it taxes the nation's vital necessity; it prevents the public from manufacturing it and destroys what nature manufactures without effort. No adjective is strong enough for characterizing this wicked dog-in-the-manger policy. From various sources, I hear tales of such wanton destruction of the nation's property in all parts of India. Maunds if not tons of salt are said to be destroyed on the Konkan coast. The same tale comes from Dandi. Wherever there is likelihood of natural salt being taken away by the people living in the neighbourhood of such areas for their personal use, salt officers are posted for the sole purpose of carrying on destruction. Thus valuable national property is destroyed at national expense and salt taken out of the mouths of the people. The salt monopoly is thus a fourfold curse. It deprives the people of a valuable easy village industry, involves wanton destruction of property that nature produces in abundance, the destruction itself means more national expenditure and fourthly, to crown this folly, an unheard of tax of more than 1,000 per cent is exacted from a starving people. This tax has remained so long because of the apathy of the general public. Now that it is sufficiently roused, the tax has to go. How soon it will be abolished depends upon the strength the people. The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi (CWMG), Vol. 49. (33.1) Why was salt law disliked by the masses ? (1) (33.2) Why were salt officers appointed by the British Government ? (1) (33.3) Why did Lord Irwin fail to understand the significance of Salt March ? (2)

answer.text:
33.1: The salt law was disliked by the masses because salt, a natural resource freely available from sea water, was monopolised by the British and Indians were not permitted to manufacture it; it was also taxed by the British Raj.
33.2: Salt officers were appointed by the British Government to keep watch along the coast so that nobody could make salt.
33.3: Lord Irwin failed to understand the significance of the Salt March because he dismissed the salt movement, thinking Gandhi would not reach the seacoast, and took the movement very lightly.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Explain the major events and movements that defined India's political condition between 1919 and 1922.

answer.text:
Major events and movements that defined India's political condition between 1919 and 1922:
The concepts of satyagraha and ahimsa marked the rise of Gandhiji as a mass leader; Khadi and Charkha became symbols of the national movement and self-reliance, promoting indigenous industry.
Gandhiji called for a nationwide campaign against the Rowlatt Act, and the Rowlatt Satyagraha was started; martial law was imposed, and in April 1919 British Brigadier Dyer ordered his troops to fire on a peaceful assembly at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar.
The Khilafat Movement, led by Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, demanded restoration of the Caliphate; Gandhiji believed that by intermixing the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movements, Hindus and Muslims could collectively bring an end to colonial rule.
Swadeshi and boycott were used as tools - students refused to attend schools and colleges, lawyers stopped going to courts, and the working class went on strike; tribes in Andhra Pradesh violated forest laws and farmers in Awadh stopped paying taxes.
In February 1922, Gandhiji called off the Non-Cooperation Movement following the Chauri Chaura incident, where several constables were burnt to death; during the movement thousands of Indians were jailed, and Gandhiji himself was arrested in March 1922, charged with sedition and given six years' imprisonment.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) Explain the significance of the Dandi March and its influence on the Independence movement.

answer.text:
Significance of the Dandi March and its influence on the Independence movement:
Gandhiji announced his plan to break the salt law; on 12 March 1930 he began his march from Sabarmati ashram to the seashore at Dandi, aiming to defy British laws for the first time.
Salt was essential for all but was monopolised and taxed by the British, and Indians were not permitted to manufacture it even for domestic use; Lord Irwin dismissed the movement, believing Gandhiji would not reach the coast.
The movement was supported by peasants, the working class, factory workers, lawyers and even Indian officials - lawyers boycotted courts, peasants stopped paying taxes, tribals broke forest laws, and there were strikes in factories/mills; nearly 60,000 Indians were arrested, including senior Congress leaders.
Rulers began to consider Gandhiji a 'Saint' and 'Statesman' using Christian acts as a weapon against men with Christian beliefs.
The Salt March was notable for bringing Mahatma Gandhi to world attention, and was widely covered by the European and American press (an American magazine, Time, wrote that the march made the British rulers 'desperately anxious').
It was the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers - the socialist activist Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay persuaded Gandhiji not to restrict the protests to men alone, and was herself among the women who courted arrest by breaking the salt or liquor laws.
The Salt March forced upon the British the realisation that their Raj would not last forever and that they would have to devolve some power to Indians.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) “Gandhiji used the ‘Salt Law’ to mobilise a wider discontent against British rule.” Support the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text:
Gandhiji used the 'Salt Law' to mobilise a wider discontent against British rule:
At the Lahore session of 1929, the Congress committed to Purna Swaraj through Civil Disobedience; Gandhiji announced he would lead a march to break the salt law, which gave the state a monopoly in the manufacture and sale of salt.
Salt was indispensable in every Indian household, but Indians were forbidden from making it and were compelled to buy it from shops at a high price; Gandhiji hoped to use the salt law to mobilise the masses, since the British monopoly on salt was seen as a fourfold curse that deprived people of a valuable, easy village industry.
On 12 March 1930, Gandhiji began walking from his ashram at Sabarmati and reached his destination three weeks later, making a fistful of salt at Dandi, in defiance of the Salt Law.
This was followed by Swadeshi and boycott, protests and demonstrations; across India peasants breached the hated colonial forest laws, factory workers went on strike in some towns, lawyers boycotted British courts, and students refused to attend government-run educational institutions.
Gandhiji called upon local officials to renounce government employment and join the freedom struggle; his meetings were well attended by villagers of all castes, and there was large-scale participation of women.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) “Gandhiji's leadership was instrumental in shaping the Non-Cooperation Movement.” Justify the statement.

answer.text:
Gandhiji's leadership was instrumental in shaping the Non-Cooperation Movement:
Gandhiji called for a countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act; following the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919, he called for a campaign of 'non-cooperation' with British rule, and Indians were asked not to pay taxes.
He joined hands with the Khilafat movement, bringing Hindus and Muslims together to end colonial rule; students stopped going to government-run schools and colleges, lawyers refused to attend court, and the working class went on strike in many towns and cities.
Hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws, farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes, and peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials.
Indians were asked to boycott institutions associated with the British; Swadeshi was promoted, foreign goods were boycotted, and the charkha was used to make people self-reliant, as Indians were asked to adhere to a 'renunciation of all voluntary association with the British Government'.
The Non-Cooperation Movement was called off because of the Chauri Chaura incident.

He worked for the abolition of untouchability and preached against child marriage, emphasising Hindu-Muslim harmony; he was both a social reformer and a politician.
In 1928 Gandhiji began to think of re-entering politics - he gave his blessings for a movement against the Simon Commission and for the satyagraha at Bardoli.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) “Various sources are essential for a complete understanding of Gandhiji's contributions in the Indian National Movement.” Justify the statement.

answer.text:
Various sources are essential for a complete understanding of Gandhiji's contributions to the Indian National Movement:
Speeches of Mahatma Gandhiji and his contemporaries, including both his associates and his political advisors; Gandhiji regularly published in his journal, Harijan.
Letters that others wrote to him - Nehru edited a collection of letters written to him during the national movement and published it as 'A Bunch of Old Letters'; autobiographies also help in framing a picture, giving an account rich in human detail.
Another important source is British government records, including fortnightly police reports prepared by the Home Department from the early 20th century, e.g. the Fortnightly Reports of the period of the Salt March.
Newspapers - contemporary newspapers published in English as well as different Indian languages tracked Mahatma Gandhi's movements and represented what ordinary Indians thought of him; accounts published in a London newspaper were often different from reports in an Indian nationalist paper. Other sources include international magazines (e.g. Time), and images, posters and photographs.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) “Gandhiji's leadership in the ‘Salt March’ of 1930 became a symbol of resistance against British colonial rule.” Justify the statement.

answer.text:
Gandhiji's leadership in the 'Salt March' of 1930 became a symbol of resistance against British colonial rule:
The British had a monopoly on the manufacturing of salt, which was very unpopular since salt was used by one and all, making it a symbol of protest; Gandhi gave advance notice of his salt march to the British, and on 12 March 1930 he started the march to break the salt law.
Gandhiji decided to launch a salt satyagraha to protest against the British, since the monopoly deprived people of a valuable village industry.
The march brought Mahatma Gandhiji to world attention and was widely covered by the European and American press; it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated on a large scale, e.g. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay.
The Salt March made the British realise that their Raj would not last forever; all sections of society participated in the march, and people made salt at Dandi to protest against the British in a non-violent protest. A number of Round Table Conferences were subsequently convened.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) “Non-Cooperation Movement became an epoch in the life of Mahatma Gandhi and that of India.” Explain the statement of Louis Fisher with examples.

answer.text:
Gandhiji got enough experience from the localised small struggles like Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad.
After the end of the First World War, the British had instituted censorship of the press and permitted detention without trial; in 1919 the Rowlatt Act was also promulgated.
Gandhiji called for a countrywide campaign against this Act; shops were shut down, schools were closed, and protests were intense in Punjab.
Gandhiji was detained while proceeding to Punjab.
The working class went on strike, students stopped attending schools and colleges, and lawyers refused to attend court.
Farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes, hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws, and peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials.
If non-cooperation was effectively carried out, said Gandhiji, India would win swaraj within a year.
As a consequence of the Non-Cooperation Movement, the British Raj was shaken to its foundations for the first time since the Revolt of 1857; the movement transformed the Indian national movement into a mass movement and Gandhiji into a popular leader.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) ‘Gandhiji started the Salt March for various reasons and it resulted in a significant movement.’ Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text:
Reasons for the Salt March: protest against the Simon Commission; the resolution to attain Purna Swaraj taken by the Congress at the 1929 Lahore Session; the decision to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Gandhiji chose salt as it was a common ingredient of household need by everybody; the salt law gave the British government the monopoly to manufacture salt, people were forbidden from making salt even for domestic use and were compelled to buy it from shops at a high price.
It involved wanton destruction of property that nature produces in abundance, meant more national expenditure, and deprived people of a valuable, easy village industry.
Significance: it brought Gandhiji to world attention and was widely covered by the European and American press; it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated; the Salt March forced the British to think that their Raj was not going to last long, and that they would have to devolve some power to Indians.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) “The Non-Cooperation Movement became an unprecedented popular movement in the history of colonial India.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text:
Gandhiji called for a countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act, which restricted people's right to assemble and allowed detention without trial for two years.
The success of the Rowlatt Satyagraha led Gandhiji to call for a campaign of 'non-cooperation' with British rule; Indians who wished colonialism to end were asked to stop attending schools, colleges and law courts, and not pay taxes.
To broaden the struggle he joined hands with the Khilafat Movement, which sought to restore the Caliphate; Gandhiji hoped that by joining the Non-Cooperation movement with the Khilafat, Hindus and Muslims could be brought together.
These movements led to popular action unprecedented in colonial India: renunciation of all voluntary association with the British government, students stopped attending schools and colleges, lawyers boycotted the law courts, hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws, farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes, and peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials.
These protest movements were carried out in defiance of the local nationalist leadership; peasants, workers and others interpreted and acted upon the call to 'non-cooperate' in ways that best suited their interests.
'Non-cooperation,' wrote Mahatma Gandhi's American biographer Louis Fischer, 'became the name of an epoch in the life of India and of Gandhiji.'

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) “The Salt Satyagraha was an all-India campaign in opposition to colonial rule.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text:
In December 1929 the Congress passed the baton of leadership to Jawaharlal Nehru and declared 'Purna Swaraj', or complete independence, as their goal; on 26 January 1930, 'Independence Day' was observed.
After the observance of this Independence Day, Mahatma Gandhi announced that he would lead a march to break the salt law - the most oppressive law, which gave the state a monopoly in the manufacture and sale of salt.
Salt was indispensable; people were forbidden from making salt even for domestic use and were compelled to buy it from shops at a high price. The state monopoly over salt was unpopular, and Gandhiji hoped to mobilise wider discontent against British rule.
Gandhiji had given advance notice of his Salt March to the Viceroy Lord Irwin, who failed to grasp the significance of the action; on 12 March 1930, Gandhiji began walking from his ashram at Sabarmati towards the ocean, reaching his destination three weeks later and making a fistful of salt.
Parallel salt marches were conducted in other parts of the country; peasants breached the colonial forest laws, factory workers went on strike, lawyers boycotted British courts, and students refused to attend government-run educational institutions.
The Salt March was notable for at least three reasons: it brought Mahatma Gandhi to world attention; it was the first activity in which women participated in large numbers; and it made the British realise that their Raj would not last forever, and that they would have to give some power to the Indians.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) Examine the causes and events of the Quit India Movement.

answer.text:
In 1935, a new Government of India Act promised some form of representative government; two years later, in an election held on the basis of a restricted franchise, the Congress won a comprehensive victory, and eight out of 11 provinces had a Congress 'Prime Minister' working under a British Governor.
In September 1939, the Second World War broke out; Congress offered support to the war effort if the British, in return, promised to grant India independence once hostilities ended, but the offer was refused, and Congress ministries resigned in October 1939.
Through 1940 and 1941, Congress organised individual satyagrahas to pressure the British to promise freedom once the war ended; the political landscape had become a three-way struggle between the Congress, the Muslim League, and the British.
In spring 1942, Churchill sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India to forge a compromise, but talks broke down after Congress insisted the Viceroy first appoint an Indian as Defence Member of his Executive Council; after the failure of the Cripps Mission, Gandhiji launched the Quit India campaign in August 1942.
Although Gandhiji was jailed at once, younger activists organised strikes and acts of sabotage all over the country; socialist members of Congress such as Jayaprakash Narayan were particularly active in the underground resistance.
In several districts, such as Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east, 'independent' governments were proclaimed; Quit India was genuinely a mass movement, bringing hundreds of thousands of ordinary Indians into its ambit, and especially energised the young, who in large numbers left college to go to jail.
It was in these years that the League began to make a mark in the Punjab and Sind provinces, where it had previously had scarcely any presence.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) Examine the causes and events of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

answer.text:
During the Great War of 1914-18, the British had instituted censorship of the press and permitted detention without trial; Gandhiji called for a countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act, and life came to a standstill in towns across North and West India in response to the bandh call.
The protests were particularly intense in Punjab, where many men who had served the British in the War expected to be rewarded but were instead given the Rowlatt Act; Gandhiji was detained while proceeding to Punjab, even as prominent local Congressmen were arrested, and the situation reached a bloody climax in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar in April 1919.
The Khilafat Movement, which sought to restore the Caliphate recently abolished by Kemal Ataturk, joined hands with Gandhiji, compounded by dissatisfaction with the 1919 Government of India Act; Gandhiji called for a campaign of 'non-cooperation' with British rule, asking Indians to stop attending schools, colleges and law courts, not pay taxes, and renounce all voluntary association with the British colonial government.
If non-cooperation was effectively carried out, said Gandhiji, India would win swaraj within a year; he hoped that coupling Non-cooperation with Khilafat would bring Hindus and Muslims together to end colonial rule.
Students stopped going to government schools and colleges, lawyers refused to attend court, and the working class went on strike in many towns and cities - there were 396 strikes in 1921, involving 600,000 workers and a loss of seven million workdays.
The countryside was seething with discontent too: hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws, farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes, and peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials, sometimes in defiance of local nationalist leadership; the movement entailed denial, renunciation and self-discipline, as training for self-rule.
In February 1922, a group of peasants attacked and torched a police station in Chauri Chaura, in the United Provinces, and several constables perished; this act of violence prompted Gandhiji to call off the movement. During the Non-Cooperation Movement thousands of Indians were jailed, and Gandhiji himself was arrested in March 1922 and charged with sedition.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (a) To what extent was the Non-Cooperation Movement successful in mobilizing the masses against the British rule ? Explain with suitable examples.

answer.text:
The Non-Cooperation Movement was a mass movement in which people from all walks of life participated; it was linked with the Khilafat movement to bring India's two major religious communities, Hindus and Muslims, together to end colonial rule.
It involved peasants, workers, students, women, tribals etc.; students stopped going to government schools and colleges, and lawyers refused to attend courts.
The working class went on strike in many towns and cities, leading to the loss of seven million workdays; Swadeshi was adopted and foreign goods were boycotted, and scholars returned awards and titles as people were asked to adhere to a 'renunciation of all voluntary association with the British Government'.
The countryside was seething with discontent too - hill tribes in northern Andhra violated the forest laws, farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes, and peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials.
Peasants, workers and others interpreted and acted upon the call to 'non-cooperate' with colonial rule in ways that best suited their interests; the movement entailed denial, renunciation and self-discipline, and was training for self-rule.

questions.chapter: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond
questions.text: (b) How are different sources to know about Gandhiji's political career helpful in understanding his contribution towards India ? Explain with examples.

answer.text:
One important source is the writings and speeches of Mahatma Gandhi and his contemporaries; many letters, though written to individuals and personal, were also meant for the public, and Gandhi regularly published in his journal Harijan letters others wrote to him.
His autobiography gives us an account of his past that is often rich in detail; another vital source is government records, since colonial rulers kept close tabs on those they regarded as critical of the government.
The letters and reports written by policemen and other officials were secret at the time but can now be accessed in archives; fortnightly reports for the period of the Salt March noted that the Home Department was unwilling to accept that Gandhi's actions had evoked any enthusiastic response from the masses, and the march was seen as a drama, an antic, a desperate effort to mobilise an unwilling people.
Contemporary newspapers, published in English and various Indian languages, tracked Gandhi's movements, reported on his activities, and represented what ordinary Indians thought of him; paintings, pictures and movies also revealed how Mahatma Gandhi was perceived by people.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : “The British element is gone, but they have left the mischief behind” — Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel said : “It is no use saying that we ask for separate electorates, because it is good for us. We have heard it long enough. We have heard it for years, and as a result of this agitation we are now a separate nation … Can you show me one free country where there are separate electorates ? If so, I shall be prepared to accept it. But in this unfortunate country if this separate electorate is going to be persisted in, even after the division of the country, woe betide the country; it is not worth living in. Therefore, I say, it is not for my good alone, it is for your own good that I say it, forget the past. One day, we may be united … The British element is gone, but they have left the mischief behind. We do not want to perpetuate that mischief. (Hear, hear). When the British introduced this element they had not expected that they will have to go so soon. They wanted it for their easy administration. That is all right. But they have left the legacy behind. Are we to get out of it or not ?” (33.1) Mention the meaning of separate electorates. (33.2) Why did Sardar Patel insist on unity ? (33.3) Why was separate electorate considered a mischief by the British ?

answer.text:
(33.1) Separate electorates were a part of the political framework under which minorities could be elected and have a meaningful voice in the administration.
(33.2) Sardar Patel insisted on unity because he was against separate electorates, feeling that they would always keep minorities as a minority.
(33.3) Separate electorate was considered a mischief left behind by the British because it laid the foundation for dividing the different communities and endangered the unity of the nation.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Explain the arguments given in favour of strong Centre in the Constituent Assembly.

answer.text: Arguments given in favour of a strong Centre in the Constituent Assembly: the issue of division of power between the Centre and the States was intensely debated; the Draft Constitution provided three lists of subjects — the Union List (Union Government could make laws), the State List (State Government could make laws) and the Concurrent List (both could make laws); in India, the Union Government was made more powerful so it could ensure peace, security and coordination on matters of vital interest; Article 356 gave the Centre power to take over a State's administration on the Governor's recommendation, and some taxes such as land and property taxes and sales tax were collected by the State while important powers stayed with the Centre; K. Santhanam from Madras said reallocation of powers was necessary to strengthen both State and Centre, since an overburdened Centre could not function properly; leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar, Gopalaswami Ayyangar and Balakrishna Sharma advocated for a strong Centre — Ambedkar declared he wanted a strong and united Centre, Gopalaswami Ayyangar said the Centre should be made as strong as possible, and Balakrishna Sharma reasoned that only a strong Centre could plan for the well-being of the country, mobilise resources, establish proper administration and defend the country against aggression, while also warning against excessive centralised power.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era

answer.text: G.B. Pant showed his concern in the Constituent Assembly for making India a unified nation: he declared that the success of a democracy was to be judged by the confidence it generated among different sections of people; every citizen in a free state should be treated in a manner that satisfied 'not only his material wants but also his spiritual sense of self-respect'; he called for understanding between the majority and minority communities and for empathy with their aspirations; he opposed the idea of separate electorates, declaring that 'it is the citizen that forms the base as well as the summit of the social pyramid' and that there should be no divided loyalties, so as to forge a strong nation and a strong State; he believed separate electorates would be suicidal.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “We are not going just to copy” — This is what Jawaharlal Nehru said in his famous speech of 13 December, 1946 : My mind goes back to the various Constituent Assemblies that have gone before and of what took place at the making of the great American nation when the fathers of that nation met and fashioned out a Constitution which has stood the test of so many years, more than a century and a half, and of the great nation which has resulted, which has been built up on the basis of that Constitution. My mind goes back to that mighty revolution which took place also over 150 years ago and to that Constituent Assembly that met in that gracious and lovely city of Paris which has fought so many battles for freedom, to the difficulties that the Constituent Assembly had and to how the King and other authorities came in its way, and still it continued. The House will remember that when these difficulties came and even the room for a meeting was denied to the then Constituent Assembly, they betook themselves to an open tennis court and met there and took the oath, which is called the Oath of the Tennis Court, that they continued meeting in spite of Kings, in spite of the others, and did not disperse till they had finished the task they had undertaken. Well, I trust that it is in the solemn spirit that we too are meeting here and that we, too, whether we meet in this chamber or other chambers, or in the fields or in the market-place, will go on meeting and continue our work till we have finished it. (33.1) Which was the revolution discussed by Nehru in the passage ? (33.2) Which qualities of the American Constitution are highlighted by Nehru ? (33.3) What was the ‘Oath of the Tennis Court’ ?

answer.text:
(33.1) It was the French Revolution that Nehru was discussing in the passage.
(33.2) Nehru highlighted that the American Constitution had stood the test of so many years and the nation had become powerful in the world; other qualities highlighted included its Preamble, democracy and Fundamental Rights.
(33.3) The 'Oath of the Tennis Court' was the oath taken by the Constituent Assembly of France when it was not given a place by the king to meet, so its members betook themselves to an open tennis court and took an oath there.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: “One of the topics most vigorously debated in the Constituent Assembly was the respective rights of the Central and the State governments.” Analyse the statement with supporting arguments.

answer.text: One of the topics most vigorously debated in the Constituent Assembly was the respective rights of the Central and State Governments: the issue of division of power between the Centre and the states was intensely debated, with Jawaharlal Nehru among those arguing for a strong Centre keeping in view the partition of the country; the Draft Constitution provided three lists of subjects - the Union List, the State List and the Concurrent List; in India, the Union Government was made more powerful to ensure peace, security and coordination on matters of vital interest, and Article 356 gave the Centre power to take over a State's administration on the recommendation of the Governor; the Constitution mandated fiscal federalism, with the Centre retaining the proceeds of some taxes, sharing others with the states, and assigning some wholly to the states, while states could levy and collect certain taxes on their own; K. Santhanam from Madras argued that reallocation of powers was necessary to strengthen both State and Centre, warning that an overburdened Centre could not function properly and that the proposed allocation of powers would cripple the provinces and impoverish them; on the other hand, leaders such as Nehru, B.R. Ambedkar, Gopalaswami Ayyangar and Balakrishna Sharma advocated for a strong Centre - Ambedkar wanted a strong and united Centre, Gopalaswami Ayyangar said the Centre should be made as strong as possible, and Balakrishna Sharma reasoned that only a strong Centre could mobilise resources, establish a proper administration and defend the country against aggression; after Partition, the pressure for a decentralised structure eased, and the violence at the time of Partition pushed leaders towards a centralised administration necessary to control secessionist tendencies.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : We say that it is our firm and solemn resolve to have an independent sovereign republic. India is bound to be sovereign, it is bound to be independent and it is bound to be a republic … Now, some friends have raised the question : “Why have you not put in the word 'democratic' here ?” Well, I told them that it is conceivable, of course, that a republic may not be democratic but the whole of our past is witness to this fact that we stand for democratic institutions. Obviously we are aiming at democracy and nothing less than a democracy. What form of democracy, what shape it might take is another matter. The democracies of the present day, many of them in Europe and elsewhere, have played a great part in the world's progress. Yet it may be doubtful if those democracies may not have to change their shape somewhat before long if they have to remain completely democratic. We are not going just to copy, I hope, a certain democratic procedure or an institution of a so-called democratic country. We may improve upon it. In any event whatever system of government we may establish here must fit in with the temper of our people and be acceptable to them. We stand for democracy. It will be for this House to determine what shape to give to that democracy, the fullest democracy, I hope. The House will notice that in this Resolution, although we have not used the word “democratic” because we thought it is obvious that the word “republic” contains that word and we did not want to use unnecessary words and redundant words, but we have done something much more than using the word. We have given the content of democracy in this Resolution and not only the content of democracy but the content, if I may say so, of economic democracy in this Resolution. — Source : Constituent Assembly Debates (CAD), Vol. I (33.1) Mention the 'firm and solemn resolve' expressed in the passage. (33.2) How does the passage emphasize the commitment to democracy ? (33.3) How is democracy explained in the context of republic in the passage ?

answer.text: 33.1 The 'firm and solemn resolve' expressed in the passage: emphasis on the commitment to democracy; reflects the will of the people; acknowledges the importance of democracy. (Any one point) 33.2 How the passage emphasizes commitment to democracy: economic democracy and justice; social equality. (Any one point) 33.3 How democracy is explained in the context of republic: republic – commitment to democracy; aligns with the aspirations of the people; guarantee of justice, equality and freedom to its citizens. (Any two points)

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: (a) Why did some members of Constituent Assembly argue for a strong Centre ? Explain.

answer.text: (a) Why some members of the Constituent Assembly argued for a strong Centre: (i) Jawaharlal Nehru advocated for a strong centre. (ii) He emphasised that a weak centre would be incapable of ensuring peace. (iii) A strong centre was a must to speak up in the international sphere. (iv) The rights of the states were most eloquently defended by K. Santhanam from Madras, who felt a reallocation of powers was necessary to strengthen both states and the Centre. (v) He described that the centre might break down with too many responsibilities. (vi) Ambedkar also supported a strong and united Centre; riots in the country could be controlled through a strong Centre. (vii) Foreign aggression could be controlled and foreign affairs guided in a balanced way if the Centre was strong. (viii) Santhanam felt the proposed power sharing would cripple the states. (ix) Reminding members of the nation's riots and violence, many stated that the Centre's powers needed to be greatly strengthened to stop communal frenzy. (x) Gopalaswami Ayyangar declared that 'the Centre should be strengthened.' (xi) Balakrishna Sharma, from the United Provinces, argued that only a strong central government could plan for the country's future, mobilise economic resources, establish proper administration, and defend it against foreign aggression. (Any eight to be explained)

questions.text: (b) Explain the important role played by some members in the Constituent Assembly.

answer.text: (b) Important role played by some members in the Constituent Assembly: (i) The Constituent Assembly had 300 members. (ii) Three were representatives of the Congress, namely Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad. (iii) Nehru moved the crucial 'Objectives Resolution' and the resolution proposing that the National Flag of India be a 'horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and dark green in equal proportion', with a wheel in navy blue at the centre. (iv) Patel worked mostly behind the scenes, playing a key role in drafting several reports and reconciling opposing points of view. (v) Rajendra Prasad's role was as President of the Assembly, steering discussion along constructive lines while ensuring all members had a chance to speak. (vi) B.R. Ambedkar, on the advice of Mahatma Gandhi, was asked at Independence to join the Union Cabinet as law minister. (vii) K.M. Munshi from Gujarat and Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar from Madras gave crucial inputs in drafting the Constitution. (viii) These six members were given vital assistance by two civil servants – B.N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India, who prepared background papers based on a close study of political systems in other countries, and S.N. Mukherjee, the Chief Draughtsman, who could put complex proposals in clear legal language. (ix) Ambedkar himself had the responsibility of guiding the Draft Constitution through the Assembly. questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: “During the debates in Constituent Assembly, B.R. Ambedkar told that he wanted a strong centre, much stronger than the centre we had created under the Act of 1935.” Analyse the statement.

answer.text:
B.R. Ambedkar wanted a centre much stronger than that created under the Act of 1935:
He reminded members about the riots and violence that had occurred.
A powerful centre was needed to control such situations and stop communal frenzy, and to keep the nation as a well-knit unit.
A strong centre was needed to mobilise available economic resources, establish proper administration, and defend the country against foreign aggression.
After partition, most nationalists were in favour of a strong centre.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Explain the central debates in the Constituent Assembly regarding federalism.

answer.text:
Central debates in the Constituent Assembly regarding federalism:
There was division of powers among the Union, State and Concurrent lists.
B.R. Ambedkar declared that he wanted a strong and united centre to stop the riots and violence that was ripping the nation apart; Gopalaswami Ayyangar declared that the centre should be made as strong as possible.
Article 356 gave the centre power to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor.
Balkrishna Sharma reasoned that only a strong centre could plan for the well-being of the country, mobilise economic resources, establish proper administration and defend the country against foreign aggression.
The Constitution mandated a complex system of fiscal federalism; states could levy and collect certain taxes on their own, such as land and property taxes, sales tax, and tax on bottled liquor.
The rights of the states were defended by K. Santhanam from Madras, who spoke for a more unitary reallocation of powers being questioned; a member from Orissa warned that the centre was likely to break since powers had been excessively centralised under the Constitution.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: How did the ‘Objectives Resolution’ of the Constituent Assembly reflect the vision of India as an ‘Independent Sovereign Republic’. Explain.

answer.text:
How the 'Objectives Resolution' of the Constituent Assembly reflected the vision of India as an 'Independent Sovereign Republic':
Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946 in the Constituent Assembly; it was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the constitution of free India and provided the framework for making the constitution.
It proclaimed India to be an 'Independent Sovereign Republic' and guaranteed its citizens justice, equality and freedom.
It provided that adequate safeguards be given to minorities and depressed castes; Nehru's plea was to make a constitution as per the needs of the people, fusing the liberal ideas of democracy with the socialist idea of economic justice.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: (a) Describe the views of the members of the Constituent Assembly on division of powers between the Centre and the States.

answer.text:
Views of the members of the Constituent Assembly on division of powers between the Centre and the States:
The issue of division of power between the Centre and State governments was intensely debated; the Draft Constitution provided three lists of subjects - the Union List (Union government makes laws), the State List (State government makes laws) and the Concurrent List (both can make laws).
In India, the Union government was made more powerful so it could ensure peace, security, and coordinate on matters of vital interest; Article 356 gave the Centre power to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor, while some taxes such as land, property and sales tax were collected by the states.
K. Santhanam from Madras said reallocation of powers was necessary - not only to strengthen the states but also the Centre, warning that if the Centre was overburdened with responsibilities it could not function properly, and that some powers should be transferred to the states, cautioning against excessive centralisation.
Many leaders, however, advocated for a strong Centre - Ambedkar wanted a strong and united Centre, Gopalaswami Ayyangar said the Centre should be made as strong as possible, and Balkrishna Sharma argued that only a strong Centre could plan for the well-being of the country, mobilise resources, establish proper administration and defend the country against aggression.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: (b) Describe the ideals expressed in the ‘Objectives Resolution’ by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly.

answer.text:
Ideals expressed in the 'Objectives Resolution' by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly:
Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the Objectives Resolution in 1946; it was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the constitution of free India and provided the framework for making the constitution.
It proclaimed India to be an 'Independent Sovereign Republic', guaranteeing its citizens justice, equality and freedom, with adequate safeguards to be provided for minorities and depressed castes.
It held that the system of government had to fit within the temper of the people, while it was also necessary to learn from the failures and successes of the West; Nehru's plea was to make a constitution as per the needs of the people.
