questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : We say that it is our firm and solemn resolve to have an independent sovereign republic. India is bound to be sovereign, it is bound to be independent and it is bound to be a republic … Now, some friends have raised the question: “Why have you not put in the word ‘democratic’ here ?” Well, I told them that it is conceivable, of course, that a republic may not be democratic but the whole of our past is witness to this fact that we stand for democratic institutions. Obviously we are aiming at democracy and nothing less than a democracy. What form of democracy, what shape it might take is another matter. The democracies of the present day, many of them in Europe and elsewhere, have played a great part in the world's progress. Yet it may be doubtful if those democracies may not have to change their shape somewhat before long if they have to remain completely democratic. We are not going just to copy, I hope, a certain democratic procedure or an institution of a so-called democratic country. We may improve upon it. In any event whatever system of government we may establish here must fit in with the temper of our people and be acceptable to them. We stand for democracy. It will be for this House to determine what shape to give to that democracy, the fullest democracy, I hope. The House will notice that in this Resolution, although we have not used the word “democratic” because we thought it is obvious that the word “republic” contains that word and we did not want to use unnecessary words and redundant words, but we have done something much more than using the word. We have given the content of democracy in this Resolution and not only the content of democracy but the content, if I may say so, of economic democracy in this Resolution. Others might take objection to this Resolution on the ground that we have not said that it should be a Socialist State. Well, I stand for Socialism and, I hope, India will stand for Socialism and that India will go towards the constitution of a Socialist State and I do believe that the whole world will have to go that way. (33.1) How did defining India as a ‘republic’ enhance democratic governance ? (33.2) How does economic democracy promote social equality within a republican framework ? (33.3) How did Jawaharlal Nehru view the role of the Constituent Assembly in shaping democracy in India ?

answer.text:
33.1: Defining India as a 'republic' enhanced democratic governance through elected representatives, with the highest authority of India being elected in the country.
33.2: Economic democracy promotes social equality within a republican framework through equal distribution of resources and equal opportunities.
33.3: Jawaharlal Nehru viewed the Constituent Assembly's role in shaping democracy in India as follows - our constitution is not copied from any other country's constitution, but will be framed according to the needs of our people; the word 'democratic' was not initially mentioned in the resolution, as the word 'republic' was considered to already contain that meaning.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Explain the main provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935.

answer.text:
The Government of India Act, 1935 was enacted by the colonial government.
The Act promised some form of representative government.
The electorate that elected the provincial bodies was limited to not more than 10-15% of the adult population; there was no universal adult franchise.
The legislature elected under the Act of 1935 operated within the framework of colonial government, and was responsible to the Governor appointed by the British.
Congress came to power in 8 out of 11 provinces.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: (a) Describe the events that shaped the vision of the Constitution of India.

answer.text:
The years immediately preceding the making of the Constitution had been exceptionally tumultuous; on 15 August 1947 India had been made free, but it had also been divided.
The Calcutta Killings of August 1946 began a year of almost continuous rioting across northern and eastern India; the violence culminated in massacres accompanying the transfer of populations when Partition was announced.
Millions of refugees were on the move - Muslims into East and West Pakistan, Hindus and Sikhs into West Bengal and the eastern half of Punjab; many perished before reaching their destination.
Another problem faced by the new nation was that of the princely states; this was the background in which the Constituent Assembly met.
J.L. Nehru presented the vision of the constitution, proclaiming India to be an independent sovereign republic, guaranteeing citizens justice, equality and freedom, and providing adequate safeguards for backward classes, minorities and tribals; Nehru referred to the American and French revolutions.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: (b) Describe the arguments given in the Constituent Assembly against the creation of separate electorates.

answer.text:
Pocker Bahadur made a powerful plea for continuing separate electorates, but many nationalist leaders opposed this idea, seeing separate electorates as a deliberate measure to divide the people.
Dhulekar opposed the idea of separate electorates; Patel declared that separate electorates were poison for the minorities, as they had seen the partition bloodbath.
Pant said separate electorates were not only harmful to the nation but also to the minorities - it was a suicidal demand that would permanently isolate the minorities, make them vulnerable, and deprive them of any effective say within the government.
Not all Muslims supported the idea of separate electorates - Begum Aizaz Rasul said the idea of separate electorates was self-destructive.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow : “Framing the Constitution” — The Indian Constitution, which came into effect on 26 January, 1950, has the dubious distinction of being the longest in the world. But its length and complexity are perhaps understandable when one considers the country's size and diversity. At Independence, India was not merely large and diverse, but also deeply divided. A Constitution designed to keep the country together, and to take it forward, had necessarily to be an elaborate, carefully-worked-out, and painstakingly drafted document. For one thing, it sought to heal wounds of the past and the present, to make Indians of different classes, castes and communities come together in a shared political experiment. For another, it sought to nurture democratic institutions in what had long been a culture of hierarchy and deference. The Constitution of India was framed between December 1946 and November 1949. During this time, its drafts were discussed clause-by-clause in the Constituent Assembly of India. (33.1) Why is the Indian Constitution regarded as the longest in the world ? (33.2) Why was the Constitution seen as essential at the time of Independence ? (33.3) How did the Constitution seek to nurture the democracy in India ?

answer.text:
33.1 The Indian Constitution is regarded as the longest in the world because it accommodated India's vast size and cultural diversity, provided comprehensive details, and included specific provisions for a diverse nation.
33.2 The Constitution was seen as essential at the time of Independence because it was to hold together a vast nation and trust in a united India, sought to heal wounds of the past and present, made Indians of different classes, castes and communities come together in a shared political experiment, and sought to nurture democratic institutions.
33.3 The Constitution sought to nurture democracy in India by establishing representative democracy, establishing principles of equality, guaranteeing fundamental rights, and promoting social and economic justice.

questions.chapter: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era
questions.text: Analyse how the Constituent Assembly of India addressed the issue of federalism.

answer.text:
The Draft Constitution provided for three lists of subjects: Union, State, and Concurrent; more items were placed under exclusive Union control than in other federations, and more placed on the Concurrent list too than desired by the provinces.
The Union also had control of minerals and key industries; Article 356 gave the Centre powers to take over a state administration on the recommendation of the Governor.
The Constitution also mandated a complex system of fiscal federalism: in the case of some taxes (customs duties and Company taxes) the Centre retained all proceeds; in other cases (income tax and excise duties) it shared them with the states; and in still other cases (estate duties) it assigned them wholly to the states; the states could levy and collect certain taxes on their own, including land and property taxes, sales tax, and the profitable tax on bottled liquor.

questions.text: Explain how the ‘Objectives Resolution’ became the basis of the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.

answer.text:
The Objectives Resolution provided the framework within which the work of constitution-making was to proceed.
It proclaimed India to be an Independent, Sovereign Republic, and assured that adequate safeguards would be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed and other backward classes.
It guaranteed citizens justice, equality and freedom.
